concepts.short_definition: An algorithm design paradigm that breaks a problem into smaller subproblems, solves them independently, and combines their solutions to solve the original problem.
A sorting algorithm that uses divide and conquer by recursively splitting an array into halves, sorting each half, and merging them back together.
Equations that define sequences recursively, often used to express the running time of divide and conquer algorithms.
A theorem that provides a solution to recurrence relations of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), used to analyze the time complexity of divide and conquer algorithms.
An efficient algorithm for finding an element in a sorted array by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half.
A measure of the amount of time an algorithm takes to solve a problem as a function of the input size.
A comprehensive assessment testing cumulative knowledge on course 6.1210.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Algorithm for Longest Increasing Subsequence
concepts.short_definition: A method to compute the longest strictly-increasing subsequence in a string using a dynamic programming approach with time complexity O(n).
A problem-solving framework to structure dynamic programming algorithm design, including steps like State, Recurrence, Task, Base case, Order, and Time complexity.
Determining prices for multiple product types to maximize total revenue, given customer constraints on quantity and maximum willingness to pay.
A model where each customer wants a specific quantity of products and is willing to pay at most a given price per product.
A principle stating that a globally optimal solution can be found by making a locally optimal choice at each step.
The optimization problem of finding the smallest set of points that 'hit' or cover all given intervals of integers.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy Algorithm for Interval Hitting Set Problem
concepts.short_definition: A greedy approach that selects points iteratively to cover intervals, typically by choosing the end point of the interval with the smallest end among remaining uncovered intervals.
A formal argument showing that the locally optimal choice in a greedy algorithm leads to a globally optimal solution.
An example demonstrating that a certain greedy choice does not work for the problem, disproving the corresponding greedy strategy.
A comprehensive review of key concepts and topics likely to be tested in the final exam for a course.
The class of decision problems that can be solved by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time.
A classification of problems to which every problem in NP can be reduced in polynomial time; NP-hard problems are at least as hard as the hardest problems in NP.

Given a list of n friends and a list of m pairs of friends who cause trouble together, decide if it is possible to invite everyone to exactly one of three parties so that no pair of troublemakers attends the same party.
A decision problem is NP-complete if it lies in NP and is NP-hard.
The class of decision problems for which a given solution can be verified in polynomial time by a nondeterministic Turing machine.
Given a graph G, decide if it is possible to color the vertices of G using 3 colors so that no two adjacent vertices share the same color.

concepts.canonical_name: Proof that INVITE-FRIENDS is in NP
concepts.short_definition: Showing that a certificate (party assignment) can be verified in polynomial time to decide if the INVITE-FRIENDS problem instance has a solution.
Showing a polynomial-time reduction from an NP-complete problem (3-COLOR) to INVITE-FRIENDS, establishing its NP-hardness.

concepts.canonical_name: Overall proof of NP-completeness of INVITE-FRIENDS
concepts.short_definition: Deduce that INVITE-FRIENDS is NP-complete by combining proofs that it is in NP and NP-hard.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Operations on Static Sequence
concepts.short_definition: The asymptotic running time of various operations (build, get_at, insert_first, insert_last, insert_at, set_at, delete_first, delete_last, delete_at) on a static sequence data structure.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Operations on Dynamic Sequence
concepts.short_definition: The asymptotic running time of various operations on a dynamic sequence data structure.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Operations on Doubly-Linked List
concepts.short_definition: The asymptotic running time of common operations (build, get_at, insert_first, insert_last, insert_at, set_at, delete_first, delete_last, delete_at) on a doubly-linked list data structure, with specific landmarks such as Θ(1) for insertion or deletion at ends.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Operations on Dynamic Array
concepts.short_definition: Asymptotic running time complexity of various sequence operations on dynamic arrays, including amortized costs for some operations.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Operations on AVL Sequence
concepts.short_definition: Time complexity of operations on an AVL balanced tree used as a sequence, with log n running times for get, insert, set, delete.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Operations on Sorted Array
concepts.short_definition: Asymptotic running times of operations on a sorted array including build, find, insert, find_min, find_prev, delete, find_max, find_next.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Operations on Direct Access Array
concepts.short_definition: Time complexities for operations on direct access arrays, with high cost proportional to universe size u for some operations.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Operations on Hash Table
concepts.short_definition: Expected amortized and worst-case time complexities of hash table operations such as build, find, insert, delete.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Operations on AVL Binary Search Tree (BST)
concepts.short_definition: Time complexities of operations (build, find, insert, find_min, find_prev, delete, find_max, find_next) on AVL BST, with logarithmic times.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Priority Queue Operations
concepts.short_definition: Time complexities for key priority queue implementations (dynamic array, sorted dynamic array, AVL tree, heap) with their build, insert, delete_max, and sorting times.
Algorithms that make locally optimal choices at each step aiming for a globally optimal solution.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Table Definition T(i, k) for LIS
concepts.short_definition: A DP state T(i, k) representing the length of an LIS in the suffix S[i:] with start value at least k.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Recurrence for T(i, k)
concepts.short_definition: Recurrence: T(i, k) = max( T(i+1, k), 1 + T(i+1, S[i]+1) if S[i] ≥ k ), defines the optimal substructure for LIS.

concepts.canonical_name: Boundary Conditions for DP Table T(i, k)
concepts.short_definition: Boundary values to initialize DP: T(n, k) = 0 and T(i, 27) = 0 for all valid i and k.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Table Definition T(i) for LIS Containing S[i]
concepts.short_definition: DP state T(i) is the length of LIS in suffix starting at i that contains element S[i].

concepts.canonical_name: Base Case for DP T(i) with i=∞
concepts.short_definition: The base case for DP T(i) when i=∞ is T(∞) = 0.

concepts.canonical_name: Precomputation of f(i,k) to Find Next Index j > i with S[j] = k
concepts.short_definition: f(i,k) = min { j : j > i and S[j] = k } found via backward pointer techniques.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity Analysis of DP with Precomputation
concepts.short_definition: Using f(i,k) and limiting 26 English letters, each Relate step takes O(1), total DP run time is O(n).
A dynamic programming approach to maximize revenue by pricing multiple types of items given customer constraints, with a time complexity of O(n^2 m).
Sorting customers in non-decreasing order based on the maximum price they are willing to pay (pi) to facilitate the dynamic programming approach.

concepts.canonical_name: Clustered Grouping Property in Pricing Problem
concepts.short_definition: The optimal partition of customers into groups for pricing is such that each group consists of consecutive customers after sorting by price willingness.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming State Definition for Pricing Problem
concepts.short_definition: DP state T(i,j,k) represents maximum revenue on subset customers[i:] after pricing j bags with the last group assigned at index k.

concepts.canonical_name: Subproblems and Recurrence of DP for Pricing Problem
concepts.short_definition: Recurrence relations defining how DP transitions are made either by adding a customer to the existing group or starting a new group with a price derived from the customer's maximum willingness to pay.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of DP Pricing Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The dynamic programming solution runs in O(n^2 m) time, given the states and transitions.
Defines T(i,j) as the maximum over choices of k between i and n of a quantity involving cumulative sums of qx and T(k+1,j-1).
Use of a prefix sum array π(k) to compute cumulative quantities Pk x=i qx in O(1) time to optimize the R step.
The concept of a hard margin in Support Vector Machines refers to finding a linear decision boundary that strictly separates two classes with no misclassification.
Soft margins in Support Vector Machines allow for some misclassification or margin violations to enable better generalization on non-linearly separable data by introducing slack variables.
A loss function often used in SVM models that measures the error or penalty for misclassified examples and for examples within the margin.
A method used in kernelized SVM to implicitly map inputs into high-dimensional feature spaces without explicitly computing the coordinates.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy Choice Property in Interval Cover Problem
concepts.short_definition: In the problem of covering intervals with the smallest set of points, the Greedy Choice Property states there exists an optimal solution that includes choosing the end point of the interval with the smallest end point.

concepts.canonical_name: Counterexample to Greedy Choice Property Variants
concepts.short_definition: Examples demonstrating why other candidate choices for the Greedy Choice Property in the interval cover problem do not hold, by showing selections that lead to suboptimal solutions.
A formal argument demonstrating that an algorithm always produces the correct output for all valid inputs.
The process of sorting a collection of intervals based on their ending points bi.

concepts.canonical_name: Sorting Time Complexity O(n log n)
concepts.short_definition: The computational complexity of sorting algorithms like mergesort or heapsort, which require O(n log n) time to sort n elements.
The process of initializing a set S to be empty and a variable b to negative infinity as part of algorithm setup.
A method for selecting the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals by scanning intervals in order and adding an interval if its start is after the last added interval's end.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity O(n) of Interval Scheduling
concepts.short_definition: The algorithm for interval scheduling that scans and selects intervals runs in linear time with respect to the number of intervals n.
A proof technique where the statement is proved for a base case and then assuming it holds for all smaller values to prove for the current value.
A method of proof where one assumes the negation of the desired conclusion and derives a contradiction to establish the original claim.
Comparing the cardinalities of two solution sets, such as a greedy solution set and an optimal solution set, to analyze algorithm performance.

concepts.canonical_name: Set of intervals not covered by a given interval
concepts.short_definition: The set of intervals that start after a specific interval bk, representing the intervals not covered by bk.
The concept that certain intervals can cover portions of a set, affecting subsequent selections.
An assumption used in mathematical induction that a statement holds for all cases smaller than a given size, here used to establish optimality for a subset I′ with size less than n.
The state of a solution being the best possible or minimal in cost/size according to a given criterion, here referring to set A being optimal over a subset I′.
The operation of removing an element from a set, denoted here as \{bk\} removed from GREEDY and S, as in |GREEDY \ {bk}| ≤ |S \ {bk}|.

concepts.canonical_name: Relationship Between Polynomial-time Reduction and P Membership
concepts.short_definition: If B can be solved in polynomial time and A reduces to B in polynomial time, then A can be solved in polynomial time.

concepts.canonical_name: Effect of Input Size Transformation on Algorithm Runtime
concepts.short_definition: The runtime of an algorithm solving problem A through a polynomial-time reduction to B depends on the input size transformation; if input size grows from n to n^2, runtime changes accordingly.
The complexity class NP consists of decision problems for which a proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time.
The process of determining the computational complexity and resource requirements of algorithms.
A logical argument that an algorithm correctly solves the problem it is designed for.
An analysis showing the maximum amount of computational time an algorithm requires as a function of input size.
Proof establishing the minimum computational time an algorithm requires.
Proof establishing the minimum memory required for an algorithm.
Requirement that algorithms be described in natural language rather than programming code for clarity.
Algorithms to find the minimum element in an unsorted array and their asymptotic optimality.
A linear time algorithm to find the minimum element in an unsorted array by iterating through all elements once and tracking the minimum seen so far.

concepts.canonical_name: Min Heap Construction and Minimum Extraction
concepts.short_definition: Building a min heap from an unsorted array, then popping the minimum element to find the minimum element.
The time complexity for inserting an n-bit string into an AVL set containing n such strings, assuming a word size of Θ(log n).
Amortized constant time operation for appending an element to a dynamic array, repeated n times yields O(n) total time.
BFS cannot solve SSSP efficiently in graphs with arbitrary positive integer weights, only when edges are unweighted or have equal weights.

concepts.canonical_name: Positive Edge Weights Constraint for Dijkstra's Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: Dijkstra's algorithm requires that all edge weights be non-negative to correctly compute shortest paths.
An algorithm that computes shortest paths from a single source in a weighted graph that may contain negative edge weights, can detect negative cycles reachable from the source.
An algorithm for APSP that can handle negative edge weights (but no negative cycles), uses Bellman-Ford to reweight edges and then runs Dijkstra's algorithm.

concepts.canonical_name: Computational Complexity Classes: P and NP
concepts.short_definition: P is the set of decision problems solvable in polynomial time; NP is the set of decision problems verifiable in polynomial time.

concepts.canonical_name: Known Relationships Among Complexity Classes: P, NP, and EXPTIME
concepts.short_definition: The established inclusions among complexity classes; for example, P is a subset of EXPTIME, NP is a subset of EXPTIME, but the strictness of these inclusions remains unknown except for known separations.
A problem for which no algorithm can decide the answer for all inputs in finite time.
The problem of determining whether a given computer program will halt or run forever on a given input, known to be undecidable and NP-hard but not NP-complete.
Comprehensive assessments administered at the end of a course to evaluate a student's overall understanding and mastery of the subject material.

concepts.canonical_name: Valid move in Number Crunch problem
concepts.short_definition: A move where two distinct uneaten indices i and j are chosen such that |A[i] - A[j]| ≤ 1, and the smaller element's index is eaten.

concepts.canonical_name: Proof of Greedy Choice Property for Number Crunch problem
concepts.short_definition: A logical argument showing that the selected greedy choice leads to an optimal solution sequence by conditioning on floor values and move sequences.
A move in the sequence that adheres to problem constraints and can be used in constructing a solution.
An ordered series of moves used to solve the problem, where order and validity matter.
An algorithm with runtime proportional to the size of its input, typically O(n).

concepts.canonical_name: Bucket Concatenation Strategy in Counting Sort
concepts.short_definition: The method of concatenating buckets after counting sort by swapping the element with the minimal key value to the beginning of each bucket before concatenation.
The condition that the algorithm stops running when the list L has fewer than two elements, preventing invalid or incomplete operations.
Sorting elements based on the floor of their values, i.e., sorting by the function i ↦ ⌊A[i]⌋ instead of by direct values or indices.
The practice of verifying that operations or moves in an algorithm meet problem constraints to ensure correctness and avoid errors.
Mistake where the last remaining value in a bucket is compared to the wrong value in another bucket, potentially causing an incorrect abort in the algorithm.
Errors occurring from attempting to simplify or incorrectly implement the greedy choice (GC) strategy in an algorithm.

concepts.canonical_name: Improper Use of Heap in Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: Mistakes made by employing a heap data structure incorrectly, especially forgetting to consider its runtime costs and impacts on the algorithm's efficiency.
A core method for solving systems of linear equations by systematically applying row operations to transform the matrix to reduced row echelon form.
A mathematical transform that decomposes a function or signal into its constituent frequencies.
Decomposition of a square matrix into eigenvalues and eigenvectors, useful in solving linear algebra problems.

concepts.canonical_name: Proper Divisors of a Positive Integer
concepts.short_definition: The set of all positive integer divisors of a positive integer x except x itself.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Complexity Classes: Linear, Polynomial, Pseudo-polynomial
concepts.short_definition: Classification of algorithm runtime based on input size or numeric value, distinguishing between linear, polynomial, and pseudo-polynomial time complexities.

concepts.canonical_name: Factor Tree of a Positive Integer
concepts.short_definition: A tree where the root node is a positive integer n, its children are the proper divisors of n, and this process continues recursively down to leaves which are the number 1.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming to Count Leaves in a Factor Tree
concepts.short_definition: A DP approach that, given n, computes the number of leaves (which are 1s) in the factor tree of n using a recursive function Ones(m) summing over proper divisors of m.
A framework for defining dynamic programs specifying: Subproblems (S), Recurrence (R), Termination condition (T), Base cases (B), Objective (O), and Time complexity (T).

concepts.canonical_name: Sum of Positive Divisors Function σ(n) and its Bounds
concepts.short_definition: The function σ(n) equals the sum of all positive divisors of n, which relates to the runtime complexity bounds of divisor-based algorithms, with known asymptotic bounds like Θ(n log log n) and O(n√n).
The particular choice of how to define the subproblems in a dynamic programming solution, which determines how the recursive relationships are built.
Rounding input coordinates to discrete grid points to enable efficient data structures and sorting in algorithms.

concepts.canonical_name: Hash Set for Constant Time Lookup
concepts.short_definition: A data structure that stores elements for expected constant time membership queries.
Defining neighbors in a 2D grid as all points within a given Euclidean distance (here within radius 10, squared distance ≤100).
Calculating the number of berries lost flying between cities as d% of current berries, with d as the distance traveled that day, rounded up.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Recurrence for Maximum Berries
concepts.short_definition: The recurrence relation for X(i), the maximum berries at city i, considering the berries after flying and nightly collection.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Recurrence for Minimum Berries
concepts.short_definition: The recurrence relation for Y(i), the minimum number of berries needed at city i to reach Shamouti without running out.
Achieving an overall O(n) expected time algorithm by combining efficient sorting, hashing, and constant size neighbor queries in dynamic programming.
Mistakes arising from neglecting necessary conditions that must hold for an algorithm or procedure to work correctly.

concepts.canonical_name: Assuming Sorted Data in Algorithmic Problems
concepts.short_definition: The mistake of implicitly or explicitly assuming that input data (e.g., city locations) is sorted when the problem does not guarantee it.
Errors that occur when a program uses a value of one type in a context where another type is expected.
Mistakes involving incorrect treatment of positive and negative signs in calculations, often leading to incorrect results.
Logical errors where an iteration or index goes one step too far or not far enough, often causing errors in loops or array accesses.
Errors arising from approximations in numerical calculations due to finite precision or rounding steps.
A model that combines L1 (lasso) and L2 (ridge) regularization penalties to encourage both sparsity and grouping in regression coefficients.
A regression technique that uses L1 regularization to encourage sparsity in the model coefficients.
A regression technique that uses L2 regularization to shrink coefficients towards zero and reduce model complexity.
A property of a regression model where many coefficients are zero, leading to simpler and more interpretable models.
A property where correlated predictors tend to be selected or shrunk together in regression models with joint L1 and L2 penalties.
A decision problem asking whether a subset of a given set of positive integers sums to a target integer T.
Decision problem given an algorithm A and input x, outputs YES iff A halts and outputs YES on input x.
ACCEPT problem is NP-hard because there is a polynomial-time many-one reduction from SUBSETSUM (an NP-hard problem) to ACCEPT.
An O(nT) time dynamic programming algorithm solving SUBSETSUM.
A perfect matching in a graph is a set of edges that matches each vertex to exactly one edge, covering all vertices without overlap.
Procedures to arrange elements in a particular order (e.g., ascending or descending).
The proof or argument that a sorting algorithm produces a correctly sorted output for all inputs.
The computational problem of determining an arrangement or sequence whereby given boxes can be nested inside one another according to dimensional constraints.
Concepts and algorithms relating to various types of trees in computer science, including properties and manipulation.
The practice of selecting, proving, and justifying runtime bounds for algorithms, prioritizing correctness over asymptotic efficiency.
Approaches to taking exams effectively, including time management, reading all problems first, and clear, concise solution writing.
An algorithm that solves a problem with running time upper bounded by a polynomial function of the input size.
Optimization problem where items with weights and values are selected to maximize value without exceeding weight capacity, with each item either taken or left.
The ratio α of the number of stored items to the number of buckets in a hash table.
Assumption that each key is equally likely to be hashed into any slot independently of other keys.

concepts.canonical_name: Expected Search Time in Hash Table
concepts.short_definition: The expected time to find an item in a hash table under SUHA depends on the load factor.
An algorithm that transforms data without using extra space proportional to input size.
An algorithm that maintains the relative order of equal elements in sorting.

concepts.canonical_name: Balanced Binary Search Tree Construction from Sorted Arrays
concepts.short_definition: Creating a height-balanced BST from the union of multiple sorted arrays, minimizing height for efficient searches.
Computational model where algorithm performance is measured by the number of key comparisons performed.
Algorithms to find shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in a graph, including Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Johnson, and Floyd-Warshall algorithms.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Density and Its Impact on Algorithm Choice
concepts.short_definition: How the number of edges relative to vertices in a graph influences the asymptotic performance of shortest path algorithms.

concepts.canonical_name: Adding Edges to a DAG and Its Effect on Topological Orders
concepts.short_definition: How extending the edge set of a DAG affects the number of possible topological orderings.
The metadata stored in nodes of an AVL Sequence data structure, including heights, depths, sizes of subtrees, or indices of sequence elements.

concepts.canonical_name: Depth-First Search (DFS) and Single-Source Shortest Path (SSSP)
concepts.short_definition: Using DFS-based approaches to solve single-source shortest path problems in certain classes of graphs like DAGs and unweighted graphs.

concepts.canonical_name: Bellman-Ford Algorithm for Negative Cycle Detection
concepts.short_definition: Using the Bellman-Ford algorithm to detect negative weight cycles by observing distance estimate changes in the final iteration.

concepts.canonical_name: Properties of Undirected Graphs with Negative Cycles
concepts.short_definition: Characteristics of undirected graphs containing negative edges and cycles as inferred from Bellman-Ford results.
Given an undirected graph G and integer k, determine if G contains a complete subgraph (clique) of size k.
Given an undirected graph G and integer k, determine if G contains k vertices with no edges between any pair of them.
The complement of a graph G on n vertices is a graph with the same vertices where two vertices are connected if and only if they are not connected in G.
An O(n²) dynamic programming algorithm to compute the maximum total value of a nesting sequence of boxes, using subproblems defined by prefixes or suffixes of the input.
Optimum solution that includes box i (if i > 0) and excludes all boxes j > i, with i ranging from 0 to n, corresponding to prefixes of the input.
Optimum solution that includes box i (if i ≤ n) and excludes all boxes j < i, with i ranging from 1 to n+1, corresponding to suffixes of the input.
A general framework for systematic dynamic programming design that involves defining Subproblems, Recurrence, Base cases, Topological order, Output, and Time complexity.
A measure of the amount of computational time an algorithm takes to run as a function of the input size.

concepts.canonical_name: Relate Step in Divide and Conquer Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: A step in divide and conquer algorithms where solutions to subproblems are combined or related to form a solution to a larger problem.

concepts.canonical_name: Data Structures for Efficient Subproblem Solutions
concepts.short_definition: Data structures that can store and retrieve solutions to subproblems efficiently to improve algorithm runtime, such as balanced binary search trees or heaps.
A binary tree where no path from the root to any leaf goes left more than k times.

concepts.canonical_name: T(n, k) for k-wonky binary trees
concepts.short_definition: The minimum height of a k-wonky binary tree on n elements.
A binary tree where no path from root to leaf goes left more than zero times; i.e., all such paths have zero left moves, effectively forming a right spine.

concepts.canonical_name: Subtrees Size and Structure in Rooted Trees
concepts.short_definition: Considering the sizes and particular properties ('wonkinesses') of left and right subtrees when designing algorithms related to rooted trees.
The squared difference between the sweetness of a sweet berry s(i) and the sourness of a sour berry t(j), i.e., (s(i) - t(j))^2.
The problem of blending n sweet and n sour berries into candies to minimize the sum of imbalances of all candies.

concepts.canonical_name: Practice Final Exam as Assessment Method
concepts.short_definition: Using a comprehensive practice final exam to evaluate understanding and readiness for the actual final exam.
The problem of determining whether a given program halts on an input is undecidable, meaning no algorithm can solve it for all inputs.
0-1 Knapsack is an NP-complete problem, and the question of its polynomial time solvability is equivalent to the open P vs NP problem.

concepts.canonical_name: Simple Uniform Hashing Assumption (SUHA) Expected Find Time
concepts.short_definition: Under SUHA and with load factor α ∈ o(1), the expected time to find an item in a hash table with chaining is Θ(1 + α), which approximates to Θ(1).
The process of combining multiple sorted arrays into a single sorted array in linear time.
An APSP algorithm efficient for sparse graphs, running in O(|V|^2 log|V| + |V||E|) time.
An APSP algorithm with cubic time complexity O(|V|^3), suitable for dense graphs.
The depth of a node measured as the distance from the root to the node within a subtree.
The height of a subtree is the length of the longest path from the subtree root to a leaf node.
The total number of nodes contained within a subtree.
Specific graph categories where DFS can correctly find shortest paths, e.g., undirected acyclic graphs and undirected graphs with only negative edges.
Relationships among problems A, B, and C such that A ≤P B ≤P C, B is NP-complete, and conclusions about NP membership.
A decision problem for which a given solution can be verified in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing machine.
The property that if problem A reduces to problem B and problem B reduces to problem C, then A reduces to C.
A method or algorithm that checks the correctness of a purported solution to a problem within polynomial time.
A notation describing an asymptotic upper bound that is non-tight; f(n) ∈ o(g(n)) means f grows strictly slower than g as n→∞.
A matrix where entry (i, j) is 1 if there is an edge between vertices i and j, and 0 otherwise.
An n × n matrix with 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere.
An n × n matrix where every entry is 1.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Subproblems in Nesting Boxes
concepts.short_definition: Defining subproblems X(i) for prefixes and Y(i) for suffixes to compute the optimum solution involving box i and excluding certain boxes.
For i > 0, X(i) = vi + max over j < i where wj < wi of X(j).
For i ≤ n, Y(i) = vi + max over j > i where wj > wi of Y(j).
Base case for subproblems X(i) is X(0) = 0.
Base case for subproblems Y(i) is Y(n + 1) = 0.

concepts.canonical_name: Topological Ordering in Dynamic Programming for X(i)
concepts.short_definition: X(i) depends on previously computed subproblems X(j) where j < i, enabling a topological order by increasing i.

concepts.canonical_name: Topological Ordering in Dynamic Programming for Y(i)
concepts.short_definition: Y(i) depends on previously computed subproblems Y(j) where j > i, enabling a topological order by decreasing i.

concepts.canonical_name: Overall Algorithm Complexity for Nesting Boxes
concepts.short_definition: The dynamic programming algorithm uses n+1 subproblems each taking O(n) time, resulting in O(n^2) total runtime.
The maximum total value V is the maximum over all i in 1 to n of X(i) or Y(i).

concepts.canonical_name: Common Mistakes in Nesting Boxes Dynamic Programming
concepts.short_definition: Mistakes include neglecting to include box i in recurrence and confusing the subproblem definitions X and Y.
A range query that finds the maximum or minimum of a value in a subset of data entries constrained by one side of a key range, useful in augmented AVL trees.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy Algorithm Error for Width-constrained Subproblems
concepts.short_definition: A mistaken greedy algorithm that chooses the next subproblem based on local comparisons without considering the correct maximization over all valid subproblems constrained by width.

concepts.canonical_name: Improved Runtime via Augmented AVL Tree for Dynamic Programming
concepts.short_definition: The use of an augmented AVL tree to achieve O(n log n) runtime in dynamic programming problems by performing efficient range queries to find subproblem maximums keyed by widths.
Number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path; conventionally the height of an empty tree is -1.
A dynamic program computing T(n,k) by conditioning on the size of the left subtree, minimizing over choices and using the subproblems T(ℓ, j−1) and T(i−ℓ−1, j).

concepts.canonical_name: Subproblem structure in k-wonky tree DP
concepts.short_definition: The left subtree of a k-wonky tree must be (k −1)-wonky, and the right subtree must be k-wonky, leading to the recurrence for DP.
The naive DP runs in O(n^2 k) time since there are O(nk) subproblems and each takes O(n) to compute min over all left subtree sizes.

concepts.canonical_name: Maximum size of a k-wonky binary tree of height h
concepts.short_definition: The largest possible number of nodes in a j-wonky binary tree with height h defined recursively.

concepts.canonical_name: Recurrence relation for maximum size of k-wonky binary tree
concepts.short_definition: A recursive formula expressing S(h,j) as S(h −1, j −1) + S(h −1, j) + 1, with base cases S(−1, j) = 0 and S(h, 0) = h + 1.

concepts.canonical_name: Topological order computation in dynamic programming
concepts.short_definition: Solving subproblems in order of increasing h because S(h, j) depends only on subproblems with smaller h.

concepts.canonical_name: Binary search optimization in dynamic programming subproblems
concepts.short_definition: Using binary search to improve runtime per subproblem from O(n) to O(log n).

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime complexity of k-wonky binary tree size computation
concepts.short_definition: The algorithm to compute the maximum size of a k-wonky binary tree with height at most h runs in O(nk) time.
A graph representing the decomposition of a problem into subproblems without cycles, used in dynamic programming.
The process of determining the height of a given tree, typically the longest path from the root to a leaf.
Correctly indexing elements during the dynamic programming solution steps, accounting for all nodes such as the root.

concepts.canonical_name: Base Case Handling in Tree Problems
concepts.short_definition: Correctly managing base cases such as leaves or empty trees in tree-based algorithms.
A greedy choice that picks the candy with the minimum possible imbalance at each step.
A greedy choice pairing the sweetest berry with the sourest berry at each step, assuming monotonic ordering.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy Algorithm for Minimum Sum Imbalance
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm using the greedy choice of pairing the sweetest berry with the sourest berry to minimize total imbalance in candies.
A non-comparative sorting algorithm that sorts numbers by processing individual digits, typically from least significant to most significant digit.
The process of determining the time complexity of individual steps within an algorithm to understand their contribution to overall complexity.
An algorithmic runtime that scales proportional to the logarithm of the input size, O(log n).
A linear data structure following Last In First Out (LIFO) principle, where the last element added is the first removed.
A linear data structure following First In First Out (FIFO) principle, where the first element added is the first removed.
A simple comparison-based sorting algorithm with average and worst-case runtime O(n^2).
A divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm with guaranteed O(n log n) runtime.
A comparison-based sorting algorithm using a heap data structure with O(n log n) runtime.
Methods to visit all nodes of a binary tree: Pre-Order (root first), In-Order (root in middle), Post-Order (root last).
A binary tree traversal order where the root node is visited first, then left subtree, then right subtree.
A binary tree traversal order where the left subtree is visited first, then the root, then the right subtree.
A binary tree traversal order where the left and right subtrees are visited first, and the root last.

concepts.canonical_name: Mean of a Subtree in a BST
concepts.short_definition: The average value of all nodes in a subtree of a binary search tree.

concepts.canonical_name: Median of a Subtree in a BST
concepts.short_definition: The middle value when the values in a subtree are sorted, used as an augmentation to nodes in a tree.

concepts.canonical_name: Mode of a Subtree in a BST
concepts.short_definition: The most frequently occurring value in a subtree of a binary search tree.

concepts.canonical_name: Sum of a Subtree in a BST
concepts.short_definition: The sum of all values in a subtree of a binary search tree, stored as an augmentation for efficient queries.
Structural and ordering properties guaranteed to be true in a max heap data structure containing n elements.
The time complexity of performing heapify-up or heapify-down operations in a heap is O(log n).
The directed acyclic graph formed by contracting each strongly connected component of a directed graph into a single node.
Key properties of the condensation graph Gc such as node count, connectivity, acyclicity, and relation of sources between Gc and G.
The selection at each iteration of the unvisited vertex with the smallest tentative distance to relax edges from in Dijkstra's algorithm.

concepts.canonical_name: Single-Source Shortest Path (SSSP) Algorithm Using Edge Subdivision and BFS
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that solves the single-source shortest path problem on positive integer weighted graphs by subdividing each edge of weight w into w unit edges and running BFS on the resulting graph.
A runtime complexity that grows at most as a polynomial function of the input size.
A runtime complexity that is polynomial in the numeric value of the input (e.g., weights), but not necessarily polynomial in the size of the input encoding.
A runtime complexity that grows exponentially with the input size.
An open question in computational complexity theory asking whether every problem whose solution can be verified in polynomial time can also be solved in polynomial time.
Categories of decision problems based on their algorithmic complexity, including P, NP, NP-complete, NP-hard, and undecidable problems.
A measure of how the runtime of an algorithm scales with the size of the input.
A graph algorithm to find the shortest paths from a source vertex to all other vertices in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights.
An abstract data type supporting operations like build, delete-min, and decrease-key, used in graph algorithms such as Dijkstra's.
The average runtime per operation over a worst-case sequence of operations, smoothing out expensive operations over time.

concepts.canonical_name: NP Problem Not Known To Be NP-Complete
concepts.short_definition: A problem in the complexity class NP for which it is unknown whether it is NP-complete or not.

concepts.canonical_name: Rectangle Decomposition into Minimum Number of Integer-Length Squares
concepts.short_definition: The problem of decomposing an a × b rectangle into the fewest non-overlapping integer-length squares covering the entire rectangle.
An algorithm that selects at each step the largest square that fits in the rectangle and recursively covers the remaining area.
Optimization principle aiming to minimize the size of a matrix decomposition by choosing parameters optimally, exemplified by setting parameter a equal to b for size 1 decomposition.
A way of breaking down a problem or structure into parts such that the overall cost or value is optimized (e.g., minimized or maximized).
A square contained within a rectangle, not aligned with the rectangle's corners, defined by side length b.
A matrix factorization that yields a solution optimized according to some criterion, possibly involving choices such as swapping components to maintain optimality.
An operation that swaps a particular component of a matrix decomposition with other components to achieve an alternative optimal solution.

concepts.canonical_name: Covering a region with multiple squares of smaller side length
concepts.short_definition: The idea that when every square in a set D has side length less than b, a region that would be covered by a greedy choice square of side b must be covered by at least two smaller squares in D.
A solution that has the best possible value or outcome for the problem being solved.
The probability pi that a coin i lands on heads when flipped, where each coin can have a different bias.
The assumption that the outcomes of each coin flip do not affect the outcomes of any other coin flips.

concepts.canonical_name: Set of Coins with Joint Probability at Least 50%
concepts.short_definition: A subset S of coins such that the probability that all coins in S land heads up is at least 0.5 (50%).

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy Algorithm for Maximizing Set Size with Joint Probability Threshold
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that selects coins in decreasing order of bias or based on some criterion to maximize the size |S| of a subset satisfying the joint probability constraint in O(n log n) time.
A sequence that can be derived from another sequence by deleting some elements without changing the order of the remaining elements.
A relation between types where one type is effective against another, allowing constant-time checking of effectiveness between pairs of types.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Representation of Cities and Passages
concepts.short_definition: Modeling cities as nodes and connections (mountain passes and rivers) as edges with constraints on traversal direction and cost.
Crossing a mountain pass reduces the number of elephants by 100; crossing a river causes 1% of the elephants to drown (rounded up).
An algorithm whose running time grows proportionally to the square of the input size, typically denoted as O(n^2).
Determining whether there exists a path between two nodes in a graph under given constraints.

concepts.canonical_name: Problem Modeling with Parameters (x, M, R)
concepts.short_definition: Formulating a problem input with variables representing the number of elephants (x), mountains (M), and rivers (R) to solve using dynamic programming.
Properties guaranteed by max heaps with n elements concerning element values positions, heap operations time complexity, and value occurrences.

Graph algorithms that run in time proportional to the number of nodes and edges, such as computing condensation graphs and certain single-source shortest path (SSSP) problems on positive-weighted dense graphs.
The greedy choice of relaxing an unrelaxed edge (u, v) where d(u) is minimal to progressively find shortest paths in a graph with non-negative edge weights.
An algorithm whose running time depends polynomially on the numeric value of the input (e.g., edge weights) but not necessarily on the input size, and thus may not be polynomial time.

concepts.canonical_name: NP-Complete Problem Solvable in Polynomial Time
concepts.short_definition: The condition that at least one NP-complete problem can be solved in polynomial time, which implies P = NP.

concepts.canonical_name: NP-Hard Problem Solvable in Polynomial Time
concepts.short_definition: The condition that at least one NP-hard problem can be solved in polynomial time.

concepts.canonical_name: NP-Hard Problem Solvable Always in Polynomial Time
concepts.short_definition: The condition that every NP-hard problem can be solved in polynomial time, which is false unless P=NP and complexity hierarchy collapses.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Complexity Classes for Decision Problems
concepts.short_definition: Possible asymptotic upper bounds on worst-case runtimes of algorithms solving decision problems, including factorial time, logarithmic time, polynomial time, and polynomial-logarithmic time.

concepts.canonical_name: Priority Queue Operations: Build, Delete-Min, Decrease-Key
concepts.short_definition: The operations on a priority queue data structure with specified runtimes for Build, Delete-Min, and Decrease-Key.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Analysis of Dijkstra's Algorithm with Given Priority Queue
concepts.short_definition: The resulting runtime of Dijkstra's Algorithm when implemented with a priority queue having specified Build, Delete-Min, and Decrease-Key runtimes.

concepts.canonical_name: NP Problems not known to be NP-complete
concepts.short_definition: Problems that are in NP but for which it is unknown whether they are NP-complete, e.g. s-t Reachability.

concepts.canonical_name: Decomposition of Rectangle into Integer Squares
concepts.short_definition: Partitioning an a × b rectangle into non-overlapping squares with integer side lengths that completely cover the rectangle.
A measure of the size of a decomposition, with smaller sizes being more optimal.
An optimal decomposition refers to a problem breakdown approach in dynamic programming where the solution is composed of optimal solutions to its subproblems.

concepts.canonical_name: Square with side length b inside rectangle D
concepts.short_definition: A square named sO which lies inside a rectangle D but does not share a corner with the rectangle.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy Choice Property in Covering Problems
concepts.short_definition: The property that an optimal solution includes the square chosen greedily to cover a region before considering alternatives.

concepts.canonical_name: Square Covering with Side Length Constraints
concepts.short_definition: The concept of covering a region using squares where each square has side length less than a fixed value b.
The process of partitioning a set of covering squares into subsets to analyze coverage properties, such as the subset D1 covering a specific area.
The condition when a greedy algorithm's solution is optimal for the problem, often proven using the greedy choice property.
A solution that satisfies all problem constraints and is valid under the problem's rules.
The probability that a set of weighted coins all land on heads, computed as the product of their individual head probabilities.

concepts.canonical_name: Monotonicity Property in Weighted Coin Sets
concepts.short_definition: A property showing that feasible solutions for the coin set problem scale recursively via adjusted probabilities when removing a coin with the highest probability.

concepts.canonical_name: Empty Set as Optimal Solution Case
concepts.short_definition: The scenario where the empty set is the only feasible solution, typically when all coins have probability less than the threshold x.
A property where improving the quality of subproblem solutions does not decrease the overall solution quality, often requiring careful definition of relevant subproblems and conditions to prove.
The set of necessary and sufficient conditions that determine whether a candidate solution can be accepted as valid or feasible within the constraints of the optimization problem.
A property where feasibility becomes strictly weaker or less likely as the set S grows, often contrasting with monotone feasibility conditions.
A prerequisite relationship where learning one concept requires prior understanding of another concept, explicitly stated in material.
Defining subproblems in DP as M(i, j), representing the maximum length of a subsequence of P[i:] where the first type is effective against j.
The step to compute M(i, j) using max of skipping current element or extending subsequence if effectiveness holds.

concepts.canonical_name: Initialization in DP for Subsequence Problem
concepts.short_definition: Base case B M(n + 1, j) = 0 for all j, representing no elements beyond index n.
Adding a dummy type ⊥ against which everything is effective to handle edge cases in the sequence.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Analysis of the DP Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The DP algorithm has O(n|T|) time complexity due to (n+1)(|T|+1) subproblems and constant work per subproblem.

concepts.canonical_name: Effective Type Relation in DP subsequences
concepts.short_definition: The condition that for subsequence S, t(si) is effective against t(si-1) for each consecutive pair.

concepts.canonical_name: Common Mistake: Omitting Dummy Type in Subsequence DP
concepts.short_definition: Not including a null type to handle the case where the first Pokémon in the optimal subsequence has a completely ineffective type.
Using as subproblem max length of subsequence of P[i:] or P[:i] whose first type is j, causing redundancy and complexity in solution.

concepts.canonical_name: Common Mistake: Assuming Effectiveness is a Strict Total Order
concepts.short_definition: Erroneous assumption that effectiveness is a strict total order and reducing problem to Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS).
Defining the DP state as the maximum number of elephants Hamilcar can have at a city i.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Traversal Constraints in Dynamic Programming
concepts.short_definition: The problem condition forcing traveling only from city i to city j with j > i, for updating DP states only from smaller to larger city indices.
Rounding up after applying percentage loss of elephants crossing a river (1% lost rounded up).
Removing unreachable cities and renumbering to ensure efficient linear time computation in DP.
A DP approach with runtime proportional to the sum of the edges of mountain passes and rivers, i.e. O(|M| + |R|).
Output condition: Hamilcar reaches Rome (city n-1) with at least 100 elephants.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming for Path Optimization with Constraints
concepts.short_definition: A quadratic time dynamic programming approach using SRTBOT framework to determine if Hannibal can reach Rome with at least 100 elephants given parameters (x, M, R).

concepts.canonical_name: Quadratic Time Complexity of DP Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The runtime complexity of the DP algorithm is O((|M| + |R|)^2) which is quadratic in the input size due to iteration over states and edges.

concepts.canonical_name: Weighted Undirected Graph Model with Monotone Edge Weights for Path Costs
concepts.short_definition: A graph formulation where V=[n]×[2], edges have monotone weight functions modeling transitions between river and mountain states with specific costs for crossing M and R edges.
An operation on two functions f and g to produce a new function where (f ⋆ g)(x) = g(f(x)).
A relation ⪯ on functions where f ⪯ g if and only if f(x) ≥ g(x) pointwise for all x.
If f ⪯ g, then for any monotone function h, we have f ⋆ h ⪯ g ⋆ h, meaning composition preserves the partial order.

concepts.canonical_name: Identity Function as Identity Element in Composition
concepts.short_definition: The identity function acts as the identity element under function composition, i.e., composing any function with the identity leaves it unchanged.

concepts.canonical_name: Pointwise Boundedness of Edge Weights by Identity Function
concepts.short_definition: Edge weights represented as functions are pointwise bounded above by the identity function.

concepts.canonical_name: Supremum Function under the Partial Order
concepts.short_definition: The supremum function ∞ maps every input to zero and is an upper bound for functions under the partial order ⪯ where f(k) ≥ 0 for all k.

concepts.canonical_name: Weight of a Path as Number of Remaining Elephants
concepts.short_definition: For a path π, the weight w(π) is a function mapping the number k of elephants starting along π to the number remaining at the end.

concepts.canonical_name: Dijkstra's Algorithm Application for Path Weight Estimation
concepts.short_definition: Running Dijkstra from (0,0) to compute δ((n−1,0))(x)≥100 where weights are functions mapping input x to remaining elephants after the path.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Complexity of Modified Dijkstra's Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The runtime when representing weights by single values w(x) is O((|M| + |R|) log(|M| + |R|)).

concepts.canonical_name: Common Mistakes in Dynamic Programming without Topological Order
concepts.short_definition: Mistakes include not addressing lack of topological order, using same subproblems incorrectly, and exponential or pseudopolynomial costs due to naive approaches.
A method of reducing a problem instance in terms of smaller instances of the same problem, used to prove correctness and efficiency in greedy algorithms.
Inserting an element into an AVL tree, maintaining balanced property with logarithmic runtime in worst and amortized case.
Appending an element to an AVL Sequence data structure.
Inserting an element into a hash table, typically expected O(1) average case runtime.
Processing a vertex and relaxing all of its outgoing edges during shortest path computation in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).
A sorting algorithm for n distinct non-negative integers presented in the class, runtime context implied.
Algorithm presented in class for deciding subset sum problem given n integers as input.
A data structure where each node has at most two children, storing elements such as integers, without necessarily following any ordering properties like BST.
The subtree consisting of node x and all of its descendants.
Additional information stored at nodes of a binary tree that can be maintained efficiently (e.g., in constant time per node during updates).
The smallest integer value contained in the subtree rooted at a given node.
The smallest integer value contained in the left child's subtree of a given node, or +∞ if no left child.

concepts.canonical_name: Smallest Value in Subtree Greater Than Node Item
concepts.short_definition: The smallest integer value in the subtree rooted at x that is strictly greater than x.item, or +∞ if none exists.

concepts.canonical_name: Smallest Value in Subtree Greater Than Constant
concepts.short_definition: The smallest integer value in the subtree rooted at x that is greater than a fixed constant (e.g., 61210), or +∞ if none exists.
A data structure used in Dijkstra’s algorithm to select the next vertex with the smallest current distance estimate.
Current estimate of the shortest distance from the source to a given vertex during the execution of Dijkstra's algorithm, denoted d(u).
The actual shortest path distance δ(u) from a source vertex to vertex u in a graph.
Given a graph G=(V,E), the graph G'=(V×V, E') where E' contains an edge from (a,b) to (c,d) if edges (a,c) and (b,d) exist in G.
A directed graph is strongly connected if there is a path from every vertex to every other vertex.
A problem with a yes/no answer, typically formalized in computational complexity theory.
An algorithm that can verify a given solution to a problem in polynomial time.
A problem is decidable if there exists an algorithm that halts with a correct yes/no answer for every input instance.
The problem of determining if there is a path from vertex s to vertex t in a given directed graph.
A rooted tree is a tree in which one vertex is designated as the root and every edge is directed away from the root.
A forest is a disjoint union of trees, i.e., a set of trees considered together without connections between them.
Vertex u is an ancestor of vertex v if u is on the path from the root to v.
An assignment of colors to vertices of a graph or tree according to some constraints.

concepts.canonical_name: Coloring Constraint in a Rooted Forest
concepts.short_definition: In a rooted forest, two distinct vertices having the same color must be related by an ancestor-descendant relationship; i.e., if u and v share a color, then u is an ancestor of v or v is an ancestor of u.

concepts.canonical_name: Optimal Coloring of a Rooted Forest under Ancestor Constraint
concepts.short_definition: A coloring of the vertices that obeys the ancestor constraint and uses the minimum possible number of colors.
A vertex in a tree graph that has no children (degree one), often used as a starting point in tree algorithms.
The computational complexity that reflects the amount of time an algorithm takes with respect to the input size, e.g., O(nk) for this DP problem.
A problem involving traveling from city 1 to city n, handing out presents according to given rules and constraints, with the goal of ending with at least 12 presents.
The process of changing an algorithm's steps or structure to achieve improved time complexity, such as reducing runtime from O(nk) to O(n log k).

concepts.canonical_name: Maximum Profit Computation in Buying and Selling
concepts.short_definition: Computing the maximum possible profit from buying and selling items over multiple days given price and buying limits.

concepts.canonical_name: State, Recurrence, Base Case, and Termination (SRTBOT) in DP
concepts.short_definition: The components of a DP algorithm design: defining states, recurrence relation, base cases, and termination conditions.
The step of proving the DP recurrence relation correctly relates subproblem solutions to construct the overall solution.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming for Maximum Profit with Storage Constraint
concepts.short_definition: A dynamic programming method to compute the maximum profit over n days when owning at most k baubles, with daily price pi and daily limit l, running in O(nk log k) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy Algorithm for Maximum Profit with Storage Constraint
concepts.short_definition: A greedy approach to compute maximum profit over n days when owning at most k baubles, with daily price pi and daily limit l, including a greedy choice and justification of greedy choice property, running in O(nk log k) time.
A method of solving a problem by breaking it down into smaller instances of the same problem.
Understanding the requirements and constraints given in a problem for algorithm design.
Adding an element to the end of a dynamic array, which may involve resizing.
The event when two or more elements are assigned to the same hash bucket, leading to a chain or bucket with multiple elements.
The process of sequentially checking each element in a hash table chain to find a target element.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Array Expansion in Hash Tables
concepts.short_definition: The process of resizing underlying dynamic arrays used to store hash values and chains within a hash table when insertions cause capacity limits to be exceeded.

concepts.canonical_name: Amortized Time Complexity of Hash Table Operations
concepts.short_definition: The average time per operation over a sequence of operations, accounting for occasional costly resizing operations that are spread out over many cheap operations, resulting in an expected Θ(1) time per operation in certain cases.

concepts.canonical_name: Hash Collisions and Their Impact on Runtime
concepts.short_definition: When multiple elements are hashed to the same hash value, the resulting chain can become long, causing insertion or search operations to require linear time, affecting the total runtime complexity of hash table operations.

concepts.canonical_name: Amortization Limits Imposed by Sorting Lower Bounds
concepts.short_definition: Because of theoretical lower bounds on sorting (like Ω(n log n)), certain operations like AVL BST insertion cannot have amortized runtime better than Θ(log n) without breaking these bounds.

concepts.canonical_name: Append Operation Time in AVL Sequence
concepts.short_definition: Appending an element to an AVL Sequence data structure always takes Θ(log n) time per append operation; running n appends differs from building an AVL Sequence from scratch.
An algorithm whose runtime is polynomial in the size of the input (number of elements), independent of numeric values of input.
Merge Sort runs in O(n log n) time, which is polynomial in input size n.

concepts.canonical_name: Johnson's Algorithm for All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP)
concepts.short_definition: Algorithm computes APSP on a graph with n vertices and runs in polynomial time O(n^2log n + n|E|).

concepts.canonical_name: Smallest Value in a Subtree Augmentation
concepts.short_definition: Augmentation storing the smallest value in the subtree rooted at a node, maintainable in constant time per node.
The process of enhancing each node of a binary search tree (BST) with extra information (augmentation) to maintain additional properties efficiently, such as minimum or maximum values in a subtree.

The property that when a vertex v is removed from the priority queue during Dijkstra's algorithm, the distance estimates d(u) for vertices u on the shortest s-v path may or may not equal the true distances δ(u), depending on edge weights and graph structure.

Dijkstra's algorithm visits vertices in increasing order of their true distance from the source, ensuring correct distance estimates when vertices are removed from the priority queue, if edge weights are positive.

concepts.canonical_name: Effect of Zero Edge Weights on Dijkstra's Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: When graph edges can have zero weight, Dijkstra's algorithm might not visit vertices in strictly increasing order of their true distance, possibly missing vertices on shortest paths during tie-breaking.

concepts.canonical_name: Johnson's Algorithm Runtime on Squared Graph
concepts.short_definition: For a graph G with n vertices and m edges, Johnson's algorithm run on the squared graph G'= (V×V, E′) with |V′|=n² and |E′|=m² has runtime O(n^4 log n + n^2 m^2).

If problem 3-COLORING polynomially reduces to problem X (3-COLORING ≤P X), then X is NP-hard, but whether X has a polynomial time algorithm or verifier is unknown and may depend on the open P vs NP problem.
Whether a problem can be decided by an algorithm; that is, whether an algorithm exists that provides a correct yes/no answer for all inputs.
A practice version of a final examination used to prepare students for the actual assessment.
A collection of one or more rooted trees, where each tree is a connected acyclic graph with a designated root vertex.
Choosing a leaf and coloring it and all ancestors with a new color preserves optimality and feasibility of the coloring under the ancestor constraint.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy Algorithm for Minimal Coloring of Forest
concepts.short_definition: At each step, pick a leaf and color it and its ancestors with a new color, then recurse on the remaining forest; repeating until all vertices are colored.

A proof technique where the solution on a problem with k leaves is built assuming correctness on smaller instances with fewer leaves, used here to prove the greedy algorithm is optimal by induction over number of leaves.
A proof method showing that the greedy coloring is optimal by induction on the number of leaves in the tree.
The step of removing a leaf from the tree to induce a smaller subgraph used for the inductive hypothesis in proving coloring optimality.
A way to represent a tree storing each vertex’s parent and a list of its children, allowing linear time initialization and processing.
An efficient linear-time method that maintains a list or queue of leaves to perform iterative operations until the tree is fully processed.
A node in a tree data structure that has no children.
The action of removing and returning an element from a data structure, typically from a stack or list.
A list data structure labeled L used to hold nodes during an algorithm.
A sequence of nodes starting from a leaf node and moving upwards to the root by iteratively replacing each node with its parent, forming a unique path.
Assigning colors to the vertices of a graph so that no two adjacent vertices share the same color.

concepts.canonical_name: Set of Vertices (S) in a Graph
concepts.short_definition: A specific subset of vertices within a graph, denoted as S in graph algorithms.
A color not yet assigned to any vertex adjacent to the current set of vertices; used to maintain proper coloring.
A disjoint set of trees, i.e., an acyclic undirected graph in which each component is a tree.
An abstract data type that stores elements in an ordered manner allowing efficient insertion and removal.
A vertex in a tree which has no parent, serving as a starting point for traversals.
A sequence of nodes in a tree starting from the root node to a leaf node, where each node is connected by edges.
The process of removing a set S of vertices from a forest and defining a set R of roots as children of removed non-leaf vertices, except those in S.
An algorithm that performs a full DFS starting from a list of root vertices R and assigns colors to vertices based on discovery and leaf status.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity Analysis of Vertex Removal and DFS in Forest
concepts.short_definition: The total runtime of removing vertices in S from a forest and performing DFS over roots in R is O(n), where n is the number of vertices.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Coloring Using DFS with Leaf-Based Color Change
concepts.short_definition: A method of coloring vertices during DFS such that a new color is assigned whenever a leaf vertex is reached, thereby implicitly identifying connected components.
The process of breaking down a graph into a forest (a collection of trees), useful for solving subproblems in algorithms.

concepts.canonical_name: Depth-First Search (DFS) Coloring Algorithm Path Property
concepts.short_definition: In a DFS-based coloring algorithm, vertices assigned the same color form a path in the DFS tree from some starting vertex u to a leaf vertex v, with no future vertices colored the same later. The starting vertex u is either a root of the DFS forest or has a parent colored with a different, earlier color.
A recursive problem-solving technique where after applying a greedy choice, the problem is reduced to a smaller instance by removing chosen elements.
The technique of removing colored vertices from the graph to maintain efficiency and correctness during coloring.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming for Holiday Migration Problem
concepts.short_definition: A dynamic programming approach to determine if Delibird can end her trip with at least 12 presents, using subproblems X(i) or Y(i), solved in O(nk) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Subproblem X(i) Definition in Delibird DP
concepts.short_definition: X(i) is the maximum number of presents Delibird can have after traveling from city 1 to city i.
X(i) = max over j in [max(1,i-k), i-1] of floor(X(j)/2) + p_i, defining the recurrence for subproblem X(i).
Y(i) = max(0, min over j in [i+1, min(n, i+k)] of 2(Y(j) - p_j)) defining the recurrence for subproblem Y(i).

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Delibird DP Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: Both DP solutions (using X(i) or Y(i)) run in O(nk) time by evaluating O(n) subproblems each requiring O(k) iterations.
A max-heap is a data structure that supports efficient access to the maximum element and allows insertion and deletion operations; used to keep track of the largest value in a set efficiently.
A data structure that allows direct access to elements at arbitrary indices and supports efficient insertion and deletion.
A min-heap is a data structure supporting efficient access to the minimum element and insertion and deletion operations, used here for storing Y(i) values.
An algorithm runtime complexity indicating the algorithm runs in time proportional to n times the logarithm of k, where n and k are problem parameters.

concepts.canonical_name: Heap Operations: Insert and Delete with Pointer
concepts.short_definition: Efficient heap operations require direct pointers to items to perform insertions and deletions in O(log k) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Usage of Floor and Ceiling Functions in Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: Discretization in algorithms where floor and ceiling functions are used to compute integer values from real numbers.
A method proving correctness of a recursive greedy algorithm by showing optimality on subproblems and extending to the entire problem.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy Algorithm for Maximum Profit in Bauble Trading
concepts.short_definition: An O(n) greedy strategy which buys the maximum allowed baubles on day 1 and sells them on the day with the maximum price, then recurses on remaining days.

concepts.canonical_name: Problem Setup: Bauble Trading with Daily Buying Limit and Known Prices
concepts.short_definition: A trading problem with n days, daily prices p_i, a fixed buying limit l per day, starting with zero baubles and unlimited money, maximizing profit by buying/selling integer baubles under constraints.
A method to compute the maximum value of a sequence iteratively by maintaining a running maximum, updated as the sequence index varies.
Method to maintain a running sum over a sequence of values, updating incrementally.
An array M where each element M(i) stores the maximum value of p_j for indices j from i to n, used to efficiently find the maximum suffix value in an array.
A method of solving problems by breaking them down into simpler subproblems and storing solutions to subproblems to avoid recomputation.
A method for trading baubles where on a selected maximal price day all owned baubles are sold and baubles are bought on each day before that day.

concepts.canonical_name: Optimal Bauble Trading Strategy on Day 1
concepts.short_definition: A strategy where on day 1, buy l baubles, then sell all owned baubles if and only if for all days i, the price pi is less than or equal to the price on day 1 (p1).
A problem of trading baubles where Sobble does not necessarily start with 0 baubles, requiring analysis to consider arbitrary initial bauble holdings.
M(i) represents the maximum profit achievable from day i onward, defined as the maximum price from day i to n+1.
X(i, j) defines the maximum profit achievable from day i with j baubles in possession, using a conditional to decide buying or selling strategy depending on future prices.

concepts.canonical_name: Optimal Selling Condition in Bauble Trading
concepts.short_definition: If current price pi is greater than or equal to the maximum future price M(i+1), it is optimal to sell all baubles on day i.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Base Case for Bauble Trading
concepts.short_definition: The base case is X(n + 1, j) = M(n + 1) = 0, meaning no profit is possible beyond day n+1 regardless of baubles owned.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Bauble Trading DP Solution
concepts.short_definition: The runtime complexity of the DP solution is linear in the number of days n, as there are n+1 subproblems, each computed in constant time.

concepts.canonical_name: O(nk^2) DP Algorithm for Maximum Profit
concepts.short_definition: A dynamic programming algorithm with time complexity O(nk^2) to solve maximum profit with storage constraints problem, considered the baseline correct solution.

concepts.canonical_name: Suffix Subproblem Definition in Dynamic Programming
concepts.short_definition: The suffix subproblem defines profit maximization starting from day i to day n, with state variable j (number of baubles owned at day i), where decisions about buying or selling are made forward in time.

concepts.canonical_name: Prefix Subproblem Definition in Dynamic Programming
concepts.short_definition: The prefix subproblem defines profit maximization from day 1 through day i inclusive, with j baubles owned at the end of day i, considering previous states and transitions backward in time.

concepts.canonical_name: Buy and Sell Variable Transformation in DP
concepts.short_definition: Transforming the subproblem decision variable from owned baubles m to buy/sell quantity b or s, to which positive values indicate buying and negative values indicate selling, for ease of representation.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Dynamic Programming Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: An analysis showing the algorithm runs in O(nk^2) time due to O(nk) subproblems each solved via an O(k) maximization iteration.

concepts.canonical_name: Common Mistakes in Dynamic Programming Formulation
concepts.short_definition: Typical errors made when setting subproblems or recurrence, including vagueness about prefix vs suffix, incorrect limits, sign errors in buy/sell, and base case misalignment.
A dynamic programming algorithm to optimize bauble trading with storage and buying limits, solving for maximum profit with states X(i,j) representing max profit at day i with j baubles.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming (DP) Optimization via Data Structures
concepts.short_definition: Techniques to speed up naive DP algorithms by using data structures such as AVL trees, heaps, prefix max arrays, and binary search to achieve improved runtimes like O(nk log k) instead of O(nk^2).
Initialization of the DP for baselines such as unreachable states (e.g. X(0,j)=-∞) or free initial baubles by setting initial states to 0 for prefix subproblems.

concepts.canonical_name: Incorrect Greedy Assumptions in Bauble Trading
concepts.short_definition: Common false assumptions in greedy strategies for buy/sell decisions such as must buy/sell max quantities or waiting to sell at max future price, which do not hold true generally for optimal solutions.
Decomposition of the DP state value in terms of F(i,m) = X(i + 1, m) - p_i m, which separates computation allowing efficient max queries over ranges.

concepts.canonical_name: Range Query for Maximum in AVL Tree
concepts.short_definition: Performing a query on an AVL tree to find the maximum F(i, m) value for m within a specified range efficiently in O(log k) time.
Precomputing prefix maximum values in an array to answer range maximum queries on prefix segments in O(1) time instead of O(log k).

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Recurrence Computation Using Range Queries
concepts.short_definition: Computing values X(i,j) using dynamic programming where each value depends on range queries over previous results F(i,m).
Method to compute prefix max array A incrementally by setting A[0] = F(i, 0) and for t > 0, setting A[t] = max{A[t−1], F(i, t)} in increasing order of t.

concepts.canonical_name: Use of Max-Heap in Algorithm Optimization
concepts.short_definition: Maintaining a max-heap data structure to store and retrieve maximum values efficiently as part of an algorithm's computation.
The process of setting initial values for the function F(i, m) over a range of m, typically to prepare for further computation or algorithmic steps.
A method using heap data structures to optimize dynamic programming by maintaining a priority queue of values to efficiently compute maximums over ranges.
An optimization that replaces a heap by storing a single running maximum value to achieve O(1) time queries instead of O(log k).
Analysis of algorithm runtime where the operations per iteration and nested loops determine total runtime, e.g., O(nk log k).
In a dynamic programming algorithm, the value of a subproblem F(i, m) depends only on subproblems with greater indices i, and these dependencies govern the order of computation.

concepts.canonical_name: Initialization of Optimal Value in Dynamic Programming
concepts.short_definition: The process of initializing the optimal function value F* as the maximum over the range of subproblem values F(i, m) for given indices, forming the basis for solution extraction.

concepts.canonical_name: Order of Subproblem Computation in Dynamic Programming
concepts.short_definition: Choosing an order (increasing or decreasing indices) in which subproblems are solved, which affects how elements are added or removed during the process.

concepts.canonical_name: Subproblem Result Removal in Dynamic Programming
concepts.short_definition: In the decreasing order computation of subproblems, after computing the current subproblem value X(i, j), the result for a future subproblem F(i, j + l) can be removed from the working set Hi.
A symmetric matrix A such that for any vector x, x^T A x >= 0 holds.
A theorem that guarantees a continuous symmetric positive semidefinite kernel corresponds to an inner product in some feature space.
An iterative optimization algorithm to minimize a function by moving in the direction of the negative gradient.
A method to decompose the expected prediction error of a model into bias, variance, and irreducible error components.
An algorithmic technique using two pointers moving through a data structure to achieve efficient computations, often linear time.
The computational time order for the described algorithm, showing that time is proportional to the product of n and k.

concepts.canonical_name: Definition of delta functions δX(i,m) and δF(i,m)
concepts.short_definition: Discrete difference functions defined as δX(i,m) = X(i,m+1) − X(i,m) and δF(i,m) = F(i,m+1) − F(i,m) to study variations of X and F over increments m.
The function δF(i,m) can be expressed as δX(i+1,m) minus p_i, highlighting their mathematical dependency.
Lemma stating that for any fixed i, the sequence δX(i,m) is non-increasing as m increases.
Proposition establishing that for any i, δF(i,m) is non-increasing in m, using the monotonicity of δX(i+1,m).

concepts.canonical_name: Existence of a turning point m* for F(i,m)
concepts.short_definition: Corollary that there exists an m* in [0, k] such that F(i,m) increases when m ≤ m* and decreases when m ≥ m*.

concepts.canonical_name: Binary search to find maximum F*
concepts.short_definition: Using the monotonicity properties, a binary search can efficiently find the maximum value F* = max_m {F(i,m) | 0 ≤ m ≤ min(k, j + l)} in O(log k) time.
The process of computing an array ∆F composed of elements δF(i, j) for j from 0 to k−1 as part of a computational task.
The property and behavior analysis of the sum of an increasing function and a decreasing function, especially that their sum need not be monotonic (first increasing then decreasing).
The method of computing values X(i, j) using a recurrence relation involving minimizing an index m* j such that a certain condition holds, to optimize computation.
Incorrect reasoning that the sum of an increasing and a decreasing function is monotonic, illustrated by counterexamples and contrast with cases involving max functions.
The property that the function F(i,m) first increases and then decreases with m, implied by Lemma 1 stating X(i+1,m) is concave and -pim is convex or linear.

concepts.canonical_name: Binary Search for Value B over A
concepts.short_definition: A method of searching by iteratively narrowing down the search space over a set A to find a value B.
An optimization technique that improves upon binary search by scanning a global turning point m* over the function ΔF and adjusting per query range, reducing runtime complexity.
