The property that the function X(i+1,m) is concave, which justifies the structure of the problem and related corollaries.
The property that the function -pim is convex or linear, contributing to analysis in the problem.

A correct greedy algorithm running in O(nk2) time naïvely, optimizing to O(nk log k) or O(nk), using a data structure A to keep track of effective value of baubles in storage and running sum S for profit.
The operation of replacing each element v in a vector with a threshold value pi if v is less than pi, and incrementing a sum S by the amount pi - v for each replacement.
Removing a specified number of the largest entries in a vector when its size exceeds a threshold defined by parameters k and l.
A representation of buying and selling baubles at specific days based on their values and replacements, with profit calculated from price differences.
A restriction ensuring that the number of baubles bought on any given day does not exceed a specified limit l, interpreted in the algorithm by counting only the l copies added in a specific step.
A limitation ensuring that the set A of baubles never exceeds size k, enforced by selling excess baubles in Step 2 within the algorithm.
The process of updating set A by replacing elements based on price changes to maximize profit, each update incrementing the profit sum S.
The process of removing excess baubles from set A to maintain its size constraint by selling them to realize actual transactions.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm Step 3: Buying l Copies of pi
concepts.short_definition: Adding l copies of the price pi to set A to represent the new baubles bought on day i, as the only actual purchases to satisfy buying limits.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Bauble Trading Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The computational complexity of the given algorithm steps, varying by data structure implementation from O(nkl) to O(nk log k) to O(nk).

concepts.canonical_name: Efficient Data Structures for Bauble Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: Use of data structures such as AVL BSTs, max-heaps, or sorted linked lists to optimize the runtime of the bauble trading algorithm.
The technique of scanning an array sequentially from the start using a pointer to perform updates until a condition is met.
The condition used to stop scanning the array, specifically when the first element v is greater than or equal to a threshold pi.
The operation of removing elements from a set or sequence, especially removing elements from the end based on a size comparison with another parameter.
Performing value insertions at specified positions in a data structure, taking O(k) time per operation, for a total of O(nk) time complexity.
Constraint limiting the number of transactions or elements (l) that can be processed or selected on a particular day i in an algorithm.

concepts.canonical_name: Correct Replacement of Values in Data Structures
concepts.short_definition: Replacing values v with pi in data structures carefully to avoid losing opportunities for future higher profits, particularly ensuring correct frequency counts.
When removing elements from a data structure as part of an algorithm, removing the largest entries instead of the smallest to maintain correct logic.

concepts.canonical_name: Computing Profit in Buy/Sell Decision Problems
concepts.short_definition: The calculation of total profit S from buy/sell decisions, which can be non-trivial when data structure operations do not directly correspond to buy/sell actions.

concepts.canonical_name: Use of AVL Set as Multiset with Frequency Tracking
concepts.short_definition: Using an AVL Set data structure that supports multiple identical items by explicitly tracking frequencies or using a multiset variant, to satisfy problem requirements.

An iterative algorithm that constructs a solution by maintaining partial schedules of changes in bauble quantities per day and baubles stored, choosing optimal days to buy and sell to maximize profit, examined in permuted orders to improve efficiency.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity Optimization Techniques for Greedy Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: Techniques to reduce the algorithmic run-time from naive O(n^3) to O(n^2 log n), O(n^2), or O(nk) by managing order of examination of days and subproblems in a greedy strategy.
A partial schedule includes δi representing change in baubles bought or sold on day i and ki representing baubles in storage at end of day i.
A permutation σi or σj(i) of days specifying the order in which days or subproblems are examined within the greedy algorithm to improve efficiency.
The problem of determining the maximum profit achievable by buying and selling stocks given their prices on different days.

The principle that when comparing stock prices on two different days i and j, if the price on day j is greater than or equal to the price on day i, buying on day j and selling on day i cannot yield a positive profit and thus can be skipped.
The maximum number of baubles that can still be bought on a given day j without exceeding the daily purchase limit l.
The maximum number of baubles that can still be bought on day j and sold on day i without exceeding the storage limit k baubles on any intermediate day t between j and i.

The concept of slack in trading constraints refers to the maximum feasible number of items (baubles) that can still be transacted on a given day without violating any imposed trading constraints, formulated as s(j) = min{f(j), g(j)} for day j.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm for Bauble Trading Profit Maximization
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm to compute maximum profit from buying and selling 'baubles' with storage constraints, involving updating storage slack and orders over days i and j.
The idea of temporarily selling a bauble on day i and buying it back later on day j, used to handle cases where j > i in the bauble trading algorithm, affecting storage slack calculation.
Storage slack g(j) represents constraints on baubles stored during intermediate days, and is computed differently depending on whether 'bauble loan' is allowed.

concepts.canonical_name: Ordering of Indices i and j in Bauble Trading Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: Sets of valid orderings for indices i and j in the algorithm that produce correct solutions, varying whether 'bauble loan' is allowed and based on sorting orders (increasing/decreasing) of i, j, and prices.

concepts.canonical_name: Use of Balanced Binary Trees and Lazy Propagation in Algorithm Optimization
concepts.short_definition: Data structures like AVL sequences or segment trees and the technique lazy propagation are used to optimize computation of storage constraints and updates in the bauble trading algorithm.

concepts.canonical_name: Maintaining Running Maximum to Optimize Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: For the bauble trading algorithm with σj(i) decreasing in j, the max quantity K := max_{t=j}^{i-1} kt can be maintained explicitly as a running maximum allowing O(n^2) time optimization.
An algorithmic technique to efficiently update the running maximum K without explicitly updating all elements every time, by using a temporary sequence to record changes and then applying updates.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity Reduction from O(n^2) to O(nk)
concepts.short_definition: The observation that only a subset of values of j close to i need to be considered reduces the inner loop complexity, improving the original O(n^2) algorithm to O(nk).

concepts.canonical_name: Initialization of Sequence with Zero Values
concepts.short_definition: The process of setting all elements in a sequence d = {d1, ..., di} to zero.
Setting a variable K to zero as a starting point in an algorithm or procedure.
The minimal slack available for a given index j, defined as the minimum between purchase limit slack f(j) and storage slack g(j).

An iterative method adjusting values dj, K, and di based on calculated slack values s(j), where increments to dj and K are balanced against decrements to di, under specific conditions involving pi and pj values.
The set of indices j considered for iteration defined as σj(i) = {i −1, . . . , max(i −⌈k/l⌉, 1)}, iterated in decreasing order.
If the priority pj of index j is greater than or equal to the priority pi of index i, the iteration skips updating j.
Updating the maximum storage used, K, by setting it to the maximum between current K and kj if pj < pi.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy Algorithm for Buying and Selling Optimization
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that iterates over buying days and tries to maximize purchase by iterating over selling days, using permutations σj and σi(j) with specific ordering rules to find optimal buy-sell strategies under constraints such as storage and bauble loans.

concepts.canonical_name: Permutation Ordering in Greedy Buying-Selling Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: Specific orderings of permutations of buying days σj and selling days σi(j) that are necessary for correctness in greedy algorithms with or without 'bauble loans' in buying-selling optimization problems.

concepts.canonical_name: Use of Bauble Loan in Buying-Selling Greedy Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: A technique called 'bauble loan' that corrects past mistakes in greedy buying-selling algorithms, allowing for relaxed ordering of permutations and more correct solutions.
The process of computing slack variables to track constraints like storage capacity, crucial for correct algorithm design and runtime efficiency in buying-selling optimization.
The time complexity characteristics of various greedy algorithms for a specific problem, including naive and optimized implementations.
A technique to optimize range update and query operations in segment trees or balanced trees like AVL by postponing updates until necessary.
A variable used to accumulate or capture a cumulative total over time during an iterative process.
A sequence representing incremental changes (deltas) applied sequentially, such as daily changes in quantity.
An algorithm for determining optimal transactions of baubles over days to maximize profit, by setting target quantities and adjusting stock based on price comparisons.

concepts.canonical_name: Target Quantity Calculation in Greedy Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: Computation of the target quantity ti to hold at the end of day i based on future higher price day and buying limits.
Determining the target day j which is the next day after day i where the price is higher than price on day i.

concepts.canonical_name: Stock Adjustment Step in Greedy Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: Adjusting the current stock S by buying or selling δi baubles on day i to meet target quantities.

concepts.canonical_name: Informal Proof of Greedy Commodity Procurement Optimality
concepts.short_definition: An informal justification that the target quantities ti computed by the algorithm lead to an optimal profit under the buying limit constraints.
The total time complexity of executing two nested loops each iterating O(n) times results in O(n^2) runtime.
A query on an AVL Balanced Search Tree that returns all elements within a specified range, making use of the AVL tree properties to achieve efficient search.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Range Query on AVL BST
concepts.short_definition: The time complexity for performing a range query on an AVL BST is O(log n), enabling overall O(n log n) runtime for the algorithm steps that use it.
Method to reduce the search space by exploiting inequalities to limit the indices checked during algorithm execution.
A technique that involves maintaining a subset of data of fixed size that moves over a larger dataset.

concepts.canonical_name: Pre-processing with Stack for Next Higher Price Day
concepts.short_definition: A technique to pre-compute for each day i the next day j(i) after i with a strictly higher price, using a stack to maintain indices with strictly increasing prices top-to-bottom, enabling efficient lookup in O(n) time.
The approach of deciding on inventory stocking within a fixed-length future window (e.g., length k/l) for each day, affecting how supplies are allocated before target days with higher prices.

concepts.canonical_name: Common Mistake: Using Maximum Price Instead of Next Higher Price
concepts.short_definition: Incorrectly setting the target day j(i) as the day after i with maximum price rather than the first day after i with strictly higher price, leading to suboptimal stocking decisions.

concepts.canonical_name: Handling Insufficient Stocking Before Target Day
concepts.short_definition: Accounting for cases where it is impossible to stock up the needed k baubles before the target day because the daily stocking limit l is too small.

concepts.canonical_name: Stock Selling Strategy at Local Price Peaks
concepts.short_definition: The strategic decision to force selling of all baubles at local maximum price days, but not necessarily at global maxima, affecting profitability.
An array in which the elements are maintained in sorted order to allow efficient binary search and access to minimum and maximum elements.
An array structure allowing direct indexing of elements using keys, often using a large enough array to map all keys directly to indices.
The study and evaluation of the resource usage (time and space) of algorithms as functions of input size.
A method to determine strategies in a zero sum game scenario.
A computational problem involving selection criteria, likely requiring optimization or algorithmic analysis.
An algorithm that processes data structure operations focusing on popping the maximum element efficiently.
A problem scenario labeled 'A Fishy Conundrum' likely requiring problem solving skills and algorithm design.
A formal assessment covering the course material up to a certain point, used to evaluate student understanding.
A sorting algorithm based on the AVL tree data structure, maintaining balanced binary search trees during sorting.
When integers 1 through n are inserted into a binary search tree in ascending order, the resulting tree is skewed to one side (a degenerate tree).
A tree operation that changes the structure of an AVL tree to maintain its balance while preserving the inorder traversal.
The property that rotations in an AVL tree preserve the inorder traversal of the tree.
Additional information stored at nodes in AVL trees that may need to be updated after rotations, potentially requiring Ω(log n) time to restore.

concepts.canonical_name: Worst-Case Runtime Upper Bound from Amortized Runtime
concepts.short_definition: The concept that given amortized O(n) runtime over n operations, the worst-case runtime of a single operation can be as high as O(n^2).
Compute an array B where each element B[i] is the sum of all elements A[k] for k from 0 to i-1 in the input array A.

concepts.canonical_name: Linear Time Algorithm for Prefix Sum
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that computes the PREFIXSUM array B from input A in O(n) worst-case time by initializing B with zeros and then iterating through A once.

concepts.canonical_name: Asymptotic Optimality of Prefix Sum Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The property that any algorithm solving PREFIXSUM must take at least Θ(n) time because it produces Θ(n) output values, hence the linear time algorithm is asymptotically optimal.
Given an array A of n integers, find indices i < j such that the sum of elements from A[i] to A[j-1] is zero, or return ⊥ if no such pair exists.

concepts.canonical_name: Linear Time Algorithm for Zero Sum
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that solves the ZEROSUM problem in expected O(n) time using a PREFIXSUM computation and hash tables to detect duplicates corresponding to zero sums.
The computational problem of finding two elements in a list whose sum equals zero.
The incorrect idea or misuse involving applying sorting directly on a hash table structure that is inherently unordered.
The performance evaluation of algorithms considering average-case (expected) time versus worst-case time, emphasizing differences and assumptions made.
An algorithm technique that uses two indices (or pointers) to sweep through data with monotonic conditions to find a target efficiently.

concepts.canonical_name: Monotonicity Properties of f(i,j) = ψi^2 − ψj
concepts.short_definition: The function f increases with i and decreases with j, so it is monotone in the first argument and antimonotone in the second.
An assertion maintained throughout the execution ensuring for all pairs with indices less than current pointers, f(i',j') != T.

concepts.canonical_name: Worst-Case Linear Time Algorithm for Finding Pair with Given Difference
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that finds indices i,j such that ψi^2 − ψj = T or returns ⊥ in worst-case linear time using sorting and two-pointer technique.
An algorithm that systematically considers every possible candidate solution to guarantee finding a correct answer if it exists.
A stack of integers supporting additional operations PEEKMAX and POPMAX to access and remove the maximum element.
Operation of MAXSTACK that outputs the maximum value contained in the stack.
Operation of MAXSTACK that outputs and removes the maximum value m, along with all elements added after the most recent maximum instance.
Implementation of MAXSTACK using two linked list stacks A and B, where A holds all elements and B tracks maximum values.
Should return the top element of stack B to get the maximum value in constant time.
POPMAX can take O(n) time worst-case as it may need to pop up to n elements until the maximum is removed.

concepts.canonical_name: Amortized runtime of POPMAX using potential function Φ = c|A|
concepts.short_definition: Using the potential function proportional to the size of stack A, the amortized cost of POPMAX is O(1), despite worst case being O(n).
The change in potential related to the number of items popped during amortized analysis, not dependent on the size of the array A.
The process of resizing a dynamic array when it becomes full, typically involving copying to a larger array, impacting amortized time complexity.
The manipulation of big-O notation expressions, which does not support subtraction, e.g., O(n) − O(n) is not defined as O(1).
A function used in amortized analysis to measure the stored energy or potential in the data structure, facilitating the analysis of operation costs over a sequence.
A formal evaluation conducted to assess students' understanding and mastery of course content at the halfway point of the term.
An operation to toggle the activation status (active/inactive) of a tower with a given unique ID in O(log n) time.
The maximal count of consecutive inactive watchtowers in the data structure returned in O(1) time.
The longest prefix of a sequence during which no active events occur.
The length of the longest suffix of a string T that is inactive (e.g., does not participate in certain processing).

concepts.canonical_name: Longest Inactive Consecutive Subsequence in AVL Tree
concepts.short_definition: The length of the longest consecutive sequence of inactive nodes in the subtree of an AVL tree.

concepts.canonical_name: Prefix and Suffix Lengths of Inactive Nodes in Subtree
concepts.short_definition: p(T) is the length of the longest prefix of inactive nodes starting from the left of subtree T, s(T) is the length of the longest suffix of inactive nodes at the right of subtree T.
Operation that uses AVL FIND to locate a key and toggles its status from active to inactive or vice versa by negating the corresponding boolean value.

concepts.canonical_name: MAXINACTIVESEQ Query in AVL Augmented Tree
concepts.short_definition: Returns the length m augmentation at the AVL root representing the longest inactive consecutive subsequence in the entire tree.
Conditions required for a function to be a valid augmentation on an AVL tree: it must be a function of the subtree and computable in constant time.
A method of visiting all the nodes in a tree data structure systematically.
In a binary search tree, the predecessor of a node is the node with the next smallest key and the successor is the node with the next largest key.
A hash table collision resolution method where each bucket points to a chain (usually a linked list or tree) of entries that hash to the same value.
A binary tree property where the height difference between left and right subtrees of any node is at most one, ensuring the tree is balanced for efficient operations.

concepts.canonical_name: Rotation Count to Transform AVL Tree to BST
concepts.short_definition: The number of rotations required to convert an AVL tree into a binary search tree with the same nodes.
An algorithmic approach describing whether inserting each element from a linked list individually into a heap is asymptotically optimal for building the heap.
The computational problem of finding the union of multiple closed intervals and expressing it as a union of disjoint closed intervals.
An algorithm to merge overlapping or contiguous intervals into disjoint intervals representing their union.

concepts.canonical_name: Linear Time Interval Union Algorithm for Integer Start Times
concepts.short_definition: An O(n) time algorithm to compute the union of intervals when each interval start time is an integer, exploiting the discrete, bounded nature of the time domain.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm for Scheduling with Interval Constraints
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that solves scheduling problems where each interval has length greater than one, aiming for an O(n) time solution.

concepts.canonical_name: Interval Length Greater Than One Constraint
concepts.short_definition: A condition in scheduling problems where each friend will play for more than one hour, i.e. bi - ai > 1, with ai not necessarily integer.
Given an array A of n integers, count how many 4-tuples of indices (w,x,y,z) satisfy A[w] + A[x] + A[y] + A[z] = 0, where indices are not necessarily distinct.
An algorithm with worst-case, amortized, or expected O(n^2) time complexity that counts the number of 4-tuples (w,x,y,z) satisfying A[w]+A[x]+A[y]+A[z]=0.
A property of a heap data structure where each parent node is less than or equal to its child nodes, ensuring the minimum element is at the root.
The concept that if an array satisfies the min-heap property and its reverse satisfies the max-heap property, then the array is sorted.
The operations insert, find, and delete on a data structure that stores unique items.

concepts.canonical_name: Most Recent Access Tracking in Data Structures
concepts.short_definition: Techniques to track and retrieve the most recently accessed element in a data structure efficiently.

concepts.canonical_name: Range Query on Augmented Search Tree
concepts.short_definition: Querying for information (e.g., most recent access) limited to keys within a specified range, implemented in logarithmic time in a balanced search tree.

concepts.canonical_name: Maintaining Augmented Data in Tree Subtrees
concepts.short_definition: Storing and correctly updating augmented information (like recent()) in each subtree to enable fast queries.
An algorithmic operation whose execution time does not depend on the size of the input; it takes a fixed amount of time.

concepts.canonical_name: Finding the Closest Pair by Absolute Difference
concepts.short_definition: The problem of identifying two items in a set whose IDs have the smallest positive absolute difference.

concepts.canonical_name: Hash table chaining with AVL trees
concepts.short_definition: A hash table using AVL balanced binary search trees for collision resolution chaining, instead of linked lists.

concepts.canonical_name: Worst-case Runtime of Hash Table Operations under SUHA
concepts.short_definition: The asymptotic worst-case time complexity for common operations (insert, delete, search) on a hash table assuming Simple Uniform Hashing Assumption (SUHA).
An algorithm for building a heap data structure from a list that has the best possible asymptotic runtime complexity.
A characterization of when an array represents a valid max-heap, where every parent node is greater than or equal to its children.
The process of computing the union of multiple closed intervals as a union of disjoint closed intervals.
A sorting and merging approach for intervals that sorts intervals by start time, discards smaller overlapping intervals, and merges overlapping intervals to form disjoint intervals.
The process of replacing any two overlapping intervals with a single merged interval that spans their combined time range.
Analysis of the maximum time an algorithm requires to run under any input of size n, e.g., worst-case Θ(n) for counting sort in this problem.
A recursive algorithm dividing the interval list into halves, solving each half, then merging the resulting intervals until none overlap.
A proof technique to show the algorithm produces the correct output for all inputs by establishing base cases and inductive steps.
A property maintained throughout the execution of the interval merging algorithm: S is a set of disjoint intervals and its union equals the union of intervals processed so far.
A counting principle stating that if n items are put into m containers, with n > m, then at least one container must contain more than one item.
A method of solving a problem by transforming it into an instance of another problem that is already solved or easier to solve.

A floating point number is represented as a  9 b where a and b are integers, with length proportional to log(1+|ab|), and can be represented in a single machine word if ab is polynomial in input size.
A practice exam mimicking the format and content of a midterm exam for preparation purposes.
A data structure that stores pairs (key, value), where the key represents a sum and the value the count of pairs of indices whose elements sum to the key.
An algorithm that counts the number of 4-tuples summing to zero in expected Θ(n^2) time using a hash set to count sums of pairs and then summing products of counts for pairs summing to k and -k.

concepts.canonical_name: Expected Amortized Runtime of Hash Table Insertion and Lookup
concepts.short_definition: Insertion and lookup operations in a hash table with constant load factor take expected constant time amortized, Θ(1).

concepts.canonical_name: Counting pairs summing to k and -k
concepts.short_definition: For each sum k, count the number of pairs of indices whose elements sum to k and multiply that count by the number of pairs summing to -k to find partial contributions to #4SUM.
An example that disproves a claimed statement or hypothesis.
A balanced binary search tree data structure (AVL tree) used to implement a set keyed by unique IDs, supporting insert, find, and delete operations.

concepts.canonical_name: Cross-linked Doubly-Linked List in AVL Tree Nodes
concepts.short_definition: Maintaining a doubly-linked list of tree nodes sorted by access time, where each tree node also has pointers to its neighbors in the list, to support O(1) retrieval of most recently accessed element.

concepts.canonical_name: recent() operation in augmented AVL tree
concepts.short_definition: Operation that returns in O(1) time the bird most recently accessed (via insert or find), using either augmentation or cross-linked list methods.

concepts.canonical_name: recent-up-to(max) operation in augmented AVL tree
concepts.short_definition: Operation that returns in O(log n) time the bird most recently accessed among those with IDs ≤ max using recursive or iterative methods making use of subtree augmentations.
Enhancing a binary search tree node to store the minimum ID value in its subtree to facilitate efficient queries.
A method that performs a query by recursively traversing a tree based on defined conditions to find a target element.

concepts.canonical_name: Closest Pair of Values in a Binary Search Tree
concepts.short_definition: The pair of elements in a BST whose IDs have the smallest positive absolute difference.

concepts.canonical_name: Auxiliary Tree Method for Closest Pair
concepts.short_definition: An approach using a second AVL tree storing pairs of adjacent birds in traversal order, keyed lex order by difference and ID, to efficiently maintain the closest pair.

concepts.canonical_name: Cross-linked Doubly Linked List in BST
concepts.short_definition: Maintaining a doubly linked list reflecting the in-order traversal of a BST, cross-linking nodes for constant time predecessor and successor access.

concepts.canonical_name: In-order Predecessor and Successor in BST
concepts.short_definition: The previous and next nodes in the in-order traversal sequence of a binary search tree.

concepts.canonical_name: Augmentation Maintenance during Insertion and Deletion
concepts.short_definition: Updating augmented information in BST nodes efficiently when insertions or deletions happen.

concepts.canonical_name: Common Mistakes in Implementing Closest Pair Augmentations
concepts.short_definition: Frequent errors when augmenting BST or related data structures to find the closest pair, like misinterpreting predecessors/successors or ignoring root cases.

concepts.canonical_name: Conceptual Understanding of Midterm Practice Problems
concepts.short_definition: The ability to correctly interpret and apply concepts tested by the Midterm 1 practice problems.
Defining a recursive algorithm by specifying its base case and recursive cases, assuming the function works on smaller inputs without redefining it repeatedly.
The condition under which a recursive function returns a direct answer without further recursive calls, preventing infinite recursion.
The part of a recursive function where it calls itself with a smaller or simpler input to solve the problem.
The justification that a recursive function works on smaller inputs, similar to induction, allowing its use in recursive definitions.
Repeating or rewriting already defined algorithms unnecessarily, reducing clarity and concision and potentially losing points.
A method commonly used for solving algorithmic problems, referenced as an example of algorithms students rewrote unnecessarily.
An algorithmic approach involving augmenting data structures or solutions, mentioned as an example of algorithms unnecessarily rewritten.
Conditions required for COUNTING-SORT to work correctly: keys must be natural numbers and bounded by O(n) for linear runtime.
Conditions required for DAA-SORT to work correctly: keys must be natural numbers and bounded by O(n); additionally keys must be distinct to avoid loss of duplicates.
Conditions required for TUPLE-SORT: auxiliary sorting algorithms must be specified and all their preconditions must be satisfied; otherwise a general comparison sort is assumed.
Conditions required for RADIX-SORT to work correctly: keys must be natural numbers and bounded by n^{O(1)} to achieve linear runtime.

concepts.canonical_name: Set of Items Keyed by a Key
concepts.short_definition: A set S containing items of type X, where each item is associated with an intrinsic key k that uniquely identifies it, and all items and their keys are distinct in S.
When the key k is not specified for a set S of type X items, the key is assumed to be the identity function, meaning the key of x is x itself.

concepts.canonical_name: Set as a Mapping from X to Y
concepts.short_definition: The concept that a set S can be considered as a set of (X,Y) pairs keyed by X, representing mappings between X and Y.

concepts.canonical_name: Function as a Set of Ordered Pairs
concepts.short_definition: A partial function can be mathematically represented as a set of ordered pairs with certain properties.

concepts.canonical_name: Total Function Waste in Set Representation
concepts.short_definition: Representing a total function x↦x.y as a set S that does nothing but waste time and space by definition.

concepts.canonical_name: Useful Set Representation of a Function
concepts.short_definition: A set representing a (partial) function such as x.y 7→x can be useful, implying nontrivial mappings with practical value.
A collection data structure similar to a set but allows duplicate keys, where find may output any item with the given key.

concepts.canonical_name: Hash Table Limitations in Multi-set Context
concepts.short_definition: Hash tables rely fundamentally on distinct keys, so they do not support multi-set behavior well because repeated keys cause collisions affecting expected runtime.
When repeated keys are stored in a hash table (as in a multi-set), collision handling replaces multiple find operations and can degrade performance making the expected runtime analysis invalid.
A property of binary trees where in-order traversal yields the keys in sorted order.
A binary tree that satisfies both Heap Properties or one Heap Property and the Binary Search Property, indicating some form of degeneracy.
The average time an operation takes with respect to a probability distribution on inputs or random choices.
Abstract data type supporting LIFO push and pop operations.
Abstract data type supporting FIFO enqueue and dequeue operations.

concepts.canonical_name: Lower Bound on Stack Implementation Using One Queue
concepts.short_definition: At least one of PUSH or POP operations must take worst-case Omega(n) time when implementing a stack with one queue using only enqueue and dequeue.
A function that is either entirely non-increasing or non-decreasing.
The time complexity of sorting an array of tuples lexicographically, where each tuple has length log log n and each integer in the tuple is bounded.
Techniques that can decrease the number of collisions in a hash table through changes in size or hash function.
Properties of a binary search tree after inserting elements in a certain order, including ancestor relationships, subtree positions, depth comparisons, and leaf nodes.
Possible positions of the third smallest element in a 1-indexed min-heap of distinct elements, considering heap properties.

concepts.canonical_name: Maximum Length List of Unique Ingredient Sets
concepts.short_definition: A longest list of recipes such that no two recipes share the same set of ingredients.
A problem where given an array A of length n ≥ 2 such that A[0] ≤ 0 and A[n−1] ≥ 0, the goal is to find an index i such that A[i] × A[i+1] ≤ 0.
The conditions A[0] ≤ 0 and A[n−1] ≥ 0 on the input array ensuring there exists an index i with A[i]×A[i+1] ≤0.

concepts.canonical_name: Existence of Correct Output in IVT Problem
concepts.short_definition: The property that under the given preconditions, there exists at least one index i such that A[i] × A[i+1] ≤0.
An algorithm designed to find a root or fixed point of a continuous function, leveraging the Intermediate Value Theorem.
A theoretical minimum (using Big Omega notation) on the runtime complexity that any correct algorithm solving a given problem must have in the worst case.
The set of topics and skills necessary to successfully complete the midterm exam 6.1210 Midterm 1.
A data structure that supports insertion of elements with values and IDs, and can return the median of their values in constant time, with efficient construction from sorted input.

concepts.canonical_name: Median of a Set (Even and Odd Cases)
concepts.short_definition: The median is the middle value of a sorted list, or for an even number of elements, the average of the two middle values.
The requirement that INSERT operation should take O(log n) time where n is the number of hats.
The GETMEDIAN operation should return the median excitingness in constant time O(1).
The BUILD operation should create the data structure from a sorted array of hats in linear time O(n).
A formal argument demonstrating the data structure and its operations correctly maintain and return the median.
Classification and analysis of the time complexity of each operation under various conditions.
An operation on a sequence that outputs the maximum sum over all prefixes of the sequence.
The process of adding additional data fields to tree nodes to enable efficient queries beyond the basic operations.
An augmentation is valid if its stored information can be correctly computed from the augmented information of a node's children and the node itself, maintaining correctness during dynamic updates.
Guidelines and rules to follow during the exam, such as what materials are allowed, rules on communication, and submission guidelines.
A function that asymptotically bounds another function above, denoted O(f(n)).
Sorting an array of tuples of integers according to the lex ordering of the tuples.

concepts.canonical_name: Hash Functions and Table Size Effects on Collisions
concepts.short_definition: Effects of changing hash functions and hash table sizes on collision counts.
Position relations of the smallest elements in a min-heap with distinct elements.
The categorization of an algorithm's running time into worst-case, expected, and amortized time complexity.
Ordering the elements of a recipe in a sorted sequence for consistent representation and comparison.

concepts.canonical_name: Keying a Recipe with a Sorted Tuple
concepts.short_definition: Using the sorted tuple of a recipe's ingredients or elements as a unique key to identify or store the recipe.
Representation of numbers in a positional numeral system with base n, where each digit's value is between 0 and n-1, and the whole number is interpreted accordingly.
The process of arranging the ingredients within a recipe in a consistent order, often as a preprocessing step before sorting recipes.

concepts.canonical_name: Iterating Over Sorted List to Remove Duplicates
concepts.short_definition: The process of traversing a sorted collection and outputting the first element and every element whose key differs from its predecessor to ensure unique output.
An algorithm's time complexity that grows linearly with the input size in the worst-case scenario.
A method of assigning a fixed-size value (hash) to data which can be used for efficient lookup or sorting.
The process of arranging the elements of a tuple in a sorted order, typically ascending.
A data structure that stores unique elements and allows efficient insertion, deletion, and membership testing.
A unique identifier used as the key to categorize or index recipes based on their ingredients.
The problem of detecting and filtering out duplicate entries in a collection based on a defined equality criterion.

concepts.canonical_name: Canonical Representation of a Small Set
concepts.short_definition: A standardized form of representing a small set, such as a sorted array or tuple, to enable comparison and hashing.
A data structure that allows expected amortized O(1) insertions and supports detecting duplicates by checking membership during insertion.
The idea that sorting a fixed small number of elements (e.g., 5) can be done in constant time, contributing to linear runtime over all recipes.

concepts.canonical_name: Hashing of Recipes in Algorithm Design
concepts.short_definition: Using hash functions to represent and distinguish recipes or ingredient sets in algorithmic problems.

concepts.canonical_name: Distinctness of Ingredient Sets vs. Disjointness
concepts.short_definition: The difference between recipes having distinct ingredients and recipes having non-overlapping (disjoint) ingredient sets, relevant to hashing and set comparison.

concepts.canonical_name: Use of Disjoint-Addressing Arrays (DAA) in Recipe Sorting
concepts.short_definition: Employing a disjoint-addressing array technique to sort or manage recipes by ingredient or recipe ID, and common inefficiencies in this approach.
An assessment instrument testing knowledge of multiple concepts in a course, typically with various questions covering the material.
If an array A satisfies A[0] ≤ 0 and A[n-1] ≥ 0, then there exists at least one index i such that A[i] × A[i + 1] ≤ 0.

concepts.canonical_name: Direct construction proof of discrete IVT
concepts.short_definition: A proof method that finds the first index k where A[k]≥0 and shows the product condition holds at indices k-1 and k or at 0 and 1 if k=0.
A proof by induction on the length of the array demonstrating the existence of an index i where the product condition holds.
A proof by contradiction assuming all adjacent products are positive, which contradicts the precondition.

concepts.canonical_name: Non-constructive algebraic proof of discrete IVT
concepts.short_definition: A proof using product of all adjacent terms and properties of the product to show existence of a non-positive product.

concepts.canonical_name: Brute force search solution for discrete IVT
concepts.short_definition: An approach that checks each adjacent pair for the product condition, analogous to the continuous Intermediate Value Theorem.

concepts.canonical_name: Induction base case for arrays of length 2
concepts.short_definition: A base case showing for an array of length 2 with A[0] ≤0 ≤ A[1], the product condition holds.
The smallest index k in array A such that A[k] ≥ 0, used as a pivot in the direct proof.
The solutions to a quadratic equation derived using the quadratic formula.
A formula to find the roots of any quadratic equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
The expression b^2 - 4ac which determines the nature and number of roots of a quadratic equation.
A method to solve quadratic equations by rewriting into a perfect square form.
A polynomial equation of degree two in the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0, where a, b, and c are constants and a ≠ 0.

concepts.canonical_name: Divide and Conquer Algorithm for IVT Problem
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that solves the IVT problem by recursively splitting the array and selecting the correct half to recurse on, achieving O(log n) runtime.

concepts.canonical_name: Correctness Proof of Divide and Conquer IVT Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: Demonstrating that the divide and conquer algorithm correctly finds an index that satisfies the IVT problem by maintaining the precondition invariants on subarrays.
Analyzing the runtime of the divide and conquer algorithm via the recurrence T(n) ≤ T(2n/3) + O(1) to show O(log n) runtime.

concepts.canonical_name: Base Case Importance in Divide and Conquer Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: The necessity of including and correctly handling the base case in recursive divide and conquer algorithms to ensure correctness.

concepts.canonical_name: Intermediate Value Theorem Algorithm Lower Bound
concepts.short_definition: Theoretical lower bound on worst-case runtime for any correct algorithm solving the Intermediate Value Theorem problem, proven to be Ω(log n).

concepts.canonical_name: Binary Input Restriction in Decision Tree Model
concepts.short_definition: Restricting inputs to binary values restricts the branching factor in decision trees, ensuring every algorithm can be treated as a comparison algorithm.
The argument that decision trees require at least Ω(log n) comparisons given Ω(n) possible outputs, establishing lower bounds for algorithms in the comparison model.

concepts.canonical_name: Data Structure for Dynamic Median Finding
concepts.short_definition: A data structure supporting insertion of elements and retrieval of the median in O(log n) and O(1) time respectively, using two heaps to maintain halves of the dataset.

concepts.canonical_name: INSERT Operation on Median Data Structure
concepts.short_definition: Add a new element or replace an existing element with the same ID in the dynamic median data structure, adjusting the heaps to maintain balance with O(log n) complexity.

concepts.canonical_name: GETMEDIAN Operation on Median Data Structure
concepts.short_definition: Retrieve the median of the current set of elements in constant time by examining the top elements of two balanced heaps.

concepts.canonical_name: BUILD Operation on Median Data Structure
concepts.short_definition: Construct a median data structure in linear time from a sorted array of elements and their median, initializing two balanced heaps accordingly.
A halfspace is one side of a hyperplane dividing a space into two parts, defined as H+ (positive side) or H− (negative side).
The number of elements or points contained within a halfspace, denoted as |H+| or |H−|.
The operator e applied to an element of a halfspace, such as e(min H+) or e(max H−), representing an evaluation or value derived from that element.

concepts.canonical_name: Outputting the average of two values
concepts.short_definition: Computing the numerical average of two numerical values, such as e(min H+) and e(max H−), to produce a result.
The process of verifying the sizes of two heaps to determine a condition or property.
The procedure of examining the roots of heaps to ensure correctness or satisfy some condition.
The process of rearranging elements of a matrix A according to a specific pattern or rule, such as in the Nesting Boxes problem with a pivot index m.
A chosen index m used to pivot or rearrange a matrix or data structure to facilitate solving problems like Nesting Boxes.
A property of a heap data structure where each parent node is ordered with respect to its child nodes according to a specific criterion (e.g., min-heap or max-heap).
Constraints on the number of elements or structural balance maintained by heap data structures during operations.
The process of constructing a heap (H− or H+) from a subset of elements (like half of set A) with worst-case linear time complexity.
An insertion method that uses a hash set I keyed by ID to track elements ('hats'), storing their heap and index information to achieve efficient amortized expected constant time for heap operations.
The operation of retrieving the median element from heaps with worst-case constant runtime.
An average-case time complexity per operation, where amortized over sequences of operations, the expected time is constant.
The procedure of deleting an element from a heap data structure by specifying its index, effectively removing it as if it were the root and then restoring heap properties.
Partitioning a hypothesis set into two subsets H+ and H− based on a threshold condition h < min H+.
An algorithmic step to restore the balance between two heaps by deleting the minimum from the larger heap and adding it to the smaller heap.
An algorithmic step to remove duplicate elements from heaps to maintain data integrity.
An algorithmic step to enforce an ordering property between elements of two heaps.

concepts.canonical_name: Amortized Time Complexity of Heap Operations
concepts.short_definition: The analysis showing that a bounded number of heap operations leads to an amortized expected time of O(log n).
A method of maintaining the median of a dataset dynamically using a min-heap and max-heap on either side of the median.
Using a hash set to allow constant time lookup and insertion of elements also stored in heaps to support efficient dynamic operations.
The asymptotic time complexity of constructing the data structure for this problem, ideally O(n) or O(n log n).
The time complexity of inserting a new element in the data structure, ideally O(log n) amortized or worst-case.
Techniques for managing elements with the same key values in data structures to avoid errors and maintain correctness.
A data structure augmentation storing the median value to speed median retrieval.
The selection of the root node in an AVL tree is not necessarily the median element; the root is chosen to maintain AVL balance properties, but need not correspond to the median key.

concepts.canonical_name: Augmentation of AVL tree for prefix maximum sum
concepts.short_definition: A technique of augmenting AVL tree nodes with additional information to support quick computation of maximum prefix sums.
An augmentation that can be maintained during all standard AVL tree operations (rotations, insertions, deletions) without violating correctness or balance.

concepts.canonical_name: Largest Prefix Sum in a Binary Tree Subtree
concepts.short_definition: The largest sum of values of any prefix in the subtree T, considering the sequence of nodes in order.

concepts.canonical_name: Tree Augmentation for Prefix Sum and Other Values
concepts.short_definition: Augmentation of tree nodes with additional information such as subtree sum and largest prefix sum to enable constant-time query operations.
Computing output directly and immediately without any optimization techniques.

concepts.canonical_name: Augmented Data Structure for Prefix Queries
concepts.short_definition: A data structure augmented with additional information to compute prefix-based queries efficiently during dynamic operations.
A recursive formula that computes prefix maxima by partitioning prefixes of left and right subtrees and combining results using associativity and distributivity.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Θ(|S|²) and Θ(|S|) Prefix Computations
concepts.short_definition: The original prefix computation requires Θ(|S|²) time, which can be optimized to Θ(|S|), but no faster without augmentation.

concepts.canonical_name: Sum Augmentation for Constant Time Summation
concepts.short_definition: An augmentation tracking subtree sums to enable constant time computation of prefix sums in recursive formulas.
The formula used to update a node's augmentation value based on its own value and its children's augmentations to maintain correctness after modifications.
Maintaining augmentations in constant time during updates such as rotations or insert/delete operations in trees.
Augmentations that incorrectly depend on information like node indices, prefix sums outside of subtree scope, or child's left subtree sums, which break augmentation correctness and maintenance.

concepts.canonical_name: Limitations of Leaf-based Base Case in Augmentations
concepts.short_definition: Why using a leaf as the base case in augmentations is problematic due to excluding empty sequences and complicating maintenance.

concepts.canonical_name: Avoiding Storage of Child-only Subtree Information in Nodes
concepts.short_definition: Best practice to avoid storing information specific only to a particular child’s subtree in a node to prevent storage waste, maintenance complexity, and correctness issues.
The study of describing the limiting behavior of a function, such as an algorithm's running time, using big-O, Theta, and Omega notations.
Analysis technique yielding amortized time guarantees for sequences of operations.
Analysis technique for expected time bounds using probabilistic arguments.
The worst-case time complexity to find a value in a sorted linked list is linear Θ(n), as linked lists lack random access.
An array A is pear-shaped if for every index i, A[i] ≤ A[i + 1210].
Algorithmic complexity for searching whether a value x is contained in a pear-shaped array A of length n.
Procedure to insert a new element into a heap while maintaining the heap property by placing the element at the end and then 'bubbling' it up.
The behavior and ordering of enqueue and dequeue operations on a queue data structure.
The behavior and ordering of push and pop operations on a stack data structure.
Data structures used for chaining in hash tables that influence the worst-case runtime of insert, delete, and find operations.

concepts.canonical_name: Linked List in Hash Table Chaining
concepts.short_definition: Using a linked list as the chaining data structure in a hash table, involving pointer-based sequences of elements.

concepts.canonical_name: Sorted Dynamic Array in Hash Table Chaining
concepts.short_definition: Using a sorted dynamic array as the chaining structure in a hash table to store elements in order.
Using a heap data structure as chaining in a hash table.
The process of devising a step-by-step procedure to solve a given computational problem.
Arithmetic involving integers where numbers wrap around upon reaching a certain value, called the modulus.
Data structures consisting of a collection of elements identified by index, storing integer values.
Selecting two different indices i and j from an array that meet a specified property.

concepts.canonical_name: Pairing of Elements with a Given Sum
concepts.short_definition: The problem of grouping elements (Pokémon auras) into pairs such that the sum of each pair equals a given value σ, with possibly one element left unpaired.

concepts.canonical_name: Linear Time Algorithm for Finding Unpaired Element
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm running in worst-case O(n) time to find the element that is not paired when the rest can be partitioned into pairs summing to σ.
Dividing a set of 2n + 1 elements into n pairs according to some pairing scheme σ, with one element left unpaired.
A collection of elements identified by index, used here to represent Pokémon auras.
The problem of finding the single unpaired element in a collection where all other elements are paired.

A data structure that supports efficient addition, deletion, and query operations on intervals, specifically enabling placement and removal of intervals and checking whether a point lies within any current intervals.
An operation that adds a given interval (Lucky Egg) to the data structure.
An operation that removes a given interval (Lucky Egg) from the data structure.
An operation that queries whether a given point (Pokémon location) is currently covered by any Lucky Egg in the data structure, returning TRUE if so.
A restricted scenario where all intervals have the form (a, a + d) for some fixed d, enabling data structures and algorithms that do not depend on d for runtime or space complexity.
Structural characteristics and format of the midterm exam.

concepts.canonical_name: Data Structure Design for Max Sum Selection
concepts.short_definition: Designing a data structure to maintain a set of athletes each with pistol and fencing ratings to support efficient updates and queries for selecting four distinct athletes maximizing the sum of two pistol ratings and two fencing ratings.
An operation to initialize a data structure from an array of elements in O(n) time.
An operation updating an element's ratings in a data structure, overwriting if existing, in O(log n) time.
An operation to output the four distinct student IDs maximizing the sum of pistol and fencing ratings in O(1) time.
Analyzing and classifying runtimes as worst-case, expected, and/or amortized, with runtime justifications.
Derivation of an analytical upper limit on the time complexity of an algorithm.
Techniques for selecting and answering easier versions of problems to receive partial credit.
Approach to managing available exam time to maximize score by first tackling problems with greatest progress potential.
Process of checking whether a value is present by examining each node sequentially in a linked list data structure.
The runtime complexity to decide whether a value is contained in a pear-shaped array, which is Θ(log n).
Classes that describe the upper and lower bounds of algorithmic growth rates, such as Big O, Big Omega, and Theta notation.
A technique for solving recurrences by representing the recursive calls as a tree and summing the work done at each level.
An upper limit on the growth rate of a function, describing the worst-case time complexity.
The process of moving an inserted element upwards in the heap by swapping it with its parent as long as it violates the heap property.

concepts.canonical_name: Valid Insert Positions in a Heap
concepts.short_definition: The possible positions where an inserted element can reside or move up to during heap insertion, constrained by the heap structure and swap rules.
The process of adding a new element to a heap data structure, starting at a specific index and maintaining the heap property by heapifying the inserted element.
The process of adjusting the heap to maintain the heap property after insertion or deletion, by comparing and swapping elements recursively as needed.

concepts.canonical_name: Order of Dequeue from a Queue
concepts.short_definition: The order in which items are removed from a queue must be identical to the order in which they were inserted, following FIFO rules, even when enqueue and dequeue operations interleave.

concepts.canonical_name: Order of Pop from a Stack
concepts.short_definition: Possible output sequences from popping items from a stack depend on LIFO ordering and the interleaving of PUSH and POP operations.

concepts.canonical_name: Chaining Data Structures for Hash Tables
concepts.short_definition: Data structures used to resolve collisions in hash tables by storing multiple entries in the same bucket, impacting runtime complexities of table operations.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm for detecting pairs with difference multiple of ceiling(log n)
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that inputs an array A of n integers and outputs a pair of indices i ≠ j such that A[i] - A[j] is a multiple of ⌈log n⌉, running in O(log n) time.
Two integers a and b are modularly equivalent modulo c if rem(a, c) = rem(b, c), i.e., a ≡ b mod c.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime analysis of algorithm using DAA for modular collision detection
concepts.short_definition: Analyzing the runtime shows worst-case O(log n) time due to at most ⌈log n⌉ + 1 insertions before collision; this bound is tight due to an example input.
A hash function mapping integer k to its remainder modulo ⌈log n⌉, used for indexing in a DAA or hash table.

concepts.canonical_name: Differences between direct addressing arrays and hash tables in collision management
concepts.short_definition: DAA uses direct mapping with no collisions except by the nature of the problem, while hash tables require handling of hash collisions and key uniqueness, affecting runtime and correctness.
Problems used for practicing the kinds of questions appearing in a midterm exam for the course.

concepts.canonical_name: Partition into σ-pairs with one left over
concepts.short_definition: Dividing the 2n+1 Pokémon into n pairs whose auras sum to σ and one unpaired Pokémon.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm to find unpaired aura given σ
concepts.short_definition: An O(n) time algorithm that computes the sum of all auras and subtracts nσ to find the unpaired aura.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm to find unpaired aura when σ unknown but σ < n1210
concepts.short_definition: An O(n) algorithm that given array A finds the unpaired Pokémon’s aura without knowing σ, using a reduction to the known σ case.
Determining if an aura is larger than a given reference aura (n1210).
Accessing elements of an array using negative indices to refer to positions relative to the array's end or mirrored indices.
The condition that for every valid index i, the sum of the element at position i and the element at position -i (a mirrored position) is constant across all i and less than a threshold (here, n1210).

concepts.canonical_name: Returning a Specific Array Element under Condition
concepts.short_definition: The method of returning the element at index 0 of the array if the array satisfies a particular condition involving symmetry and a bound.
The matrix that, when multiplied with the original matrix A, yields the identity matrix.
An algorithm that determines pairs of auras in a sorted array based on a threshold σ defined as the sum of the smallest and largest elements.
Proof that every paired aura in the algorithm is less than the sum σ of the smallest and largest auras, ensuring correctness of pairing based on position and σ.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Analysis of Aura Pairing Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The analysis showing that the aura pairing algorithm runs in linear time based on linear scans in steps 1, 3, 4, and conditional linear time in steps 2 and 5.

concepts.canonical_name: Finding the Largest Element in a Set
concepts.short_definition: The process of identifying the maximum element in a collection or set of elements.

concepts.canonical_name: Deleting an Element from a Set
concepts.short_definition: Removing a specified element from a collection or set.
The computation of sample variance σ as the average of squared deviations over the sample size n.
The process of verifying that for every index i in array A, the sum of elements at A[i] and A[2n-1 - i] equals a constant σ.

concepts.canonical_name: Proof of Correctness via Pairwise Sum Checking
concepts.short_definition: The reasoning that the largest element in the array is unpaired iff deleting it leaves an array partitionable into n pairs each summing to constant σ, verified by step 4.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Complexity of Theta(n) for Array Operations
concepts.short_definition: The analysis showing that steps including scanning, deleting, and pair checking in the algorithm run in worst-case linear time relative to n.

concepts.canonical_name: Augmented AVL Tree for Interval Management
concepts.short_definition: An AVL binary search tree augmented with subtree maximum end values to manage intervals efficiently.

concepts.canonical_name: PLACE Operation on Augmented AVL Tree
concepts.short_definition: Insertion of an interval node in an augmented AVL tree, maintaining balanced BST properties and updating max subtree values.

concepts.canonical_name: BREAK Operation on Augmented AVL Tree
concepts.short_definition: Deletion of an interval node in an augmented AVL tree, maintaining balanced BST properties and updating max subtree values.

concepts.canonical_name: HAPPY Query Operation on Augmented AVL Tree
concepts.short_definition: Query to determine if a point x lies within any interval stored in the augmented AVL tree using subtree maximums for pruning.
The concept of comparing a node's item attribute 'a' with a value x to decide traversal direction in a binary search tree.
Ordering nodes in AVL trees based on a lexicographical ordering of tuple keys to facilitate specialized query operations.

concepts.canonical_name: Specialized Querying on Balanced Binary Trees
concepts.short_definition: Techniques to efficiently query properties of a set by using balanced binary trees keyed in specific ways to partition the search space.

concepts.canonical_name: Data Structure Operations: Insertion and Deletion in AVL Trees
concepts.short_definition: Standard operations to add or remove nodes from AVL trees while maintaining balance and order.
Computing the index (number of elements before a given element) in an AVL-based sequence data structure using size augmentations.
An operation that finds the largest key strictly less than a given value k in a data structure.
A boolean condition outputting TRUE iff more intervals start at or before position x than those ending before x, ensuring x is covered by at least one interval ending at or after x.
The augmentation in an AVL tree storing the maximum b value in the subtree rooted at a node, used to speed up interval searching.
A method to handle keys with the same a value during insertion to maintain correctness, avoiding overwriting or ambiguous node locations.
An expression describing how to update the maxb augmentation of a node from its children's augmentations and the node's item.
Ensuring correctness in searching for intervals covering a point by checking appropriate nodes and their ancestors and subtrees.
The process of removing a node from a binary search tree while maintaining its binary search property.
The method to find the immediate predecessor of a given element in a data structure, preferably by implementing it manually rather than using black-box functions.
A practice exam for Midterm 1 in course 6.1210, consisting of 16 questions to prepare students.
An operation to update or record new information, here to record or overwrite the ratings of an athlete by student ID in O(log n) time.
An operation to select elements maximizing a certain score in constant O(1) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Data Structure Using Hash Table and Max-Heaps for Efficient Team Selection
concepts.short_definition: A data structure that uses a hash table to store athlete records keyed by student ID and two max-heaps keyed by pistol and fencing ratings respectively to perform updates and selection in the required time complexities.
The operation of finding a record x in a dataset ROSTER using a specified key s.
An ordered collection of elements, possibly of different types, used to group related data items together.
A data structure with named fields, similar to a tuple but with named components for easier access.
The operation of assigning or accessing elements of an array using indices.
The process of assigning a value to a variable or a data structure element.
A method that systematically enumerates all possible candidates for the solution to a problem and checks whether each candidate satisfies the problem's criteria.
The runtime complexity of the BUILD operation on HEAP data structures, which is worst-case O(n) time.
The expected amortized runtime complexity of the RATE operation on HEAP data structures, which is O(log n) time.
The runtime complexity of the SELECT operation which operates on a constant size prefix of a HEAP.

concepts.canonical_name: Use of HEAP data structure for efficient team selection
concepts.short_definition: Using HEAPs to efficiently select sports team members with highest ratings, where top elements represent the athletes with the best ratings.

concepts.canonical_name: Complexity differences between HEAP and AVL BST implementations
concepts.short_definition: Replacing HEAPs with AVL BSTs increases the BUILD and SELECT operation costs multiplicatively by log n unless optimizations are used, such as storing largest elements redundantly.

concepts.canonical_name: Limitations of AVL BST operations for sorted data
concepts.short_definition: AVL BSTs cannot be built in O(n) time and their building in such time would violate comparison sort lower bounds.

concepts.canonical_name: Hash Table usage for efficient lookup
concepts.short_definition: Using a Hash Table is necessary for expected O(1) time lookup operations, as HEAPs or AVL BSTs cannot find items in O(log n) time efficiently for this problem.
Heap deletion does not take constant time; it is not a constant-time operation.

concepts.canonical_name: Conflict of data structure properties in trees
concepts.short_definition: A tree cannot simultaneously satisfy AVL, BST, and heap properties.
A mistake or misconception that students repeatedly make regarding a topic or problem.
A straightforward problem-solving approach that tries all possible candidates or solutions without optimization.
The awarding of some points even if the solution is incomplete or does not meet all criteria, typically for correctness or effort shown.

concepts.canonical_name: Clarity and Concision in Recursive Definitions
concepts.short_definition: The importance of avoiding redefinition, ambiguity, and unnecessary complexity when writing recursive algorithms.
Mistakes such as vague underspecified attempts at repetition and replacing recursion with imprecise hand-waving, leading to overcomplicated or incorrect algorithms.

concepts.canonical_name: Total function as a set keyed by function value
concepts.short_definition: A total function expressed as a set S where each element x maps to x.y; such a set does not add value by definition because it merely duplicates the data (wastes time and space).

concepts.canonical_name: Useful set representing function by projecting key component
concepts.short_definition: A SET representing a function by mapping the pair x.y to x (i.e., keyed by x.y), can be useful as it provides meaningful data representation or operations.
An abstract data type that stores unique keys without duplicates.

concepts.canonical_name: Expected runtime analysis of hash tables
concepts.short_definition: Analysis that guarantees average efficient operations in hash tables assuming distinct keys and uniform hashing.
A binary tree with the AVL Property that enables efficient representation as arrays, typically satisfying heap properties.
Closed-form asymptotic solution of recurrence relations defining algorithm runtime.
The amortized (average) time complexity of inserting multiple items into a dynamic array, considering occasional resizing.
Analysis of recursive algorithms defined by divide-and-conquer recurrences to find asymptotic runtime.
The condition in AVL trees restricting the allowed skew (balance factor) of any node to |s| ≤ 1.
A proposed variant of AVL trees where balancing skew is relaxed to |s| ≤ 2 instead of |s| ≤1.

concepts.canonical_name: Minimum height of AVL2-tree with n nodes
concepts.short_definition: The smallest height possible for an AVL2-tree containing n nodes.

concepts.canonical_name: Maximum height of AVL2-tree with n nodes
concepts.short_definition: The largest height possible for an AVL2-tree containing n nodes.
The process of constructing a Set AVL-tree data structure with n items, typically requiring O(n log n) time using standard insertions.
The computational complexity in terms of n for constructing an AVL-tree, commonly O(n log n) using naive insertions, with questions about the possibility of achieving O(n).

concepts.canonical_name: Hash Function h(k) = k^2 mod m
concepts.short_definition: A specific hash function mapping an integer key k to the remainder when k squared is divided by m, used in hashing schemes.
A set of three positive integers (a, b, c) that satisfy the equation a^2 + b^2 = c^2.

concepts.canonical_name: Naive Algorithm for Detecting Pythagorean Triples
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that checks all possible triples of values in an input set to find Pythagorean triples, with a runtime of O(n^3).
Technique using a hash table data structure to achieve average case time efficiency for searching and lookups, often reducing expected runtime of algorithms.
Algorithmic techniques involving sorting input data and using binary search to achieve worst-case time guarantees like O(n^2 log n).
A review activity or document preparing students for the midterm exam in course 6.1210.
Dates on which guests arrive or depart from the resort, including the number of guests arriving or departing on each date.

concepts.canonical_name: Maximum Number of Guests Eating Lunch Together
concepts.short_definition: The highest count of guests present at the resort at lunchtime (1 P.M.) on any given day, considering guests arrive before 10 A.M. and leave after 5 P.M.

concepts.canonical_name: Guest Count Calculation from Arrival and Departure Data
concepts.short_definition: The method or process of computing the number of guests present simultaneously based on unordered and possibly repeated arrival and departure records.
Determining the maximum number of overlapping intervals (e.g., guest stays) at any point in time.

concepts.canonical_name: O(n log n) Interval Overlapping Algorithm with Sorting
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm to find the maximum number of overlapping intervals by sorting arrival and departure dates and scanning them in order, running in O(n log n) time.

concepts.canonical_name: O(n) Interval Overlapping Algorithm with Fixed Date Range
concepts.short_definition: An optimized algorithm to find maximum overlapping intervals in O(n) time by leveraging a fixed finite date range (e.g., two years) and using specialized data structures like arrays or counting vectors.
A problem involving n people arranged in a circle where every m-th person is removed iteratively until none remain, producing a Josephus permutation.

concepts.canonical_name: Analysis of Data Structure Efficiency for Josephus Problem with Constant m
concepts.short_definition: Determining the best data structure to output the Josephus Permutation in O(n) time when m is constant (m=O(1)).

concepts.canonical_name: Using Recursive Calls in Tree Operations
concepts.short_definition: A method where recursive queries obtain results from subtrees and combine them to derive answers at parent nodes, applicable in augmented trees.
An assessment format where the respondent selects the correct answer(s) from several options.
An assessment format requiring brief, descriptive answers rather than multiple choice or essay responses.
Advice and strategies for efficiently allocating time to problems during an exam based on point values and difficulty.
A technique to prove upper and lower bounds on recurrences through induction by guessing and verifying a bound.
A technique in amortized analysis where the total amortized cost is the sum of the actual cost and the change in a potential function, used to analyze algorithms.
A function mapping the state of a data structure to a real number used in amortized analysis to represent stored credit or debt, which helps in analyzing average costs per operation.
The average running time per operation over a worst-case sequence of operations, often expressed as actual cost plus change in potential function.
Constraint that the potential function Φ must have a constant lower bound to ensure correct amortized cost analysis and avoid negative infinite amortized costs.
Exams administered during the course timeline to assess understanding of course materials covered up to that point.

concepts.canonical_name: In-order Traversal of a Binary Search Tree
concepts.short_definition: A traversal method of a binary search tree that returns the nodes' keys in sorted order and takes O(n) time.
A theoretical lower bound that any comparison-based sorting algorithm requires at least Ω(n log n) comparisons.
Collision in a chaining hash table occurs when two keys hash to the same cell, causing multiple entries in that cell's chain.
The average running time of an algorithm over all inputs.

concepts.canonical_name: Hash table for sum of squares pairs
concepts.short_definition: A data structure storing sums of squares a² + b² indexed by pairs to quickly check for Pythagorean triples.

concepts.canonical_name: Two-pointer algorithm on sorted squared list
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm using a sorted list of squared numbers and two pointers to find pairs summing to a target c².

concepts.canonical_name: Merge sort and binary search for sum of squares
concepts.short_definition: Sorting sums of squares with merge sort and searching c² with binary search to find Pythagorean triples.

concepts.canonical_name: Maximum Number of Guests at Lunch
concepts.short_definition: The maximal count of guests present simultaneously at lunch time on any given day, based on arrival before 10 A.M. and departure after 5 P.M.

concepts.canonical_name: Guest Arrival and Departure Dates Representation
concepts.short_definition: A data format listing guest arrival and departure records as tuples containing the event type (arrival or departure), date, and number of guests.
A method of determining the number of guests present at a particular time by counting overlapping arrival and departure intervals.

concepts.canonical_name: Sorting and Merging Algorithm for Interval Counting
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that sorts arrivals and departures separately or combined and merges them to count simultaneous guests efficiently in O(n log n) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Counting Sort for Interval Counting within Limited Date Range
concepts.short_definition: An algorithmic improvement using counting sort to achieve O(n) runtime when all dates lie within a fixed known small range (e.g., two years).

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity O(n log n) for Josephus Problem with variable m
concepts.short_definition: Using an AVL tree, the (n, m) Josephus Permutation can be output in O(n log n) time if m is not constant.
Assigning and updating a timer-based timestamp to nodes upon insert or find access to track access recency.
A recursive algorithm returning the most recent bird accessed with ID ≤ max by considering left subtree, current node, and right subtree recursively.
An iterative method using FIND to locate the largest ID ≤ max, then comparing timestamps from that node and relevant ancestors and subtrees to find the most recent accessed bird.
A query that finds the minimum ID in a subtree or structure to optimize search operations.
A recursive function that searches the AVL tree keyed by timestamp to find the most recent item with ID less than or equal to max or returns ⊥ if none exists.

concepts.canonical_name: Cross-linked doubly-linked list of in-order traversal for efficient augmentation
concepts.short_definition: Use a doubly-linked list cross-linked with Falkner’s tree nodes to maintain predecessor and successor relationships efficiently for closest pair queries and augmentations.

concepts.canonical_name: In-order traversal predecessor and successor in AVL trees
concepts.short_definition: The concept of predecessor and successor nodes in the in-order traversal order of AVL trees, important for maintaining adjacency information.
Proof that an algorithm cannot run faster than a certain time complexity.
Common operations performed on data structures such as initialize, build, access, insert, delete, and set.
The asymptotic time complexities associated with common dynamic operations on a doubly-linked list data structure.
The asymptotic time complexities of operations on a sorted array including find, insert, delete, and order operations.
Expected and amortized asymptotic running times for operations on a hash table including find, insert, and delete.
Algorithms for finding shortest paths from a single source vertex to all other vertices in a graph.
An algorithm for shortest paths in Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAG) working in topological order in time Θ(|V| + |E|).
An efficient algorithm for single-source shortest paths on graphs with non-negative edge weights using a Fibonacci heap data structure with running time Θ(|V| log |V| + |E|).

concepts.canonical_name: Min-Heap and Valid Heap Array Representation
concepts.short_definition: Min-heap is a binary heap where the value of each node is less than or equal to the values of its children, and can be represented as an array that satisfies the min-heap property.

concepts.canonical_name: Bellman-Ford Algorithm and Negative Weight Cycles
concepts.short_definition: Edges that are successfully relaxed on the last iteration of Bellman-Ford algorithm indicate the presence of negative weight cycles in the graph.

concepts.canonical_name: Maximum Weight Path in Directed Graphs with Positive Weights
concepts.short_definition: Computing the maximum weight path in a directed graph with positive weights does not have the same complexity as shortest path algorithms; the stated complexity claims if true would indicate efficient maximum path computation.

concepts.canonical_name: DFS Finishing Order and Tree Traversals
concepts.short_definition: In a binary tree, the finishing order of Depth-First Search matches post-order traversal when children are processed left to right.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Representation of Roads and Cities
concepts.short_definition: Modeling cities as nodes and roads as edges in a graph, enabling algorithmic routing.
Setting a toll price on a specific road to influence route choice optimally.
Choosing the path between two cities that minimizes total toll cost, with tie-breaking rules.
Designing an efficient algorithm to determine the maximum toll price that keeps a specific road on the cheapest route.
Finding a path between two nodes in a graph that has the minimum total weight or length compared to all other paths.
Finding paths in a graph that must satisfy additional conditions such as always maintaining connection to a subset of nodes or hotspots.
