Removing nodes and edges from a graph that do not satisfy certain constraints, to focus on feasible paths only.
Finding a path in a graph that differs from a given path in at least one edge, often to find new or diverse routes.
The requirement that two paths differ in at least one edge or tunnel to be considered distinct.
A review session or document covering concepts likely to be tested on the second midterm exam.

concepts.canonical_name: Path Planning with Constraints in Graphs
concepts.short_definition: Designing a route through a network of cities with constraints on the number of steps and visits, including repeated cities, and alternate payment conditions.
A method to find an optimal path under constraints using state definitions and recursive relations.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph with Repeated Node Visits Allowed
concepts.short_definition: Allowing multiple visits to the same city in a path by permitting cycles for optimization purposes.
Sequence of payments where players alternate paying each other each night for the current city’s M’s Donots count.

concepts.canonical_name: Bound on Maximum Number of Nights
concepts.short_definition: Constraint on the total number of nights (100) allowed before the destination must be reached for the path plan.

A pathfinding problem where a robot moves on an n × n grid from (1,1) to (n,n), collecting coins with values at grid points, moving only right or up, and the goal is to maximize the sum of collected coin values.

concepts.canonical_name: Formulating Robot Coin Collector as a Shortest Paths Problem
concepts.short_definition: Representing the Robot Coin Collector problem as a shortest paths problem by modeling the grid and possible robot moves as graph vertices and edges with appropriate weights, allowing use of shortest path algorithms to find the maximum coin value path.

concepts.canonical_name: Using BFS to solve Robot Coin Collector with uniform coin values
concepts.short_definition: When all coins have value 1, the Robot Coin Collector problem can be solved using BFS by exploiting the fact that any path from (1,1) to (n,n) has exactly 2(n-1) moves.

concepts.canonical_name: Running Time of Operations on Sequences
concepts.short_definition: Time complexities (worst-case, amortized, or expected) for operations like build, get_at, insert_first, insert_last, insert_at, set_at, delete_first, delete_last, delete_at for data structures such as Static Sequence, Dynamic Array, Doubly-Linked List, and AVL Sequence.

concepts.canonical_name: Running Time of Operations on Set Data Structures
concepts.short_definition: Time complexities of operations including build, find, insert, find_min, find_prev, delete, find_max, and find_next on data structures like Sorted Array, Direct Access Array, Hash Table, and AVL BST.

concepts.canonical_name: Single Source Shortest Path (SSSP) Algorithms and Their Running Times
concepts.short_definition: Algorithms for computing shortest paths from a source vertex including BFS, DAG shortest path, Dijkstra with Fibonacci Heap, and Bellman-Ford, with their respective running times and order of relaxation.
A set of rules and guidelines specific to the administration and conduct of the Midterm 2 exam for 6.1210 Fall 2025.
Assessment problems in multiple choice format that evaluate various concepts relevant to the Midterm 2 exam.
A specific exam problem involving 'Tricky Tolls' worth 15 points, testing problem-solving skills related to toll-related concepts.
A specific exam problem named 'Spelunking Online' worth 30 points, testing relevant problem solving and understanding from the course.
An exam problem called 'Road Trip' worth 15 points, assessing skills or concepts relevant to travel or routing topics from the course.
An exam problem titled 'Robot Coin Collector' worth 16 points, testing integration of concepts related to robot movement, coin collection, or algorithms.

concepts.canonical_name: Relaxation Step in Shortest Path Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: An operation where an edge's distance estimate is updated if a shorter path is found; an edge is successfully relaxed if d(v) > d(u)+w(u,v) and is updated accordingly.
A subgraph consisting of all nodes reachable from a given source node in a graph.
A maximal subgraph of a directed graph in which every vertex is reachable from every other vertex.
A maximal connected subgraph of a graph where any two vertices are connected by a path.
An artificial node added to a graph that connects multiple other components or nodes, used to simplify traversal or connectivity analysis.
A directed graph with no cycles, meaning there is no way to start at any node and follow a sequence of edges that eventually loops back to the starting node.

concepts.canonical_name: Distance in a graph from a source node
concepts.short_definition: The length of the shortest path from the source node to each other node in the graph.
A technique for computing shortest paths in a DAG by relaxing edges in topological order to find minimum distances from a source node.

concepts.canonical_name: Relationship Between DFS Finishing Order and Post-Order Traversal in Binary Trees
concepts.short_definition: The identity that for binary trees, the finishing order of depth-first search matches the post-order traversal order when processing children left to right.

concepts.canonical_name: Minimum Cost Path in Unweighted Graph
concepts.short_definition: The shortest path in an unweighted, undirected graph computed using BFS.
Constructing the reverse of a directed graph to perform BFS on reversed edges.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Duplication Technique for Tracking Road Usage
concepts.short_definition: Constructing a duplicated graph with stateful nodes to track whether a special edge has been used, enabling BFS to find distances with and without use of that edge.
The Big-O runtime complexity for BFS and graph construction, often O(m + n) for graphs with n nodes and m edges.
A special artificial node added to a graph connected to multiple nodes with edges of zero weight, used in shortest path computations to aggregate multiple sources into one.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Pruning to Maintain Connectivity Constraint
concepts.short_definition: Removing nodes and edges from a graph based on distance constraints to ensure a path maintains a required property, such as phone signal reception.
A technique of duplicating graph vertices into multiple layers to track additional path properties, such as whether a deviation from a specific path has occurred.

concepts.canonical_name: Shortest Path Differing from a Given Path
concepts.short_definition: Finding a shortest path between two nodes in a graph that differs by at least one edge from a previously found path.
A method of transforming a graph problem by creating a new graph with nodes representing original nodes combined with additional state information, enabling modeling of more complex constraints.
Using edge weights in a directed graph to represent the amount of money paid on each night, positive or negative depending on the turn.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Construction for Road Trip Problem
concepts.short_definition: Constructing a graph with nodes representing city and night indices and edges connecting valid moves with proper weights modeling payments and trip termination conditions.

concepts.canonical_name: Edge Splitting Technique for Modeling Weighted Edges in Unweighted Graphs
concepts.short_definition: A technique to convert edges with weight 2 into two edges each with weight 1 by splitting edges to create an unweighted graph for BFS use.

concepts.canonical_name: Maximum Coin Collection Path Length Relation
concepts.short_definition: The relation between shortest path length in the modified graph and maximum number of coins collected: l = 2(n-1) + r, number of coins is 4(n-1) - l, where r is number of visited points without coins.
The force of attraction between two masses, proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
Law stating that the acceleration of an object is proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass.

concepts.canonical_name: Heap Data Structure: Min-Heap and Max-Heap
concepts.short_definition: A min-heap is a binary tree where the key at the root must be minimum among all keys in the tree; a max-heap is similarly defined where the root key is maximum. Reversing the array representation of a min-heap does not necessarily yield a max-heap.
A type of reduction between computational problems where problem A is solved using an algorithm for problem B as a subroutine, allowing multiple calls.
The problem of determining whether a graph contains any cycles.
A graph in which edges have direction and each edge has an associated positive weight or cost.

concepts.canonical_name: One-way Navigable Sea Routes as Directed Edges
concepts.short_definition: Edges representing navigation routes between islands that allow movement in only one direction, with a travel time cost.

concepts.canonical_name: Swimming and Flying with Delay Constraint
concepts.short_definition: Wingull can swim on routes taking t(i,j) minutes, or fly in one minute per route, but must then rest for 1 hour and 7 minutes before flying again, modeling multi-modal edge costs and a rest waiting requirement.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph-based Algorithm Design for Minimum Time Mission
concepts.short_definition: Designing an algorithm to compute the minimum mission completion time by modeling island routes and constraints as graph problem for shortest path computation.

concepts.canonical_name: State Space Representation in Graph Search
concepts.short_definition: A method of representing the states of a problem using vertices where each vertex encodes multiple elements of the state (e.g., location, item collection status, remaining time).
A path that follows directed edges from a source vertex u to a target vertex v in a graph.
A directed edge representing a swimming transition from vertex (u, s, r) to (v, s ∨ [v ∈ T], max(0, r - t(u, v))) with a cost equal to t(u, v).
A directed edge from (u, s, 0) to (v, s ∨ [v ∈ T], 67) with a fixed cost of 1 representing flying transition.
Transforming a weighted directed graph into an unweighted directed graph by replacing any edge with travel cost t>1 by a chain of t unit-cost edges.

concepts.canonical_name: Modeling Waiting via Self-Loop Edges in Graph
concepts.short_definition: In the state graph, for any vertex with resting time r > 0, adding an edge to the same vertex with r decreased by 1 represents waiting/resting in place for one unit time.

concepts.canonical_name: Bounding Maximum Edge Cost to Ignore Non-Optimal Transitions
concepts.short_definition: Using an upper bound on edge costs (135 minutes) to ignore swimming edges with cost exceeding this bound since waiting and flying alternatives will be no worse.

concepts.canonical_name: State Representation in Graph for Resting and Sandwich Acquisition
concepts.short_definition: Representing the problem state as (vertex, sandwich possession status, resting time) to capture all relevant parameters for BFS traversal.

concepts.canonical_name: Breadth-First Search on Expanded State Graph
concepts.short_definition: Running BFS on the unweighted expanded graph G′ to find the shortest path and minimum mission time from the start state to any end state.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Complexity Analysis of State Graph BFS
concepts.short_definition: Analyzing that the BFS on expanded graph G′ runs in linear time O(m + n) due to bounded number of states and edges after unrolling.
Combining segments of paths from different computations or routes, potentially leading to incorrect solutions if done improperly (e.g., teleporting between paths).
The methodology for allowing or disallowing resting in place during path computations, affecting solution correctness.
A constraint or limit on edges in a graph that restricts the search space or computations in shortest-path problems.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Construction from Rooms and Doors
concepts.short_definition: Representing rooms as vertices and doors as edges in an undirected graph to model movement possibilities.
A method where the pursuer moves along the prefix of the shortest path from their location to the target's last known location to catch them efficiently.
Using periodic tracker updates to know the target's last known location in a pursuit problem.
Analyzing and proving that the pursuer can catch the target within a specified time bound based on movement speeds and distances.

concepts.canonical_name: Use of Parent Pointer Matrix in APSP
concepts.short_definition: Maintaining parent pointers during BFS to reconstruct shortest paths in all-pairs shortest path computations.
A graph where edges have a direction from one vertex to another.
The concept of collecting at most one Rare Candy from each vertex in a directed graph along a path starting from a specified vertex.

For each vertex v in the graph, the maximum number of Rare Candies Wooper can have at vertex v that can be collected starting from s along a path that may revisit vertices but collects at most one candy per vertex.
A sequence of vertices connected by directed edges from one vertex to another, possibly allowing repeated vertices.
Confusing the maximum number of candies collectible at vertex v with the maximum candies collectible if starting from v, instead of from s.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Weighting by Negative Intersection Size
concepts.short_definition: Weighted edges in the condensation graph are assigned weights equal to the negative cardinality of the intersection of the set R with the SCC, i.e., −|R ∩ x|.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Algorithm for Computing Vector r in Linear Time
concepts.short_definition: A linear time algorithm involving creating a condensation graph, adding a source node, weighting edges, performing DAG shortest path from the source, and outputting r(v) based on shortest path values.

concepts.canonical_name: Non-positive cycle detection for infinite resource traversal
concepts.short_definition: Determining whether a graph contains a cycle whose total adjusted edge weight is non-positive, indicating the possibility to traverse indefinitely without running out of resources.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph edge reweighting with potential functions
concepts.short_definition: Adjusting edge weights by subtracting node potentials (distances) to simplify cycle detection and remove positive edges, enabling zero-weight cycle detection via DFS.

concepts.canonical_name: Slime cost and Rare Candy mechanics in graph traversal
concepts.short_definition: Modeling resource consumption on edges by slime costs and resource gains by Rare Candy as edge weights (s(u,v)−r(u)) to analyze traversal feasibility.

concepts.canonical_name: Lexicographic ordering for negative cycle detection
concepts.short_definition: Using lexicographic ordering on ordered pairs of edge weights to detect nuanced cycle conditions (e.g., considering both slime cost and traversal count).

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime complexity of Bellman-Ford and DFS in cycle detection
concepts.short_definition: Analyzing the total runtime as O(|V||E|) combining edge weighting, Bellman-Ford (O(|V||E|)), and DFS for cycle detection.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Types for Shortest Path Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: Classification of graphs by properties (weighted/unweighted, directed/undirected, acyclic) influencing best shortest path algorithms.
Graphs that are directed, acyclic, and have weighted edges.
Directed graphs with edges that have no weights.
Undirected graphs with edges that have positive weights.
Algorithms used to compute a topological order of a DAG efficiently.
An algorithm to find strongly connected components in a directed graph.
The condensation graph of any directed graph is acyclic (a DAG).
The condensation graph is unique up to relabeling of vertices.
Algorithms that solve the s-t reachability problem in linear time, such as BFS and DFS.
BFS can be used to determine s-t reachability in linear time.
DFS can be used to determine s-t reachability in linear time.
Two vertices u and v in a directed graph are semi-connected if there exists either a path from u to v or from v to u (or both).
The property of whether every pair of vertices in a DAG is semi-connected or not.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm for Checking Semi-connectedness in DAG
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that determines if two vertices in a DAG are semi-connected by finding a pair that is not semi-connected or confirming all pairs are.
A formal demonstration that the runtime of an algorithm does not exceed a certain asymptotic time complexity, such as O(|V| + |E|).
A graph property where the graph has no cycles; i.e., there is no path from a vertex back to itself through other vertices.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Model of MIT Rooms and Doors
concepts.short_definition: Representation of MIT as a graph where rooms are nodes and doors between rooms are edges, with m edges and n nodes where m ≥ n.
Each door is guarded by one or more Psyducks; passing through requires feeding each Psyduck a cookie.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm to Compute Minimum Cookies to Reach Exam
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that finds the path from the dorm to the exam that minimizes the sum of cookies needed to feed all Psyducks guarding the doors on the path.

concepts.canonical_name: Minimum Cookies Path Algorithm with Confused Guard
concepts.short_definition: An algorithmic method to compute the minimum number of cookies required to pass through doors guarded by Psyducks, where one Psyduck is confused and offers a dozen cookies instead of demanding one upon first passage.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm Design for Minimum Resource Allocation
concepts.short_definition: Designing an algorithm to compute the minimum number of resources (cookies) needed to satisfy certain conditions involving entities (Psyducks) in groups (rooms).
Instructions and guidelines provided to students for taking the midterm exam, including allowed materials and conduct rules.
A formal demonstration that a given algorithm or method meets its specification or correctness criteria.
Different types of questions included in the exam, such as multiple choice and problem-solving questions.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm to Find Non-Semi-Connected Vertex Pair in a DAG
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that, given an acyclic directed graph G, finds and outputs a pair of vertices that are not semi-connected, or returns ⊥ if no such pair exists.
The concept and process of determining if there exists a path from vertex u to vertex v in a directed graph.
The function δ that records the shortest path distances from a source vertex to other vertices in a graph.

concepts.canonical_name: Correctness of Vertex Sorting by Distance
concepts.short_definition: The property that if two distinct vertices have the same distance, there is no path between them, and if no collisions exist, all vertices are semi-connected.
A graph in which for every pair of vertices u and v there is a path from u to v or from v to u; implied here when a path covering all vertices exists with edges of weight -1.
The method of initializing all distances to zero when calculating shortest paths in a graph algorithm, instead of adding a supersource node.
Finding two vertices in a graph that are consecutive in topological order but not adjacent by an edge.
A directed graph that is connected when considered as an undirected graph, ignoring edge directions.
Determining if there is a path from every vertex u to vertex v in a directed graph for all pairs (u,v).

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm for Finding Non-Semi-Connected Vertex Pair in Directed Graphs
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that finds and outputs a pair of vertices in a directed graph that are not semi-connected, or returns ⊥ if all pairs are semi-connected.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Algorithm for Shortest Distance to Differently Colored Vertex
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm to find, for every vertex in a weighted directed graph, the shortest distance to a vertex with a different color.

concepts.canonical_name: Counting Edges and Vertices in Graphs
concepts.short_definition: The relationship and notation regarding the number of edges (|E|) and vertices (|V|) in a graph, especially in context of algorithm complexity analysis.
A data structure consisting of vertices (nodes) connected by edges (links).
The operation of creating a new graph G' by reversing the direction of every edge in a directed graph G.
A method of modifying a graph by adding a supersource vertex connected with zero-weight edges to specific subsets of the graph vertices.

concepts.canonical_name: Shortest Path Distances in Weighted Graphs
concepts.short_definition: The minimal sum of edge weights along any path from a source vertex to a target vertex in a weighted graph.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Construction and Time Complexity Analysis
concepts.short_definition: The process of constructing a modified graph G' and analyzing the time complexity of algorithms running on it, particularly for shortest path computations.

concepts.canonical_name: Handling Vertices with No Outgoing Edges in Shortest Path Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: Strategies to manage vertices without outgoing edges during shortest path computations to avoid incorrect results or infinite distances.

concepts.canonical_name: Johnson's Algorithm for All-Pairs Shortest Paths
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that uses reweighting to find shortest paths between all pairs of vertices efficiently, especially for sparse graphs.
A conceptual vertex connected to certain vertices (e.g., those of a specific color) to facilitate computations like shortest paths in modified graphs.
Analyzing the runtime complexity of the Bellman-Ford algorithm, often stated as Θ(|V||E|), where |V| is the number of vertices and |E| is the number of edges in the graph.

concepts.canonical_name: Correct Problem Formulation for Shortest Path
concepts.short_definition: Correctly defining the shortest path problem requirements, such as solving for all vertices from a source, rather than incorrectly solving for a single vertex or only the shortest edge.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Bound Compliance in Algorithm Solutions
concepts.short_definition: Ensuring the solution meets the chosen runtime performance bound, as failure to do so can result in an incorrect or rejected solution.

concepts.canonical_name: Minimum Cost Path in a Weighted Graph
concepts.short_definition: Finding a path from a start node to a target node in a graph minimizing the total sum of weights on edges along the path.
A graph where each edge has an associated numerical weight representing some quantity.
An element of the set V representing a node or point in a graph, such as a room in a building.
An element of the set E representing a connection between two vertices in a graph, such as a door between rooms.
A numerical value associated with an edge in a weighted graph, representing quantities like cost, distance, or in this case, the number of Psyducks guarding a door.
The notation n and m representing the number of vertices and edges in a graph respectively, used to analyze algorithm runtime complexity.
The time complexity for running Dijkstra's algorithm on a graph with n vertices and m edges is Θ(n log n + m) when using a priority queue (e.g., binary heap).

concepts.canonical_name: Minimum Cost Path Algorithm with Special Node
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm designed to find the minimum cost (in cookies) to pass through a series of doors guarded mostly by Psyducks, where one door is guarded by a confused Psyduck that changes the cost the first time you pass through it.
The matrix G constructed in the previous step, typically used in optimization algorithms or problem settings as a key component.
The operation of creating a new graph by removing a specific edge from an existing graph.
A cycle in a graph where the sum of edge weights is negative, causing shortest path algorithms to fail to find a well-defined shortest path because the path can be made arbitrarily short.
Finding shortest paths in a graph while correctly accounting for additional costs or penalties, such as door costs in the problem context, without violating shortest path algorithm assumptions.

concepts.canonical_name: Incorrect Usage of Dijkstra's Algorithm on Negative Weights
concepts.short_definition: The mistake of applying Dijkstra's algorithm to graphs with negative edge weights, which leads to incorrect shortest path computations.

concepts.canonical_name: Directed Graph Construction from Rooms and Doors
concepts.short_definition: A method to construct a directed graph where each room occupied by k entities is represented by a directed path of k vertices, and edges connect these paths according to door connections between rooms.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Representation with Vertices and Edges
concepts.short_definition: A graph G is modeled with vertices representing states (e.g., vf being in room v) and edges representing possible transitions, with m vertices and 3m−n edges in the given graph.
A pair of directed edges between two vertices in opposite directions.
A technique of duplicating vertices in a graph to transform or simplify the graph problem under consideration.
A technique of duplicating edges in a graph which can increase the size of the graph significantly and lead to computational inefficiency in some problems.
A generalized graph where edges (called hyperedges) can connect any number of vertices, unlike simple graphs where edges connect only two vertices.
All shortest paths in the graph are simple, i.e., contain no repeated vertices.

concepts.canonical_name: Edge Weight Constraints in Shortest Path Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: Conditions on edge weight values that affect the computational complexity of shortest path algorithms.

concepts.canonical_name: Paths Fully Contained in Strongly Connected Components
concepts.short_definition: Properties regarding paths between vertices being fully contained inside an SCC.

concepts.canonical_name: Depth-First Search (DFS) Discovery and Finishing Order
concepts.short_definition: Discovery order is the order vertices are first visited; finishing order is the order vertices complete exploration in DFS.

concepts.canonical_name: Possible Finishing Orders of a Full-DFS on an Undirected Graph with Discovery Order
concepts.short_definition: The different possible finishing orders of vertices given a discovery order in a DFS on an undirected graph.

The concept that gossip spreads through a network where nodes represent agents (Psyducks) and directed edges represent a follower relationship, enabling information to flow from one agent to others following them.

concepts.canonical_name: Follower Addition Operations for Gossip Domination
concepts.short_definition: The operations Maggie and Selina can perform each day to add followers to their follower lists or to other Psyducks’ follower lists, affecting how gossip spreads.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm for Minimizing Days to Gossip Domination
concepts.short_definition: An efficient algorithmic approach to compute which person, Maggie or Selina, requires fewer days to succeed in dominating the gossip mill given their follower addition abilities.

concepts.canonical_name: Asymptotic Runtime Analysis of Gossip Domination Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: The analysis of the time complexity of algorithms determining days needed for Maggie or Selina to dominate the gossip mill, used to evaluate algorithm efficiency.

concepts.canonical_name: Shortest Path in Directed Graph with Edge Weights and Vertex Costs
concepts.short_definition: Finding shortest paths in a directed graph where each edge has an associated cost or reward, and each vertex has a fixed visitation cost (tax).
A graph where edges have no direction, connecting vertices bidirectionally.
A sequence of vertices connected by edges in a graph.
A path from a source vertex s to a target vertex t in a graph.
A number divisible by a fixed integer, here specifically 6121.
An algorithm with runtime bounded by a constant times the product of number of vertices and edges in a graph.
The process of updating the shortest path estimate d(v) of a vertex v by considering an edge (u,v) and potentially improving d(v) based on d(u) plus the edge weight.
An estimate of the shortest path distance from a source vertex s to a vertex v.
The true shortest path distance from the source vertex s to vertex v in the graph.
A sequence/order of edges such that relaxing edges in that order updates shortest path estimates to their true shortest path distances.

concepts.canonical_name: Shortest Paths in Graphs without Negative Cycles
concepts.short_definition: The property that shortest paths can be computed with a limited number of edge relaxations (at most |V| -1) if the graph contains no negative-weight cycles.

concepts.canonical_name: Existence of an Edge (u,v) That Improves d(v)
concepts.short_definition: Given conditions on d(s) and d(v), the existence of an edge (u,v) such that relaxing it will update d(v) to its shortest path distance δ(v).

concepts.canonical_name: Relaxation Order with at Most |V|-1 Edge Relaxations
concepts.short_definition: The existence of an order of at most |V|-1 edge relaxations that leads all d(v) to equal δ(v).
A proof or argument about the memory usage limits of an algorithm to solve a problem.
Guidelines for how to approach exam algorithm problems, focusing on statements of known results and efficient problem solving.
A path in a graph which does not contain repeated vertices (no cycles).
Cycles in a weighted graph whose total edge weight sums to zero, which affect shortest path computations.

concepts.canonical_name: Edge Weights and Time Complexity for SSSP
concepts.short_definition: Properties of edge weights affect the computational complexity of shortest path algorithms.
The sequence in which vertices are first visited during a Depth-First Search traversal.
The sequence in which vertices finish their DFS visit (i.e., all descendants are explored and the vertex is exited).
Modeling Psyducks and their follower relationships as vertices and directed edges in a graph where an edge (P1, P2) indicates P2 is a follower of P1.

concepts.canonical_name: In-Degree and Out-Degree Counting in Condensation Graph
concepts.short_definition: Counting the number of vertices with zero in-degree and zero out-degree in the condensation graph to assess reachability properties for Maggie's and Selina's success conditions.
A numerical value assigned to an edge representing cost or profit, defined here as w(u, v) = t(v) − d(u, v) combining taxes and donations.

concepts.canonical_name: Cycle Length Invariance in Directed Graph
concepts.short_definition: The property that the length of any cycle in a directed graph is independent of the starting vertex, relevant in deciding possible routes through ports.
Time complexity of Johnson's algorithm is O(n^2 log n + n^3), dominated by O(n^3) for dense graphs.
The process of determining the correct home port in a routing or logistics context, which involves careful interpretation of given problem definitions.
Understanding that calculations involving routes must consider travel to and from a destination, not just one-way trips.
The necessity of specifying which port a tax applies to in order to correctly compute costs or logistics.
Incorrectly treating donations as only being applicable on a single route instead of possibly multiple routes or different interpretations as per problem context.
A statistical method to model the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables by fitting a linear equation to observed data.
A closed-form solution to linear regression parameters that minimizes the cost function without iterative updates.
A modeling error in machine learning where a function corresponds too closely to a limited set of data points, and may fail to fit additional data or predict future observations reliably.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Construction with Vertex Duplication Modulo an Integer
concepts.short_definition: Constructing a graph G' from original graph G by duplicating vertices for each residue class modulo an integer, with edges connecting duplicated vertices according to transition of residue classes induced by edge weights modulo that integer.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Analysis of Graph Algorithms Using Vertex Duplication
concepts.short_definition: Analyzing runtime complexity when operating on a graph constructed by vertex duplication mod k, showing that runtime scales by constant factor k relative to original graph.

concepts.canonical_name: Depth-First Search For Reachability and Checking Negative Edges
concepts.short_definition: Using DFS from source to test reachability of destination and detect presence of reachable negative edges in a graph.
The concept of interpreting edge weights modulo a number (e.g., 6121) and using path weights equivalent modulo this number.

concepts.canonical_name: Linear Time Algorithm for Minimal Equivalent s-t Path Weight Modulo 6121
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm running in O(|V| + |E|) time that outputs the smallest positive integer x ≤ 6121 equivalent modulo 6121 to some s-t path weight.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Construction for Path Weight Modulo Problem
concepts.short_definition: Constructing an augmented graph G′ to track s-t paths with weights modulo 6121 via vertex and edge modifications.
The integer j satisfying (2w(u,v)) * j ≡ 1 (mod 6121), used to construct paths with specific weights mod 6121.

concepts.canonical_name: Use of Cycles to Adjust Path Weights modulo 6121
concepts.short_definition: Constructing s-t paths with desired weights mod 6121 by concatenating cycles multiple times to adjust total path weight.

concepts.canonical_name: Relaxation Order in Shortest Path Computation
concepts.short_definition: The existence of an order of edge relaxations in a graph without negative cycles, of length at most |V| - 1, that correctly computes shortest path distances from a source vertex s to all vertices.
For a vertex v, a condition d(v) ≥ δ(v) where δ(v) is the true shortest path distance from s to v, and equality means the estimate is correct.
The lemma or property that relaxing an edge (u,v) when d(u)=δ(u) will set d(v) to δ(v).

concepts.canonical_name: Existence of Relaxable Edge with Incorrect Distance
concepts.short_definition: Given distance estimates with at least one incorrect vertex, there exists an edge (u,v) such that relaxing it sets the estimate d(v) to the correct shortest path distance δ(v).

concepts.canonical_name: Iteration Bound for Shortest Path Computation
concepts.short_definition: At most |V| - 1 edge relaxations ordered in the right way are sufficient to compute all shortest path distances correctly from s, assuming no negative cycles.
Finding the second shortest path from a single source to all destinations in a graph, which is a variant of the shortest path problems.
Methods used to explore the nodes and edges of a graph such as depth-first search, breadth-first search, and Dijkstra’s algorithm.
Applying algorithmic techniques to solve specific graph problems presented as exam questions.
Skill of analyzing and selecting correct options for multiple choice questions in the context of the exam.
Conditions under which the SSSP can be computed in time proportional to the size of the input graph (O(n + m)).
Conditions under which SSSP is computed in O(nm) time, often related to Bellman-Ford algorithm performance.
Relevant graph algorithms such as BFS, DAG shortest paths, Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, and Johnson's algorithm used in shortest path computations.
Graph features such as acyclicity, edge weights positivity, number of strongly connected components, and edge count impacts on shortest path algorithm complexity.
Concept relating full depth-first search graph traversals and the discovery of back edges indicating cycles.
A directed connection from one vertex to another in a directed graph.

concepts.canonical_name: t-s Path in a Directed Graph
concepts.short_definition: A path in a directed graph starting at vertex t and ending at vertex s.

concepts.canonical_name: Bisharp's Movement Capabilities on a Chessboard
concepts.short_definition: The set of possible moves from any square (x, y) is to any diagonally adjacent square (x ± 1, y ± 1) on an n × n chessboard.

concepts.canonical_name: Feasible Path under Constraints on Chessboard
concepts.short_definition: A path on the chessboard where Bisharp does not occupy squares containing Kingambit and stays within the board boundaries.

concepts.canonical_name: Maximum Coin Collection Problem on Grid with Obstacles
concepts.short_definition: The problem of finding a path that collects the maximum number of coins on an n × n grid while avoiding Kingambit squares and not revisiting coins more than once.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm Design for Maximum Coin Collection under Movement and Occupation Constraints
concepts.short_definition: The process of creating a method that runs in time O(n^2) to find the maximum coins Bisharp can collect without stepping on Kingambits or leaving the board, moving only diagonally.
A type of problem involving finding paths on a grid from a starting location to ending locations under constraints and optimizing certain criteria.
Each edge of the graph has one of a specified set of colors, and every vertex has exactly one incident edge of each color.

concepts.canonical_name: Shortest Path Problem in Colored Graphs
concepts.short_definition: Finding the shortest path between two vertices in a graph such that the path contains edges of at least a specified number of different colors.

concepts.canonical_name: Shortest Path Problem with Costs and Rewards
concepts.short_definition: Finding a path between cities minimizing the net cost considering flight costs and lecture rewards, subject to constraints on consecutive lectures.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm Design for Constrained Shortest Path
concepts.short_definition: Developing an efficient algorithm to find a path minimizing net cost with constraints such as no consecutive lectures in the same city and non-negative flight and reward costs.
Evaluating and minimizing net travel costs by accounting for both expenses and earnings along a path.

concepts.canonical_name: Travel Path Constraints — No Two Consecutive Lectures in the Same City
concepts.short_definition: A rule forbidding delivering lectures in the same city on two consecutive stops in the travel path.

concepts.canonical_name: Cycle Avoidance and Cost Minimization in Round Trips
concepts.short_definition: Understanding why the cheapest trip that starts and ends at the same city without infinite profit is the trip that does not leave the starting city.
An algorithm that takes as input a directed graph and two vertices s and t, and computes the second-shortest path length from s to t in O(|V| log |V| + |E|) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Tracking Path Deviation for Second-Shortest Paths
concepts.short_definition: A technique to track whether a candidate path has deviated from all shortest paths to help identify the second-shortest path.
Time complexity of various operations (build, get_at, insert_first, insert_last, insert_at, set_at, delete_first, delete_last, delete_at) on dynamic arrays, including amortized costs.

concepts.canonical_name: Sorted Array Operations Complexity in Order Sets
concepts.short_definition: Time complexity of operations such as build, find, insert, find_min, find_prev, delete, find_max, find_next in a sorted array used for an ordered set.

concepts.canonical_name: Master Theorem Cases for Recurrence Solution
concepts.short_definition: Cases of the Master Theorem to solve recurrences of the form T(n) = a T(n/b) + Θ(n^c), with solutions based on comparison of c and log_b a.

The Bellman-Ford shortest path algorithm runs in O(nm) time and can use the Path Relaxation Lemma or iterative rounds to keep track of paths with a bounded number of edges, allowing correctness under assumptions of bounded simple path lengths.

concepts.canonical_name: Conditions for Linear Time SSSP via Bounded Simple Paths
concepts.short_definition: If all simple paths in a graph contain at most a fixed number of edges (e.g., 1434), then SSSP can be computed in linear time using the bounded rounds approach of Bellman-Ford or DAG relaxation modification.

concepts.canonical_name: Dijkstra's Algorithm for SSSP with Positive Edge Weights
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm for solving the Single-Source Shortest Path problem in O(n log n + m) time when all edge weights are positive, using a priority queue data structure.
An edge in DFS traversal that connects a vertex to an ancestor in the DFS tree, indicating a cycle in the graph.
A path starting and ending at the same vertex in a directed graph with all edges oriented consistently.

concepts.canonical_name: Effect of Adding Vertex and Edges on Condensation Graph Size
concepts.short_definition: Statements relating how adding a vertex v and edges (s,v), (v,t) to graph G affects the size of its condensation graph compared to G's condensation graph, conditional on paths between s and t or t and s in G.
Bisharp collects coins by moving onto squares containing coins; each coin can be collected only once regardless of how many times Bisharp re-enters the square.
Squares containing Kingambit must never be occupied by Bisharp; these are disjoint from coin squares and are forbidden for movement.
The process of creating a graph where vertices represent squares without Kingambits and edges connect squares diagonally adjacent, reflecting allowed movements.

concepts.canonical_name: Iterating Through Vertices of a Connected Component
concepts.short_definition: The process of visiting each vertex in a connected component to perform computations such as counting associated elements (e.g., coins).

concepts.canonical_name: Symmetry of Movements in a Graph
concepts.short_definition: If a move from vertex u to vertex v exists, then the reverse move from v to u also exists, making the graph undirected.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Construction with Vertex Degree Constraints
concepts.short_definition: A graph where each vertex has at most 4 incident edges, leading to |E| ∈ O(n^2) when there are |V| ∈ O(n^2) vertices.

concepts.canonical_name: Maximum Coins Collection in a Connected Component
concepts.short_definition: The maximum number of coins that can be collected by traversing a single connected component in the graph, since all coins within the CC can be reached and retraced.
A directed graph representing possible movements with direction specified on edges.

concepts.canonical_name: Number of coins in an SCC
concepts.short_definition: The count of coins associated with the vertices in a strongly connected component (SCC) of a graph.
A super source is an added vertex in a flow network that connects to multiple source vertices via edges, enabling simplification or transformation of the flow problem.

concepts.canonical_name: Edge Weight Assignment in Cost Graph
concepts.short_definition: Assigning edge weights in a cost graph by setting the weight of an edge from A to B as the negative of the cost of node B, including edges originating from the source node S.
The graph in which the SSSP computation is performed using DAG Relaxation.

concepts.canonical_name: Directed Edge in a Grid Graph
concepts.short_definition: An edge in a directed grid graph that connects vertex (x, y) to vertex (x + 1, y + 1) when x and y satisfy certain bounds.

concepts.canonical_name: Number of Edges in Kingambit-Free Graph
concepts.short_definition: The count of edges in a graph without Kingambits: 2(n-1)^2 if undirected, 4(n-1)^2 if directed.
Subsets of vertices in a directed graph where replacing all directed edges with undirected edges makes the subset connected.
A BFS or DFS traversal starting from a single given source vertex, exploring reachable vertices from that source.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Modeling for Coin Collection Problem
concepts.short_definition: Representing coins and reachable paths in a graph, with consideration for traversal constraints such as collecting coins once, and graph structure.
Using condensation graphs to understand strongly connected components for coin collection, considering no edges between SCCs.
A grid navigation problem where a character named Pawniard moves on an n × n chessboard with coins on certain squares, collecting coins by moving according to specified rules.
An algorithm design approach for computing a path or maximum collection on a grid according to movement rules, here specialized for Pawniard's movement constraints.
The construction of a directed graph representing possible pawn moves from each square, including a supersource vertex connecting to the initial row.
Assigning weights to edges based on target node attributes, such as negative weights if the target node contains a specific item like a coin, and zero otherwise.
The properties of the graph including number of vertices n^2 and constant in-degree affecting algorithm complexity.
In grid graphs where paths collect coins, maximum coin collecting paths may end before the last row but there exists an equally optimal path ending in the front row (row n-1).

concepts.canonical_name: Proof Strategy Using Graph Closure Property (GCP) Arguments
concepts.short_definition: Using arguments related to the Graph Closure Property (GCP) to prove existence of certain optimal paths in the problem context.
An ordering of sequences based on the alphabetical order of their components, similar to dictionary order.

A method of constructing a graph G=(C,E) where vertices represent squares from files, and edges represent specific sequential relationships between squares in consecutive files based on ordering constraints.

concepts.canonical_name: Shortest Path in Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)
concepts.short_definition: Finding the shortest path from a start node s in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) with given edge weights.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming on Paths in a DAG
concepts.short_definition: Approach to find optimal paths in Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAG) by considering properties of valid movement paths and using induction to prove sufficiency of ending paths in a specific row.

concepts.canonical_name: Prefix of a path in grid coin collection
concepts.short_definition: A path prefix constructed by including squares up to a certain coordinate, used to compare coin collection outcomes in grid paths.

concepts.canonical_name: Coin collection score equality of paths
concepts.short_definition: The phenomenon where two different paths collect the same number of coins after a certain shared prefix in a grid.

concepts.canonical_name: Path Modification to Increase Coin Collection
concepts.short_definition: A method of modifying a path through a grid to collect more coins by adjusting the route to include a coin at a certain coordinate.

concepts.canonical_name: Path with Maximum Number of Coins
concepts.short_definition: A path in a grid that collects the maximum possible number of coins along its route.
Using a previously assumed property about sub-paths to prove properties about larger paths in a grid coin collection problem.

concepts.canonical_name: Construction of Path Q From Path Q'
concepts.short_definition: Extending a path that ends at a coin by adding steps to collect additional coins and continue forward, to maintain or increase the number of collected coins.

concepts.canonical_name: Property 1 in Grid Coin Collection Path Problem
concepts.short_definition: A property stating that for any path, there exists an at least as optimal path ending at a specific row with maximum coins.
Finding the shortest path between vertices s and t in a colored, positive-weighted undirected graph where the path contains edges of at least three distinct colors.
An algorithmic method to track additional state information (like colors seen) by duplicating the graph multiple times to represent different states along paths.
Shortest path problem variant where the path must satisfy color constraints such as containing edges of at least k distinct colors.

concepts.canonical_name: Directed Graph Construction with Color Sets
concepts.short_definition: Constructing a directed graph G' = (V', E', w') from an original graph G = (V, E, w), where vertices in V' are pairs of original vertices and relevant color sets, and edges in E' connect these pairs based on original edges and augmented color sets.
The process of mapping paths or results from a modified or expanded graph back onto the original graph structure.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity Analysis of Dijkstra's Algorithm for Modified Graph G'
concepts.short_definition: Analyzing the runtime of Dijkstra's algorithm on a transformed graph G' that has increased number of vertices and edges, resulting in a total runtime of O(|V| log |V|).

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Duplication Techniques for Color-Constrained Shortest Paths
concepts.short_definition: Method of duplicating graphs multiple times to handle constraints such as colors seen along paths in shortest path problems.

concepts.canonical_name: Midterm Examination in Calculus or Engineering course
concepts.short_definition: A formal examination consisting of problems assessing knowledge and problem-solving skills in subject matter relevant to the course, in particular for the midterm 2 practice.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Model for City and Flight Network
concepts.short_definition: Representation of cities as nodes and flights as directed edges with associated costs in a graph.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Algorithm for Constrained Shortest Path
concepts.short_definition: An efficient algorithm to find shortest paths under constraints, such as no two consecutive same city lectures.

concepts.canonical_name: No Consecutive Lectures in Same City Constraint
concepts.short_definition: A constraint that Erik cannot give two consecutive lectures in the same city.

concepts.canonical_name: Net Cost Minimization in Path Planning
concepts.short_definition: Calculating the total cost as flight costs minus earnings from delivering lectures, aiming to minimize this net cost.

A graph G = (V, E) where V is the set of nodes (e.g., cities) and E is the set of directed edges with weights representing some value (e.g., cost or profit) associated with traveling from one node to another.

concepts.canonical_name: Edge Weight Definition in Flight Graph
concepts.short_definition: The weight of an edge from city u to city v is defined as pu,v − rv, where pu,v might represent a flight property such as price or profit, and rv some cost or value at city v.
The time complexity of the Bellman-Ford algorithm is O(nm), where n is the number of vertices and m is the number of edges in the graph.
Representing all cities (vertices) as integers in the range [1, n] to optimize graph algorithms.
A path in a graph that starts and ends at the same vertex (a cycle).

concepts.canonical_name: Cheapest Tour Avoids Leaving Start Vertex
concepts.short_definition: An explanation that a cheapest tour starting and ending in a vertex does not leave that vertex when zero-cost self-looping is possible because leaving would lead to non-optimality or infinite profit cycles.
A function that describes the likelihood of each outcome in the sample space of a random experiment.
The probability of an event occurring given that another event has already occurred.
A theorem that relates conditional probabilities of events and allows the computation of one from the other using prior probabilities.
The weighted average or mean value of a random variable's possible outcomes, weighted by their probabilities.
A variable that takes numerical values determined by the outcome of a random experiment.

Given a directed graph with non-negative edge weights and vertices s and t, compute the minimal path length ∆(s,t) that is strictly longer than the shortest path distance δ(s,t), or infinity if no such second-shortest path exists.
The method of adjusting the weights of edges in a graph using a potential function δG(s, −) applied to each edge.
The process of translating or replicating edges from an original graph to a duplicated graph with vertex copies, with specific inclusion rules depending on edge weights.
A technique to modify edge weights in a graph so that shortest path computations can be simplified or improved, often used in algorithms like Johnson's algorithm.
A method of constructing an auxiliary graph G′ with duplicated vertices and edges to facilitate or analyze algorithms for shortest paths or related problems.
The shortest path from all vertices to a single destination vertex in a graph.
The process of initializing a running minimum variable to positive infinity before starting a minimization procedure.

concepts.canonical_name: Edge Weight in a Weighted Graph
concepts.short_definition: The assigned weight w(u, v) associated with an edge between vertices u and v in a graph.
The sum of shortest distances from source to u, edge weight from u to v, and shortest distance from v to target.
The concept of outputting the best or optimal decision variable δ* in a decision-making or optimization context.
A proof demonstrating the correctness of a modification to Dijkstra's algorithm ensuring it correctly computes desired shortest path metrics under given constraints.

concepts.canonical_name: Incorrect Approach to Shortest Path Using δ(s,v) + δ(v,t)
concepts.short_definition: An approach that checks every vertex v and computes the sum of shortest distances δ(s, v) + δ(v, t), which is incorrect as a method to find the shortest path from s to t.
Functions d1(v) and d2(v) representing the shortest and second-shortest distance estimates from a source node s to any node v in a graph, initialized with d1(s)=0 and all others to infinity.
A priority queue data structure whose priority values can be changed or updated after insertion.
Ordering elements in a priority queue by comparing their keys lexicographically, i.e., first by the first key element, then by the second as a tiebreaker.

concepts.canonical_name: Second Shortest Path Algorithm Using Modified Dijkstra
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that computes the second shortest path distances d2(t) in a graph by maintaining two distance estimates d1 and d2 per vertex, using modified priority queue operations with at most 2|V| DELETE-MIN and up to 4|E| DECREASE-KEY operations, running in O(|V| log |V| + |E|) time.
A conceptual approach for shortest path computation where vertices are duplicated as v0 and v1 to maintain two distance estimates d1(v) and d2(v), facilitating second shortest path calculations.

concepts.canonical_name: Priority Queue Operations in Modified Dijkstra Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: Operations such as BUILD, DELETE-MIN, and DECREASE-KEY on a priority queue tailored to maintain two distance estimates per vertex in the second shortest path algorithm variant.

concepts.canonical_name: Common Mistakes in Second Shortest Path Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: Typical incorrect assumptions leading to wrong or inefficient second shortest path algorithms, including uniqueness of shortest path, only modifying last edge, or using incorrect relaxation strategies.

concepts.canonical_name: Bellman-Ford Algorithm Runtime for Second Shortest Path
concepts.short_definition: When attempting to fix correctness of second shortest path algorithms by modifying edge relaxation beyond Dijkstra, the runtime degrades to O(|V||E|), as in Bellman-Ford algorithm.

concepts.canonical_name: Edge Checking Method for Second Shortest Path
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm technique that tests edges not on the shortest path to find the second shortest path length.

concepts.canonical_name: Dijkstra's Algorithm Modification for Second Shortest Path
concepts.short_definition: A modification of Dijkstra's algorithm that tracks shortest and second shortest distances to nodes.
Technique denoting distances d1(v) as shortest distance and d2(v) as second-shortest distance estimates to vertex v.

concepts.canonical_name: Prefix Path Property of Second Shortest Paths
concepts.short_definition: Any prefix subpath of a second-shortest path is itself either a shortest path or a second-shortest path to that vertex.

concepts.canonical_name: Order of removal in a data structure
concepts.short_definition: The concept that elements with a specific associated value are removed before other elements according to a given fact or rule, as exemplified by the removal order of (d1(v), v, 1) occurring before (d2(v), v, 2).
Notation defining the shortest path distance as δ1(v) and the second-shortest path distance as δ2(v) from source to vertex v.

concepts.canonical_name: Priority Queue Operations in Shortest Path Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: Operations involving adding and removing elements from a priority queue during algorithm execution, ensuring that shortest or second-shortest path distances are correctly updated.
Basic experience programming in Python 3.
Solid knowledge of set theory, relations and logic, combinatorics, proofs, recursion, number theory, graph theory, probability, and asymptotic notation.
A short quiz covering specific lectures, intended as practice and preparation for exams.
A weekly graded assignment designed to practice algorithms, data structures, and proof techniques introduced in lectures and recitations.
A programming assignment within a problem set which requires coding one of the algorithms presented in class.
Guidelines and advice regarding timely submission of homework and handling late assignments.
Guidelines outlining allowed and disallowed forms of student collaboration on problem sets, including crediting collaborators and producing individual work.

concepts.canonical_name: Homework Submission Timing and Its Impact on Learning
concepts.short_definition: The effect of submitting problem sets late on understanding subsequent material and performance on future problem sets.
The requirement to credit collaborators by including their names for each problem or stating None if no collaboration occurred.

concepts.canonical_name: Individual Authorship of Problem Set Solutions
concepts.short_definition: Requirement to produce solutions in one’s own words reflecting individual understanding, even after collaboration to arrive at answers.

concepts.canonical_name: Appropriate Use of Piazza for Course Questions
concepts.short_definition: Guidance on using Piazza public posts for clarification questions and private posts for individual solution queries until solutions are posted.

concepts.canonical_name: Effect of Reviewing Homework Solutions on Exam Performance
concepts.short_definition: Understanding differences in solutions, especially proofs, aids exam preparation and helps learning.
The rules and procedures for requesting a regrade on midterm or final exams including requirements and restrictions.
The weighted average scheme allocating percentages to problem sets, midterms, and final exam for the overall course grade.
The rule reducing the weight of the lowest exam score by 10 percentage points in computing the overall grade.
The minimum average exam score required to pass the course, typically about 30% weighted across all three exams.

concepts.canonical_name: Effective Learning Strategies for Conceptual Material
concepts.short_definition: Recommended study practices for mastering conceptual course material such as reviewing notes, spreading out problem solving, and engaging deeply with problem sets before solutions are provided.
Measure of an algorithm's resource usage such as number of operations or memory; an algorithm is optimal if it uses the smallest possible resources for the problem it solves.
Computational problem to compute the sum of two integers each represented with n digits from 0 to 9, output represented with n+1 digits.
An algorithm that performs integer addition by incrementing one number by 1 repeatedly y times.

concepts.canonical_name: Grade School Algorithm for Integer Addition
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that adds two integers by adding their least significant digits, storing the result digit and a carry, progressing digit by digit.
A single-digit arithmetic operation counted towards the running time of an addition algorithm.
The fact that grade school addition algorithm achieves the best possible asymptotic basic operation count O(n) and no algorithm can do addition with fewer than O(n) basic operations.
Recursive function incrementing a digit array representing a number by one, handling carry appropriately.
A fundamental computational step involving reading or writing a digit in integer addition or multiplication.
The minimum number of basic operations required to add two n-digit integers is Ω(n).
The task of computing the product of two n-digit nonnegative integers, producing their product also as digits from 0 to 9.
Computing multiplication by repeated addition, i.e., adding x to itself y times; an exponential-time algorithm.
The traditional multiplication method involving multiplying each digit of one number by each digit of the other, then summing with proper place value shifts to form the product.
An algorithm for multiplying n-digit integers by performing O(n^2) single-digit multiplications and additions, reflecting the typical multiplication taught in school.
The computational complexity of grade-school multiplication is Θ(n^2), meaning it requires on the order of n^2 basic operations.
The hypothesis proposed by Andrey Kolmogorov that any correct algorithm for integer multiplication must require at least Ω(n^2) basic operations, implying the grade-school method is optimal.
An application of divide-and-conquer to multiplication by splitting numbers into halves, recursively multiplying parts, and combining results to multiply large integers.
An algorithm to multiply two n-digit numbers using 4 multiplications of n/2-digit numbers plus additional additions and shifts, resulting in a recurrence T(n) ≤ 4T(n/2) + Cn.
Recurrence relation expressing the time complexity as T(n) ≤ 4T(n/2) + Cn for the multiplication algorithm.
Methods to determine asymptotic solutions to recurrence relations, including recurrence tree method, guess-and-check method, and the Master theorem.

concepts.canonical_name: Padding with Zeros to Make n a Power of 2
concepts.short_definition: A technique that ensures input size n is a power of two by adding zeros before starting recursive integer multiplication, so that recursive calls operate on evenly sized chunks, maintaining O(n²) complexity.

concepts.canonical_name: Padding with Zeros at Each Recursion Step to Ensure Even n
concepts.short_definition: A method of making recursive integer multiplication work by adding at most one zero at each recursion step to ensure n is even, proving T(n) ≤ 4T(⌈n/2⌉) + Cn and thus O(n²) complexity.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity Recurrence Relation for Karatsuba's Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The recurrence T(n) ≤ 3T(n/2) + Cn captures the number of elementary operations required by Karatsuba's algorithm to multiply two n-digit integers.
Karatsuba's algorithm runs in time O(n^log2(3)) ≈ O(n^1.59), which is faster than the classical O(n^2) multiplication algorithm.
Python's integer multiplication selects among grade school, Karatsuba, and FFT multiplication algorithms depending on operand size.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm Selection Based on Input Size
concepts.short_definition: Choosing the optimal multiplication algorithm for integer multiplication based on the number of binary digits, balancing constant factors and asymptotic improvements.
An integer multiplication algorithm using the Fast Fourier Transform to achieve O(n log n log log n) basic operations.
A fast algorithm to compute the discrete Fourier transform, used as a tool in algorithms such as Schönhage-Strassen for efficient integer multiplication.

concepts.canonical_name: Harvey and van der Hoeven integer multiplication algorithm
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm for integer multiplication achieving O(n log n) basic operations, discovered in 2019.
Computing a high-precision representation of a division a/b, often by first computing a high-precision representation of 1/b.
A high-precision integer approximation of 1/b, such as ⌊R/b⌋ for a large R that is easy to divide by, used as a key step in high-precision division.
An iterative method to compute a high precision reciprocal R/b by finding the zero of the function f(x) = 1/x - b/R using Newton's method iteration.
The iterative update χ_{i+1} = 2 χ_i - b χ_i^2 * R, applied for reciprocal computation in high-precision division.
A method of problem-solving that involves understanding and creating algorithms rather than memorizing formulas.
A rate of convergence of an iterative method where the number of correct digits approximately doubles with each step.
Representing numbers in base-2 numeral system, using only digits 0 and 1.

concepts.canonical_name: Iterative Method for Computing Square Roots
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm using successive approximations to find the square root of a number, updating guesses via a formula.
The technique of reducing a complex problem to a simpler version that is still unsolved and working on that simpler problem to make progress towards solving the original.

concepts.canonical_name: Taking Breaks to Improve Problem Solving
concepts.short_definition: The strategy of taking breaks when stuck on a problem, to allow subconscious processing and avoid unproductive repetitive thinking.
An algorithm is correct if it gives a correct answer for every possible input.
An algorithm is efficient if it uses few resources such as running time and memory.
A method of measuring the running time or resource usage of an algorithm based on the worst possible input of a given size.
A theoretical computational model that assumes algorithms operate on words of fixed size; used to analyze algorithm efficiency.
The observation that an algorithm's running time can vary significantly based on the specific input provided.
The analysis and measurement of the computational resources (like time) used by an algorithm, independent of the hardware executing it.
A mathematical abstraction defining what basic operations an algorithm can execute, representing a computer's operation set.
An indivisible basic action defined within a model of computation, counting toward algorithm runtime analysis.
A w-bit unit of data in the word-RAM model that can represent numbers, characters, or binary data.
The number of bits per word, determines addressable memory size; typically w = O(log n) for input size n to allow growing memory access.
Basic operations executed by the processor per time step including integer arithmetic, logical operators, bitwise operators, memory load/store, conditional branches, and halt.
A constant-length list of instructions stored in read-only memory executed sequentially by the processor.

concepts.canonical_name: Input and Output in Word-RAM Model
concepts.short_definition: Input is initially stored in the first n words of memory; output is defined as contents of memory cells M[0] to M[R[0]] when the program halts.

concepts.canonical_name: Relationship Between Word-RAM Steps and Real-World Running Time
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm running in T(n) steps on a word-RAM model can be converted into a program running in O(T(n)) steps on real computers, reflecting practical performance and hardware independence.

A model where algorithms are written in a higher-level language (English prose or Python-like pseudocode) instead of low-level word-RAM instructions, requiring mental compilation to word-RAM for running time analysis.

concepts.canonical_name: Running Time of Integer Addition in Pythonic Model
concepts.short_definition: The running time is Θ(|x| + |y|), where |x| and |y| represent integer lengths in words, based on schoolbook addition.

concepts.canonical_name: Running Time of Integer Multiplication via Karatsuba Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The running time using the Karatsuba method is 𝑂((|x| + |y|)^{log 3}) where |x| and |y| are lengths in words.
Appending an element to a list in Python using table doubling has an amortized cost of Θ(1).
Concatenation of two lists, L1 + L2, costs Θ(|L1| + |L2|) by iterating over both lists.

concepts.canonical_name: Running Time of List In-Place Concatenation
concepts.short_definition: In-place concatenation (L1 += L2) runs in Θ(1 + |L2|) by iterating over the second list only.

concepts.canonical_name: Running Time of Membership Test in List
concepts.short_definition: Testing if x is in list L requires iterating over entire list, costing Θ(|L|).

concepts.canonical_name: Running Time of Length Retrieval in List
concepts.short_definition: Retrieving the length of a list is Θ(1) because the list stores length in an internal field.
Sorting a list L with a comparison-based sort runs in Θ(|L| log |L|).
Dictionary insertion and membership test have Θ(1) amortized expected running time for word-sized keys and values based on hashing.
Set operations have the same amortized expected cost as dictionary operations since sets are dictionaries with values all equal to 1.

concepts.canonical_name: Impact of Implementation on Operation Cost
concepts.short_definition: Even simple operations like deleting the first element of a list (del L[0]) can be costly depending on implementation.
An index i in an integer array A such that A[i] is at least as large as its neighbors.
Given an integer array A of length n, find an index i that is a peak in A.
The first or last index is a peak if its neighbor is less or equal; there may be multiple peaks; the global maximum index is a peak; every list has at least one peak.
An array A where A[i] < A[i+1] for every i in 0 to len(A)-2.
Checklist for describing an algorithm: English description, optional pseudocode, and correctness proof.

concepts.canonical_name: Exhaustive Search Algorithm for Finding Peak
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm scanning an entire array from left to right checking each index to determine if it is a peak and returning the first found peak index.
The minimum time an algorithm takes on any input of size n, asymptotically described (e.g. O(1)).
An element in an array that is greater than or equal to its neighbors.
An algorithm that calls itself with smaller inputs until a base case is reached.

concepts.canonical_name: Recursive Peak-Finding Algorithm Using Binary Search
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that finds a peak element in an array by checking the middle element, then recursively exploring the half of the array where a peak must exist based on neighbor comparisons.

concepts.canonical_name: Strong Induction Method for Recursive Algorithm Correctness
concepts.short_definition: A proof technique which assumes correctness of recursive calls to prove correctness of the overall recursive algorithm.
A divide-and-conquer algorithm that finds a peak element in an array by recursively searching a subarray and comparing neighbors, running in O(log n) time.
A mathematical relation defining the time complexity T(n) of recursive algorithms as T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1), leading to O(log n) runtime.
The tight bound notation denoting that the algorithm runs both in O(log n) and Ω(log n) time, written as Θ(log n).
Technique of replacing recursive calls with a while loop to improve practical runtime and avoid call stack overhead.
In Python, slicing a list like A[0:j-1] takes O(j) time because it creates a new list copy, impacting algorithm efficiency if used naively in recursive calls.

A measure of the computational resources (such as time or memory) that an algorithm uses relative to the size of its input, often expressed in terms of exponential, polynomial, or logarithmic time complexity.
A data store combined with methods for accessing and manipulating the stored data.
A mathematical specification for a data structure defining the types of objects represented and the required behavior of operations.
How a data structure is represented in memory together with algorithms for the required operations of an interface.
Last In First Out order for accessing elements where the most recently added element is accessed first.

A pointer-based data structure for stacks where each node contains an item and a pointer to the next node below it, maintaining a head pointer to the top of the stack allowing Θ(1) time insertion and deletion at the top.
A contiguous memory chunk used to implement a stack by maintaining a pointer to the next empty cell, enabling push and pop operations in Θ(1) time for fixed size.

concepts.canonical_name: Static Array Limitation for Stack Implementation
concepts.short_definition: A limitation where a static array can only store a fixed number of elements, which is problematic if the number of elements is unknown or the array fills up.

A stack implementation that uses a dynamic array that resizes by allocating a new array and copying elements, typically doubling the array size when full to ensure amortized efficient push operations.

concepts.canonical_name: Amortized Cost of Push Operation in Dynamic Array
concepts.short_definition: The average cost per push operation in a dynamic array sequence, which is constant (Θ(1)) due to amortization despite occasional expensive resizes.
Analyzing the total runtime of a sequence of operations on a data structure, starting from an empty state, to understand aggregate and amortized costs.
The additional memory used beyond the memory required to store the actual data, expressed as a function of the number of elements stored.
The memory overhead of dynamic arrays is Θ(n) because they may allocate space up to twice the number of stored elements (2n) when doubling capacity.
The additional memory overhead involved in storing elements in a linked list, including memory used by pointers to link nodes together.
The operation of removing the last element from a dynamic array, with cost Θ(1) per pop.

concepts.canonical_name: Infinite Memory Overhead from Empty Large Arrays
concepts.short_definition: When popping all elements from a large array, the underlying allocated array size remains large and empty, effectively resulting in infinite overhead.

concepts.canonical_name: Resizing Strategy to Restore Θ(n) Overhead
concepts.short_definition: The strategy to resize the array when deleting elements, such as halving its size when it is underutilized, to maintain Θ(n) memory overhead.

concepts.canonical_name: Halving Array on Quarter Full Condition
concepts.short_definition: The resizing rule where the array is halved when its usage drops to one quarter to maintain efficient memory usage and constant amortized operation costs.

concepts.canonical_name: Amortized Analysis of Push and Pop Sequences
concepts.short_definition: The technique of analyzing sequences of push and pop operations on dynamic arrays to show the overall average cost per operation remains constant despite occasional costly resizing.

concepts.canonical_name: Amortized Cost Analysis using Potential Functions
concepts.short_definition: An analysis technique bounding the average cost of operations over sequences via a potential function representing stored 'credit' in the data structure.
A potential function for dynamic arrays defined as ϕ(A) = c|n − m/2|, where n is elements count, m is capacity, c a constant, used to analyze amortized costs of push and pop operations.

concepts.canonical_name: Amortized Cost of Pop Operation in Dynamic Arrays
concepts.short_definition: The amortized cost of pop operation without resizing is O(1) with potential change at most c.
An abstract data type that maintains a sequence of items and supports operations such as build, iteration, getting/setting items by index, insertion, and deletion at arbitrary positions.
An abstract data type that allows insertion and deletion of elements at both the front and back ends efficiently.
A dynamic data structure where elements are nodes linked by pointers, allowing efficient insertions and deletions at the front but linear time access by index.
A fixed-size array data structure that provides constant time access to elements but requires O(n) time for insertions and deletions in the middle due to shifting elements.
A data structure that extends dynamic arrays to allow insertions and deletions at both the front and back in amortized Θ(1) time.

An interface that maintains a collection of unique keys with associated items, supporting operations such as insertion, deletion, membership queries, as well as order-based queries like finding minimum or maximum.

concepts.canonical_name: Set Operations: build, len, find, insert, delete
concepts.short_definition: Basic operations on the Set ADT include: build(A) to construct from iterable A; len() to return count; find(k) to get item with key k; insert(x) to add item; delete(k) to remove item with key k.

Operations on an ordered Set that rely on the key ordering: iter ord() to iterate in key order; find min() and find max() to get smallest and largest keys respectively; find next(k) and find prev(k) to get adjacent keys in order.
A variation of the Set interface that allows duplicate keys; find operations return one of the elements with the given key.
A simple implementation of a set by storing elements sequentially in an array with operations having specific time complexities.
An implementation of set where the array storing elements is sorted by keys, enabling logarithmic search times but linear insertion and deletion times.
The problem of arranging elements of an array into a sorted order based on a key comparison.
An arrangement of the same elements in a different order.
A sorting algorithm using only O(1) extra space beyond the input array.
Sorting which preserves the input order of elements with equal keys.
A proof that insertion sort correctly sorts an array using induction and case analysis on the insertion of the last element.
Analysis of insertion sort run-time using recurrence relations and induction, showing it has O(n^2) worst-case time complexity.
Insertion sort is stable, preserving the relative order of equal elements during sorting.
Insertion sort grows the sorted region of the array one element at a time.
The recurrence relation S(i) = S(i-1) + O(1), with base case S(1) ∈ Θ(1), describes the runtime for inserting the last element into a sorted portion of the array.
The recurrence relation T(i) = T(i-1) + O(i), with base case T(1) ∈ Θ(1), describes the runtime for insertion sort on i elements.
The subproblem of finding the index of the maximum element in the prefix A[:i+1] of an array A, used within selection sort.
A recursive implementation of selection sort that sorts the prefix A[:i+1] by swapping the maximum element to position i and then sorting A[:i].
Proof by induction that prefix_max correctly returns the index of the maximum element in the prefix A[:i+1].
