Insertion sort has runtime S(1) in Theta(1) and S(i) in O(i), with a lower bound of Omega(i) on adversarial input, showing its time complexity behavior.
Proof by induction that selection sort correctly sorts by placing the largest element last and recursively sorting the rest.
Selection sort has runtime T(1) in Theta(1) and T(i) in O(i^2), with a lower bound of Omega(i^2) on adversarial input, reflecting its quadratic time complexity.
A merging technique for merge sort that uses two indices from the ends of sorted lists, selecting larger elements stepwise to build a merged sorted list.
The procedure that merges two sorted subarrays into a single sorted array segment.

concepts.canonical_name: Recurrence Relation for Merge Sort Runtime
concepts.short_definition: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) represents the runtime of merge sort.

concepts.canonical_name: Recursion Tree Analysis for Merge Sort
concepts.short_definition: A method analyzing the recursion tree of merge sort showing total work is O(n log n).

concepts.canonical_name: Base Case in Merge Sort Correctness Proof
concepts.short_definition: The base case that for n ≤1, the array is already sorted and thus trivially correct.

concepts.canonical_name: Inductive Step in Merge Sort Correctness Proof
concepts.short_definition: Assuming the algorithm works correctly for smaller arrays and using merge's correctness to prove overall correctness.

concepts.canonical_name: Merge Procedure Correctness Proof by Induction
concepts.short_definition: Proof that merge correctly merges by taking the largest item from the sorted arrays and recursively merging remainder.
The runtime of the merge procedure is linear, O(n), where n is the total length of the arrays being merged.
The merge procedure requires at least Omega(n) time on every input.
Merge sort preserves the relative order of equal elements during sorting.
The process of combining two sorted arrays into one sorted array during merge sort.
Finding an index (i, j) in a two-dimensional array where the element is greater than or equal to its neighbors.

concepts.canonical_name: Divide and Conquer Algorithm for 2D Peak Finding
concepts.short_definition: A divide and conquer method applied to 2D arrays to locate a peak by dividing the array into subarrays based on columns.
An element in a 2D array that is greater than or equal to all its neighbors.
An algorithm that finds a peak element in a 2D array by recursively checking midpoint columns and their maximum elements, deciding which subarray to recurse into.

concepts.canonical_name: Induction Proof for Correctness of 2D Peak-Finding Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: A proof technique that shows the 2D peak-finding algorithm is correct by using induction on the number of columns in the array.
Proof of correctness for binary search using base case and induction on array size.
Analysis showing binary search runs in O(log n) time using recursion relations and substitution.
A model of sorting algorithms where the only permitted operations to gain information about input items are binary comparisons between pairs of items.
Sorting algorithms that determine the sorted order solely by comparing pairs of elements using comparison operators such as <, ≤, >, ≥, =, and ≠.
The running time of merge sort algorithm, which is Θ(n log n) in the worst case.
The running time of selection sort algorithm, which is Θ(n²) in the worst case.
Modeling any algorithm as a decision tree where internal nodes represent binary comparisons, leaves represent algorithm termination, and root-to-leaf paths represent executions.

concepts.canonical_name: Binary Tree Height and Leaves Relationship
concepts.short_definition: In a binary tree, the minimum height h for N leaves is at least log N, and the maximum number of leaves for height h is at most 2^h.

concepts.canonical_name: Merge Sort Optimality in Comparison Model
concepts.short_definition: Merge Sort achieves the theoretical lower bound of Ω(n log n) running time among comparison-based sorting algorithms, making it optimal within this model.
Height of decision tree with branching factor b and Ω(N) leaves is Ω(log_b N), influencing the running time complexity of sorting algorithms.
Using Word-RAM model's O(1) random access indexing on words of size w enables algorithms with linear branching factor, breaking the Ω(n log n) comparison model lower bound for sorting.

A sorting algorithm that inserts each item into a direct access array at the index corresponding to the item's key and then outputs the items in key order, achieving a running time of Θ(u) where u is the range of keys.

concepts.canonical_name: Sorting by Least Significant Key First
concepts.short_definition: A technique in lexicographic sorting where sorting is performed starting from the least significant key to the most significant, using a stable sort at each step.

concepts.canonical_name: Sorting by Most Significant Key First
concepts.short_definition: A technique in lexicographic sorting where sorting is performed starting from the most significant key to the least significant, sorting equivalent elements by remaining keys.
Representing a key k as a tuple (a, b) such that k = an + b, where a and b are digits in base n, used for radix sorting keys with larger ranges.
The property that Radix Sort can sort n keys in O(n) time when the number of digit components is constant and each digit is in range 0 to n-1.
The range or universe of possible key values from which the elements to sort can be drawn; important in analyzing the time complexity of counting sort and radix sort.
Time complexity expression for radix sort typically given as Θ(n + n log_n(u)) which can be linear if the domain of keys u is Θ(n^c).

Operations such as initialize, static, dynamic, order, set, build, find, insert, find min, find prev, delete, find max, and find next performed on a direct access array data structure, with their time complexities.

Operations such as initialize, static, dynamic, order, set, build, find, insert, find min, find prev, delete, find max, and find next performed on a hash table data structure, with their time complexities including expected and amortized times.

concepts.canonical_name: Use of Sorted Array for Range Queries
concepts.short_definition: The data structure choice where a sorted array is preferred for range queries, e.g., retrieving all elements with keys between two values.

concepts.canonical_name: Use of Hash Table for Key Lookups
concepts.short_definition: Using hash tables for efficient key lookups, typically for retrieving individual elements by exact key match.

concepts.canonical_name: Decision Tree Analysis for Search Lower Bounds
concepts.short_definition: A technique to prove lower bounds on searching complexity in the comparison model by modeling comparisons as nodes and search outcomes as leaves of a binary tree.
A data structure that uses a gigantic array of size u to store items with keys from [u], allowing constant worst-case time find operations by using keys as array indices.
A function that maps keys from a large universe [u] to indices in a smaller array [m], often causing collisions when m<u due to the Pigeonhole Principle.
The event where two distinct keys map to the same index under a hash function, which complicates hash table design and operations.
A collision handling strategy in hash tables where colliding items are stored in other slots within the same table, often using linear probing to find an empty slot.
A type of open addressing collision resolution where the next available slot is found by sequentially checking adjacent slots.
Techniques to handle cases where multiple keys hash to the same array index.

concepts.canonical_name: Running Time of Find Operation in Chaining Hash Table
concepts.short_definition: The find operation takes Θ(1 + L) amortized time, where L is the length of the chain at the hashed index.
The length of the linked list (chain) of keys hashed to the same index in a hash table.
A hash function fixed before hashing that always produces the same output for a given input key.
The principle stating that if more keys than buckets exist, some bucket must have multiple keys, causing collisions.

concepts.canonical_name: Worst-Case Performance of Fixed Hash Functions
concepts.short_definition: The property that fixed hash functions can lead to large sets of keys colliding and causing operations to run in linear time.
A hash function chosen at random to ensure good average-case performance on hash table operations, assuming keys are independent of the chosen function.
The expected length of the chain at the location of the hash for a new key \(k_{new}\) is \( E[L] = 1 + \frac{n}{m} \), where \(n\) is the number of elements and \(m\) the table size.

concepts.canonical_name: Hash Table Resize and Amortized Insertion
concepts.short_definition: The technique of resizing a hash table (such as doubling its size) when the load factor is too large, reinserting all keys, which takes \( \Theta(n) \) time, but results in \( O(1) \) amortized insertion time.
A cryptographic-style hash function used by Python with a random seed that changes per process to provide randomized hashing behavior.
A randomized and keyed hash function family which guarantees that for any two distinct keys, the probability of collision under a randomly chosen hash function is at most 1/m.

concepts.canonical_name: Hash Collision Probability in Universal Hashing
concepts.short_definition: The property of universal hashing that for any two distinct keys, the probability of hash collision is exactly 1 divided by the number of bins m.
A function that defines which slot to try next when a collision occurs in open addressing hashing.
An operation that places a key into the hash table by following the probing scheme until an open slot is found.
An operation to find a key in the hash table by following the probing scheme until the key or an empty slot is found; if an empty slot is found first, the key is not in the table.
A deletion technique where deleted entries are replaced with a special marker key treated as occupied when searching but empty when inserting to avoid disrupting key searches.
A probing scheme in open addressing using the function ℎ(𝑘, 𝑖) = (ℎ′(𝑘) + 𝑖^2) mod 𝑚, which helps spread out collisions in the hash table.
A probing scheme in open addressing using two distinct hash functions ℎ′ and ℎ′′ with the function ℎ(𝑘, 𝑖) = ℎ′(𝑘) + 𝑖· ℎ′′(𝑘), often better than linear or quadratic probing.
The unique node in a binary tree that does not have a parent node.
A single element of a binary tree, which acts as the root of the subtree rooted at that node.

concepts.canonical_name: Ancestor of a Node in Binary Tree
concepts.short_definition: All nodes on the unique path from the root to the given node, excluding the node itself.

concepts.canonical_name: Descendant of a Node in Binary Tree
concepts.short_definition: All nodes in the subtree rooted at the given node, excluding the node itself.

concepts.canonical_name: Depth of a Node in Binary Tree
concepts.short_definition: The number of ancestors the node has; the root node has depth 0.

concepts.canonical_name: Left Child and Right Child in Binary Tree
concepts.short_definition: Classification of a node based on whether it is the left or right child of its parent.
The time complexity of traversing a binary tree with n nodes is Θ(n), where the traversal visits every node exactly once.
An abstract data type that stores unique items and supports operations like search, insert, and delete.
In a binary search tree of height h, all search operations can be performed in time O(h).
Techniques used to keep the height h of a binary search tree to approximately log n to ensure efficient operations.
A tree T has the BST property if, for every node n, all keys in n's left subtree are smaller than n's key, and all keys in the right subtree have larger keys.

concepts.canonical_name: Find Operation in a Binary Search Tree
concepts.short_definition: Searches for a node with key k in a BST, comparing k with the current node's key and recursively searching the left or right subtree accordingly, returning the node if found or None otherwise.
The time complexity of the find operation in a BST is O(h), where h is the height of the tree.
An extension of find that returns two nodes m and M such that m.item.key is the largest key ≤ k, and M.item.key is the smallest key ≥ k.
Operations that implement the order-related interface in a BST, such as iteration in order.
A method to find the node with the minimum key in a binary search tree by recursively going to the left subtree until no left child exists.
A method to find the node with the maximum key in a binary search tree, treated symmetrically to find_min() by recursively going to the right subtree.
The time complexity of in-order traversal is Theta(n), where n is the number of nodes in the tree.
The time complexity of find_min method is Theta(h), where h is the height of the tree.
A method to find the successor of a node x in a BST, defined by two cases depending whether x has a right child or not.
A method to find the predecessor of a node x in a BST, treated symmetrically to find_next(x).

concepts.canonical_name: Successor when node has right child
concepts.short_definition: If node x has a right child, its successor is the minimum node in x's right subtree.

concepts.canonical_name: Proof of successor properties in BST
concepts.short_definition: The proof argument that explains why the successor of a node without right child is the first ancestor reached via a left child by eliminating existence of possible intermediate nodes.
A proof technique involving analyzing the lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a binary tree to argue about properties of the tree.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime of Tree Operations Relative to Height
concepts.short_definition: The runtime of certain tree operations is proportional to the height of the tree, Θ(h), depending on whether you traverse down or up the tree.
Pointers in each tree node that reference the node's parent, which are necessary for certain operations such as finding the successor of a node in in-order traversal.
An algorithm which finds the next node after a given node in the in-order traversal of a binary tree, using conditions on right children and climbing parent pointers.

concepts.canonical_name: In-order Traversal Defines Tree Element Order
concepts.short_definition: The order relation on elements in a binary tree can be defined by the order in which they appear in an in-order traversal, allowing ordering without comparisons.

concepts.canonical_name: Insertion Operation in Binary Search Trees
concepts.short_definition: The procedure to insert a new node into a binary search tree by comparing keys and placing the new node as a leaf in the appropriate subtree, preserving the BST property.
The time complexity of inserting a new node into a binary search tree is Θ(h), where h is the height of the tree.

Procedure to delete an element with a given key from a Binary Search Tree while maintaining BST properties, dealing with cases of leaf nodes, nodes with one child, and nodes with two children by swapping with successor or predecessor as needed.

concepts.canonical_name: Node Deletion in a Binary Search Tree
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm to remove a node from a BST by swapping it with its successor (minimum node in right subtree) and deleting the successor to preserve BST properties and in-order traversal order.
Process to create a binary search tree from an array by either insertion with balancing or building from a sorted array recursively using the middle element as root.
The length of the longest path from the root to a leaf node in a tree.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Binary Search Tree Operations
concepts.short_definition: The running time of operations such as build, find, insert, delete in a BST depends on the height h of the tree; balanced BSTs aim for h in Θ(log n).
A specific tree rotation operation that moves a node down to the left and its right child up to maintain balance in a binary tree.
The measure of balance in a tree node defined as the difference in height between the right and left child subtrees, used to enforce the AVL property that this skew must be between -1 and 1.

concepts.canonical_name: Minimal AVL Tree of Height h
concepts.short_definition: The smallest AVL tree with height h, denoted n_h, used in proofs of AVL tree height properties.
A property defined as the difference of heights between the left and right subtrees, used to determine balance in AVL trees.

concepts.canonical_name: Data Structure Augmentation with Height Field
concepts.short_definition: Augmenting each node in the tree with an additional 'height' field to store its height for constant time calculation of skew in AVL trees.

concepts.canonical_name: Updating Node Heights on Insertion in AVL Trees
concepts.short_definition: The process of updating the height field from the inserted leaf node back up to the root after an insertion, only for affected ancestors to maintain AVL properties.
Deletion of a node from an AVL tree, updating heights and possibly rotating to maintain tree balance.
Updating the height of a node by setting it to max(height of left child, height of right child) + 1 after insertion or deletion.
A violation of the AVL property occurs when the skew (balance factor) of a node is 2 or -2, meaning the tree is unbalanced.
Different scenarios for skew factors (+1, 0, -1) in tree nodes that dictate which rotations are applied to maintain tree balance.
A rotation operation applied at a node to rebalance the tree when the skew factor is +1 or 0.
A rotation operation involving two rotations (e.g., rotate right then rotate left) used to rebalance the tree in cases where a single rotation is insufficient, such as when skew factor is -1.

concepts.canonical_name: Height of a Node in a Binary Tree
concepts.short_definition: The length of the longest path from the node down to a leaf, used to compute skew factors and maintain balance.

concepts.canonical_name: Insertion in AVL Tree and Violation Fixing
concepts.short_definition: When a node is inserted into an AVL tree, if a skew violation occurs (absolute skew >1), rotations fix it without requiring further ancestor rotations.

concepts.canonical_name: Deletion in AVL Tree and Violation Propagation
concepts.short_definition: Deleting a node in an AVL tree may cause skew violations that propagate up the ancestors, possibly requiring multiple rotations up the tree.
A sorting algorithm that inserts each element into an AVL tree (representing a SET), leveraging AVL's O(log n) insertion to achieve efficient sorting.
Implementing a set data structure by using an AVL tree that also satisfies the binary search tree property, allowing efficient operations and ordered traversal.
Implementing a sequence data structure using an AVL tree without enforcing the binary search tree property, enabling efficient ordered operations without sorted order.
A binary search tree (BST) or AVL tree augmented with a size field in each node, storing the number of internal nodes in the subtree rooted at that node, allowing order-statistic operations.

concepts.canonical_name: Subtree Size Field in Order-Statistic Tree Node
concepts.short_definition: The field x.size in a node x of an order-statistic tree stores the number of nodes in the subtree rooted at x, defined as x.left.size + x.right.size + 1, with size of None defined as 0.
Procedure OS-Select(x, i) returns a pointer to the node containing the ith smallest key in the subtree rooted at x by recursively using subtree sizes to guide search.

concepts.canonical_name: Rank of a Node in its Subtree
concepts.short_definition: The rank r of a node x in its subtree is defined as the number of nodes in the left subtree plus one, i.e., r = x.left.size + 1.

concepts.canonical_name: Retrieving the ith Smallest Element in an Order-Statistic Tree
concepts.short_definition: Using OS-Select to find the ith smallest element by comparing i to the rank r of the current node and recursively searching in either left or right subtree accordingly.
The use of recursive calls in OS-Select to navigate the tree by updating the node and rank parameters to find the target element.
The worst-case running time of the OS-Select procedure is proportional to the height of the order-statistic tree, which is O(lg n) if the tree is balanced (e.g., AVL tree).
An algorithm that returns the rank of a node x in an order-statistic tree by accumulating sizes of left subtrees and ascending the tree.

concepts.canonical_name: Rank of a Node in a Binary Search Tree
concepts.short_definition: The position of the node in the linear order determined by an inorder traversal, i.e., the number of nodes having keys less than or equal to the node's key.

concepts.canonical_name: Subtree Size Maintenance in Order-Statistic Trees
concepts.short_definition: The process of maintaining the size metadata in each node that records the number of nodes in the subtree rooted there to allow efficient rank and selection operations.

concepts.canonical_name: Maintaining Subtree Sizes in AVL Trees
concepts.short_definition: The process of updating the size fields of nodes during traversal, insertion, deletion, and rotations in AVL trees to keep track of subtree node counts.

Theorem stating that if a field f in an AVL tree node can be computed using only node x and its children’s values in constant time, then f can be maintained during insertions and deletions without affecting O(lg n) performance.
During AVL tree deletions, rotations occur in logarithmic number requiring O(1) time to update augmented fields per rotation, preserving overall O(lg n) operation time.
An AVL tree augmented to maintain a dynamic set of intervals, supporting efficient interval queries and updates.
Representation of intervals as pairs [t1, t2] with t1 ≤ t2, and the trichotomy that any two intervals either overlap, are to the left, or to the right of each other.
Operation that adds an element x with a non-empty interval field into an interval tree T.
An operation that removes a specific element x from an interval tree T.
An operation that returns a pointer to an element in an interval tree T whose interval overlaps with the given interval i, or None if no such interval exists.
Two intervals overlap if they share at least one point - specifically, the search tests if i overlaps [x.low, x.high].
The justification for why the Interval-Search procedure correctly finds an overlapping interval or returns None if none exists, based on the maximum endpoint values and AVL tree properties.

An algorithm to search for an interval overlapping a given interval in an interval tree by traversing a single path from the root, moving left or right based on interval overlaps and subtree maximum endpoints.
The maximum high endpoint of any interval stored in the left subtree of node x in an interval tree, used to guide search decisions.
The justification that the interval search procedure only examines a single path from the root and guarantees finding an overlapping interval if one exists in the tree.

concepts.canonical_name: Non-overlapping Intervals Property in Interval Tree Search
concepts.short_definition: If no interval in the left subtree overlaps the query interval, and the left subtree maximum endpoint is greater or equal to the query's low endpoint, then no intervals in the right subtree can overlap the query interval in an AVL-based interval tree keyed by low endpoints.
An edge represented by an ordered pair (u, v) of vertices in a graph.
An edge represented by an unordered pair {u, v} of vertices in a graph, where (u, v) and (v, u) represent the same edge.
A graph where edges are distinct pairs of distinct vertices with no multiple edges or loops; edges occur only once and connect different vertices.
Practical uses of graphs including modeling networks (road, computer, social) and state spaces of discrete systems like puzzles and workflows.
The set of vertices v in V such that there is an edge from u to v, denoted Adj+(u) = {v ∈ V | (u, v) ∈ E}.
The set of vertices v in V such that there is an edge from v to u, denoted Adj−(u) = {v ∈ V | (v, u) ∈ E}.
The number of outgoing edges from a vertex u, defined as deg+(u) = |Adj+(u)|.
The number of incoming edges to a vertex u, defined as deg−(u) = |Adj−(u)|.
In an undirected graph, the incoming neighbor set equals the outgoing neighbor set, and the in-degree equals the out-degree, i.e., Adj−(u) = Adj+(u) and deg−(u) = deg+(u).
When no superscript is used, adjacency means outgoing adjacency and degree means out-degree, i.e., Adj(u) = Adj+(u) and deg(u) = deg+(u).

A graph can be stored using a matrix indexed by vertices u and v, where each entry specifies whether an edge exists between u and v, allowing constant time lookup for edge existence but linear time for adjacency iteration.

A graph can be represented by mapping each vertex u to its adjacency list Adj(u), which stores its neighbors, allowing efficient iteration and linear space complexity with respect to vertices and edges.

concepts.canonical_name: Space Complexity of Graph Storage Using Adjacency Lists
concepts.short_definition: The space complexity of storing a graph using adjacency lists is Θ(|V| + |E|), where |V| is the number of vertices and |E| is the number of edges.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity for Iterating a Graph
concepts.short_definition: For graph algorithms, linear time usually means Θ(|V| + |E|), corresponding to the size of the graph when represented with adjacency lists.
The sum of degrees of all vertices in a graph is at most twice the number of edges, i.e., ∑u∈V deg(u) ≤ 2|E|.

concepts.canonical_name: Use of Hash Tables for Fast Edge Lookup
concepts.short_definition: Using a hash table for each adjacency list Adj(u) can allow checking if an edge (u, v) exists in expected O(1) time.
The number of edges in a path.
The problem of determining if there exists a path between two specified vertices in a graph.
The problem of finding the shortest path and its distance between two specified vertices in a graph.
A tree containing shortest paths from a source vertex to every other vertex in a graph.
Data structure to represent graph edges; can be an array of lists or a hash table mapping vertices to their adjacent vertices.
In an undirected graph, each edge appears as two directed edges, one in each direction, between the connected vertices.

A tree structure representing shortest paths from a source vertex to every reachable vertex in a graph, storing for each vertex v its parent P(v), the second to last vertex on a shortest path from source s to v, with P(s) = null.

Sets Li = {v | d(s,v) = i} grouping vertices by their distance i from source s in BFS, where each vertex in Li is adjacent to some vertex in Li-1, used to inductively compute shortest paths and parents.

concepts.canonical_name: Parent Function P(v) in Shortest Paths
concepts.short_definition: A function mapping each vertex v (other than source s) to its parent vertex on a shortest path from s to v, i.e., the second to last vertex on the path; with P(s) = null.
An analysis showing that the Breadth-First Search algorithm runs in O(|V|+|E|) time by exploring vertices and edges in a graph once to compute shortest paths.
Use of dynamic arrays or linked lists to store layers L_i with Θ(|L_i|)-time iteration and O(1)-time insertion; sets and hash tables for constant time checks and insertions of vertices during BFS.
A tree constructed during DFS represented by parent pointers P mapping each vertex to its predecessor; shows reachable vertices and their path back to the source s.
In DFS, a recursive visit(u) function calls itself on unexplored adjacent vertices, setting their parent pointer before calling visit on them, implementing depth-first traversal.
Proof that DFS visits every vertex reachable from the start vertex and correctly assigns predecessor pointers, using induction on distances from the start vertex.
DFS visits each vertex once and spends constant time on each adjacency leading to total work proportional to O(|E|), the number of edges in the graph.
A tree formed by the set of parent pointers returned by a depth-first search, representing the order in which vertices were discovered during DFS.
A tree formed by the set of parent pointers returned by a breadth-first search, representing the shortest paths in an unweighted graph.
A graph representation format where each vertex has a list of adjacent vertices (neighbors).

concepts.canonical_name: Node colors in DFS (white, gray, black)
concepts.short_definition: Colors used to mark each node's state during DFS: white for undiscovered, gray for unfinished, and black for finished.
The time complexity of DFS is O(|V| + |E|), where |V| is the number of vertices and |E| is the number of edges in the graph.
A First-In-First-Out (FIFO) data structure used by BFS to determine the next node to visit, ensuring level-order traversal.
A Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) data structure used by DFS to determine the next node to visit, enabling deep-first traversal.
DFS finishing time is the timestamp recorded when a DFS call finishes exploring a vertex and all its descendants, used in algorithms like Kosaraj-Sharir.

concepts.canonical_name: Single-Source Shortest Paths in Unweighted Graphs
concepts.short_definition: The problem of finding shortest paths from a single source vertex to all other vertices in an unweighted graph, solvable via BFS.
Determining which vertices are reachable from a given source vertex in a graph, solvable via BFS or DFS.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm to Find Connected Components using Single-Source Reachability
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that finds all connected components by running single-source reachability (using BFS or DFS) from unvisited vertices and collecting reachable vertices as components.

concepts.canonical_name: Running Time of Connected Components Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The running time of the connected components algorithm is O(|V| + |E|), linear in the number of vertices and edges in the graph.
An approach to identify strongly connected components by running single-source reachability from each vertex and grouping mutually reachable vertices.
An algorithm to find all vertices reachable from a given source vertex in a directed graph.
An algorithm that finds strongly connected components using a single pass of full DFS with a more complicated analysis.
A strongly connected component vertex in the condensation graph with no outgoing edges.
An algorithm that runs DFS on each unexplored vertex in a graph until all vertices are explored, taking time O(|V| + |E|).
The time at which Full-DFS has finished exploring a vertex and all of its neighbors.

concepts.canonical_name: Strongly Connected Component Sink Vertex Identification
concepts.short_definition: The process of finding a vertex within a strongly connected component that has no out-going edges (sink component) by cleverly using DFS on the reversed graph.

concepts.canonical_name: Finishing Time Ordering of Strongly Connected Components
concepts.short_definition: If there is an edge from SCC C to SCC C', then the largest finishing time in C is greater than that in C' after running Full-DFS.
A graph obtained by reversing the direction of every edge in the original directed graph G.
An algorithm that identifies strongly connected components in a directed graph using two passes of depth-first search and a reversed graph.
A depth first search algorithm applied to the graph fully to compute finishing times and leaders for vertices.

concepts.canonical_name: Finishing Time in Depth First Search
concepts.short_definition: Order in which vertices finish being explored in a depth-first traversal, used to order processing in algorithms like SCC.

concepts.canonical_name: Topological Ordering Exists iff Graph is a DAG
concepts.short_definition: A directed graph admits a topological ordering if and only if it is a directed acyclic graph (DAG).

concepts.canonical_name: Reverse of Finishing Order is Topological Order in a DAG
concepts.short_definition: If G=(V,E) is a DAG, then the reverse of a finishing order from a depth-first search is a topological order.
A transformation that converts problem A into problem B such that solving B yields a solution to A, indicating A is no harder than B.

concepts.canonical_name: Squaring problem as reduction to multiplication
concepts.short_definition: Expressing squaring a number as the problem of multiplying two numbers, specifically multiplying the number by itself, without specifying how to multiply.
Expressing multiplication of two numbers using squares and arithmetic operations: a × b = ((a + b)^2 - a^2 - b^2)/2, given the model allows addition, negation, and bit shift.

concepts.canonical_name: Hardness comparison between problems using reduction
concepts.short_definition: Interpreting reduction A ≤ B as indicating that problem A is no harder than problem B, because a solution to B provides a solution to A.
A Turing reduction from problem A to B where A is solved using B as a subroutine with polynomially bounded runtime.

concepts.canonical_name: Polynomial Time Complexity of Combined Reductions
concepts.short_definition: If A ≤T B in time f(n), and B can be solved in time g(n), then A can be solved in time f(n) · g(n + f(n))

concepts.canonical_name: Utility of Reductions in Graph Problems
concepts.short_definition: Using reductions to transform graph problems into standard forms to avoid redesigning complex algorithms.
Given a graph G and two vertices s and t, find the shortest s-t path of even length, possibly non-simple.
A modification of BFS to track the parity of the path length from a source vertex to handle problems like shortest even-length path.
A reduction approach to shortest even-length path by computing shortest paths in G' = (V, E^2) using adjacency matrix multiplication and doubling results.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Duplication Reduction for Parity Tracking
concepts.short_definition: The reduction that duplicates graph G into G' = (V x {0,1}, E') to track parity of path length by extending vertices with parity bits and edges alternating parity bits.
The output of the Single-Source Shortest Paths (SSSP) problem can be represented either as the distance function δ(s, -) or as a shortest path tree P.
The process of converting between the two output forms of SSSP: from the distance function δ(s, -) to the shortest path tree P, and vice versa.
Pointers that represent the predecessor of each vertex in graph traversal trees such as the shortest path tree or DFS tree; can be used to track paths implicitly.
A directed graph G=(V,E) is semiconnected if for every pair of vertices u,v in V, either there is a path from u to v or a path from v to u.
The computational problem of determining whether a given directed graph is semiconnected.

concepts.canonical_name: Trivial Semiconnectedness Problem on Topologically Sorted DAG
concepts.short_definition: Determining semiconnectedness for graphs restricted to topologically sorted Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), where vertices are ordered so edges only go forward.
In a topologically sorted DAG, the graph is semiconnected if and only if all edges of the form (v, v+1) are present for vertex indices v.

concepts.canonical_name: Many-One Reduction via Topological Sorting for Semiconnectedness
concepts.short_definition: Reducing the problem of determining semiconnectedness of any DAG to the trivial version by obtaining a topological order via DFS and applying the trivial condition.
An algorithm that determines whether a graph is semiconnected by using the condensation graph, topological sorting, and edge checks, running in linear time.
A linear ordering of the vertices of the condensation graph such that for every directed edge (u,v), u comes before v in the ordering.
A priority queue where the element with the maximum key is deleted upon the delete max operation; a variant of priority queues focused on maximum rather than minimum.
An implementation of a binary heap data structure where the tree is represented compactly as an array rather than with pointers, supporting priority queue operations efficiently.
The operation of initializing a priority queue from an iterable collection of elements.
The operation of inserting a new element into a priority queue.
The operation of returning and deleting the element with the largest key from a priority queue.
A sorting algorithm that uses a priority queue to sort elements by repeatedly deleting the maximum element and collecting them in order.
Improving the priority queue build operation to run in O(n) time instead of O(n log n), matching dynamic operation times.

concepts.canonical_name: Balanced Search Tree implementation of Priority Queue
concepts.short_definition: Using balanced search trees, such as AVL trees, to implement priority queues with build time Θ(n log n) and dynamic operations in Θ(log n).

concepts.canonical_name: In-place Priority Queue Representation Using Arrays
concepts.short_definition: Representing a priority queue in-place within an array by viewing the array as a compact binary tree and organizing the priority queue structure on it.

concepts.canonical_name: Array Representation of Compact Binary Trees
concepts.short_definition: Mapping the elements of an array in level order (top to bottom, left to right) to nodes of a compact binary tree, producing a balanced tree where height h ≤ log n + 1.

concepts.canonical_name: Height Bound of Compact Binary Trees in Arrays
concepts.short_definition: The height h of a compact binary tree constructed from n elements in an array satisfies h ≤ log n + 1, ensuring the tree is balanced.

concepts.canonical_name: Implicit Binary Tree Representation in Arrays
concepts.short_definition: A method to represent a binary tree using an array where the parent and child relationships are computed using arithmetic operations on indices instead of pointers.
Advantages of representing heaps using arrays, including faster arithmetic pointer computation, reduced space overhead by omitting explicit pointers, and improved memory access due to contiguity.
An operation on a heap that restores the Heap Property by moving a node downwards if its key is smaller than one of its children's keys.
An operation that removes the maximum key (root) from a max heap, replaces it with the last leaf, and restores the Heap Property by heapifying down.
A representation of a heap using an array where the root is at index 1 and children/parent relationships are computed by indices, with A[0] defined as infinity to simplify calculations.
The time complexity of heap insert and delete max operations, given correct heapify procedures, is Θ(log n) where n is the size of the heap.

concepts.canonical_name: Strong Induction for Correctness of Heapify Up
concepts.short_definition: A proof technique that uses induction on node index x to show the heapify up procedure restores the heap property.
Building a heap from an unsorted array by applying heapify down operations in a bottom-up manner starting from the last non-leaf node.
The analysis showing that building a heap bottom-up by heapify_down calls has better runtime than inserting elements one by one.
In a heap, the count of nodes at each height i is 2^(k-i), where k is such that n+1=2^{k+1}.
An in-place sorting algorithm that uses a heap data structure, running in worst-case Θ(n log n) time by building a heap and repeatedly deleting the max element.

concepts.canonical_name: Shortest Path Distance Function δ(s, t)
concepts.short_definition: The length of the shortest path from source vertex s to target vertex t, defined as infinity if no path exists.

concepts.canonical_name: Limitations of BFS for Weighted Graphs
concepts.short_definition: BFS does not find correct shortest paths in graphs where edges have non-uniform weights.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Duplication Technique for Weighted Graphs
concepts.short_definition: Technique that replaces weighted edges by multiple edges of weight 1 to transform weighted graph to unweighted graph with longer paths.
Graph duplication requires integer edge weights and causes large runtime and size increase.
A prefix of a shortest path is itself a shortest path.

concepts.canonical_name: Key Question in Shortest Path Algorithm Design
concepts.short_definition: Determining intermediate vertices on shortest paths to find shortest path from source to target.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm Design Approach: Reduction to Easier Special Case
concepts.short_definition: A common method of simplifying the shortest path problem by restricting the input graph to identify intermediate vertices.

A framework in shortest path algorithms maintaining distance estimates d(v) for each vertex v that are always greater than or equal to the shortest path distances δ(v) and updated via edge relaxations.
The inequality δ(a, c) ≤ δ(a, b) + δ(b, c) used as a foundation for edge relaxation correctness in shortest path algorithms.
The proof or argument that at the end of Dijkstra's algorithm the final distance estimates d(v) equal the true shortest path distances δ(v) for all vertices v.

concepts.canonical_name: Proof of Correctness of Dijkstra's Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: A strong induction proof that shows that when a vertex v is removed from the priority queue Q, d(v) equals the shortest path distance (v).

concepts.canonical_name: Decrease Key Operation in a Min-Heap
concepts.short_definition: The operation that lowers the key value of a node in a min-heap and restores heap property by the bubble up (heapify-up) procedure.

concepts.canonical_name: Priority Queue Implementations for Dijkstra's Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: Different data structures (Array, Binary Heap, Fibonacci Heap) used to implement the priority queue in Dijkstra's algorithm, affecting its time efficiency.

concepts.canonical_name: Decrease Key Operation in Priority Queues
concepts.short_definition: An operation to reduce the key value of an element in a priority queue, maintaining the heap property by swapping to restore order.

concepts.canonical_name: Generalization of Edge Weights and Operations in Dijkstra's Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: Dijkstra's algorithm can be generalized for edge weights over a set with a total order and an associative binary operation, given specific properties such as the triangle inequality and identity, enabling broader metric definitions.

concepts.canonical_name: Generalized Dijkstra's Algorithm for Different Metrics
concepts.short_definition: A conceptual extension of Dijkstra's algorithm where the standard operations (≤, +, 0, ∞) are replaced with different operators (⪯, ⋆, ⊥, ⊤) allowing computation of shortest paths according to various path metrics.
Various ways to measure the cost of paths in a graph, such as minimizing the sum, product, maximum, or minimum of edge weights along a path.

concepts.canonical_name: Special Values and Operators in Generalized Shortest Path Computations
concepts.short_definition: Use of symbolic values (⊥, ⊤) and operations (⪯, ⋆) to represent generalized ordering and aggregation in path cost calculations.

concepts.canonical_name: Effect of Negative Edge Weights on Priority Queue Removal in Dijkstra's Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: In Dijkstra's algorithm, once a vertex is removed from the priority queue because it has the minimum current distance estimate, its distance estimate should not decrease; however, negative edge weights violate this assumption causing errors.

concepts.canonical_name: Adding Large Weights to Edges to Remove Negativity is Incorrect
concepts.short_definition: Modifying a graph by adding a large constant to all edge weights to eliminate negativity can change shortest paths and lead to incorrect results.
The weight of a path in a weighted graph is the sum of edge weights along the path.
A shortest path between vertices s and t in a weighted graph is a path with minimum total weight among all s-t paths.
The infimum is the greatest lower bound of a set and may not be achieved by any element of the set, used to define shortest-path distance when no minimum exists.

concepts.canonical_name: Effect of Negative-Weight Cycle on Shortest Paths
concepts.short_definition: If a path from s to t passes through a negative-weight cycle, then the shortest-path distance δ(s, t) is negative infinity.

concepts.canonical_name: Optimal Subproblem Property for Shortest Paths
concepts.short_definition: Subpaths of shortest paths are themselves shortest paths.
When the source vertex s is fixed, δ(s, v) is abbreviated as δ(v), representing shortest path distance from s to v.
For all vertices u, v, x, the shortest-path distance satisfies δ(u, v) ≤ δ(u, x) + δ(x, v).
Proof that the DAG Relaxation algorithm computes the shortest path distances correctly for all vertices in a DAG by induction on topological order.

concepts.canonical_name: Running Time of DAG Relaxation Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The total running time of DAG Relaxation is O(|V| + |E|), including initialization and topological sort.
DAG Relaxation algorithm does not work if the graph contains cycles since a topological order does not exist in that case.
A vertex on or reachable from a negative-weight cycle used to detect the existence of that cycle via comparison of k-edge distance values.
The minimum weight of any path from s to v using at most k edges.
A construction of multiple levels of the graph, each representing vertices reachable with at most a given number of edges, producing a DAG used in Bellman-Ford's shortest path computation.
A proof that Bellman-Ford algorithm correctly computes shortest paths or detects negative-weight cycles, often employing induction on number of edge relaxations.
The process of iteratively updating shortest path estimates by checking and updating distances via edges, repeated |V| times over all edges.
The subgraph of vertices and edges reachable from a source vertex s, used to optimize shortest path algorithms.
The procedure of removing vertices unreachable from the source s to optimize the runtime of SSSP algorithms.
The computational complexity of algorithms solving the single-source shortest path problem, e.g., Bellman-Ford's O(|V||E|).
An element −⊤ that acts as the best (lowest) element in the order under generalized operations for shortest path computations.

concepts.canonical_name: Generalization of Bellman-Ford Using Algebraic Structures
concepts.short_definition: Extending Bellman-Ford by replacing the usual ≤ and + operations with more general order ⪯ and operation ⋆, requiring an infimum element instead of non-negativity.
A shortest path of length |V| in graph G that contains a negative-weight cycle, indicating no well-defined shortest path exists with fewer vertices.
Space-saving technique for Bellman-Ford storing only O(|V|) space by tracking distances for previous and current iteration vertices rather than full tables.
Assumption that all edge weights in the graph fit comfortably into word-sized integers, simplifying arithmetic and runtime analysis.
Reasons why APSP is studied including practical querying over large networks and its equivalences to other problems.

concepts.canonical_name: Equivalence of APSP to Other Problems
concepts.short_definition: APSP is computationally equivalent to problems such as finding negative triangles, minimum-weight cycles in graphs, and replacement-paths problem.
Allowing graphs to have negative edge weights can be useful for problems like finding most-beautiful paths or modeling battery charge change in EV travel.

concepts.canonical_name: Reweighting Graph Edges by Adding a Constant
concepts.short_definition: Adding a constant to every edge weight in a graph does not preserve path lengths or shortest paths.

concepts.canonical_name: APSP Algorithms for General Directed Graphs with Negative Weights
concepts.short_definition: Best known algorithms for APSP in general directed graphs with negative weights run in approximately cubic time with respect to the number of vertices.

concepts.canonical_name: Open Question on Improving APSP Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: It is an open question whether APSP can be solved in less than cubic time, for example, in |𝑉|^{2.9999} time.

concepts.canonical_name: APSP Algorithms for General Directed Graphs with Non-Negative Weights
concepts.short_definition: Running Dijkstra's algorithm from every node achieves time complexity O(|V|^2 log|V| + |V||E|) for APSP in graphs with non-negative edges.

concepts.canonical_name: APSP Algorithms for Undirected Graphs with Bounded Integer Weights
concepts.short_definition: For undirected graphs with weights in {0, 1, ..., M}, there is an algorithm running in time roughly M · |V|^{omega} (with some logarithmic factors).

concepts.canonical_name: Strongly Connected Components and Kosaraju-Sharir Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: A graph decomposition into maximal strongly connected subgraphs, computed using Kosaraju-Sharir algorithm.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Reweighting that Preserves Shortest Paths
concepts.short_definition: A transformation on a graph's edge weights by adding a function 𝜙 on vertices such that shortest paths between any two vertices are preserved.
The new weight of an edge (u,v) after reweighting is 𝑤′(𝑢,𝑣) = 𝑤(𝑢,𝑣) + 𝜙(𝑢) − 𝜙(𝑣).
The sum of added and subtracted 𝜙 values on a path telescopes so that the total path weight changes by 𝜙(source)−𝜙(destination).

concepts.canonical_name: Reweighting to Eliminate Negative Edge Weights
concepts.short_definition: Finding a function 𝜙 such that the reweighted graph has no negative edge weights.

concepts.canonical_name: Use of a New Vertex s to Compute 𝜙
concepts.short_definition: Adding a new vertex s connected by zero-weight edges to every vertex and defining 𝜙(v) as the shortest path distance from s to v.

concepts.canonical_name: Claim that Reweighting by 𝜙 Gives Non-Negative Edges
concepts.short_definition: After reweighting by the 𝜙 function defined by shortest paths from s, all edges have non-negative weight.
The construction of a modified graph G' from an original graph G to assist in shortest paths computations.

concepts.canonical_name: Running Time Complexity of All Pairs Shortest Paths
concepts.short_definition: The total computational time required for solving all pairs shortest paths problem using a specific method combining Bellman-Ford and Dijkstra's algorithms and graph transformation.
The computational complexity of multiplying two n-by-n matrices, ranging from naive O(n^3) to clever algorithms with O(n^ω) for ω<2.372.

concepts.canonical_name: All Pairs Shortest Paths Algorithm by Repeated Squaring
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm to compute path existence between all pairs of vertices in a graph using repeated squaring of the adjacency matrix, reducing positive entries to 1 after each multiplication.
For any graph, the entry (u,v) in the ℓ-th power of the adjacency matrix A counts the number of paths from vertex u to vertex v of length ℓ.
The time complexity of computing powers of the adjacency matrix by repeated squaring is O(|V|^ω · log |V|), where ω is the exponent of matrix multiplication complexity.

concepts.canonical_name: Length-\ell Path Count Using Adjacency Matrix Powers
concepts.short_definition: The number of paths of length \ell from vertex u to vertex v in a graph is given by the (u,v)-th entry of the \ell-th power of the graph's adjacency matrix A.
Reachability between vertices u and v can be determined by checking if any entry in the |V|-th power of the adjacency matrix A is non-zero, representing the existence of a path regardless of length.

concepts.canonical_name: Using Matrix Multiplication to Solve Graph Problems
concepts.short_definition: Many graph problems can be formulated and solved efficiently by expressing them as matrix multiplication problems.

A technique to compute shortest paths in graphs that may contain negative weight cycles by identifying strongly connected components (SCCs) with negative cycles and adjusting shortest path computations accordingly.
The process of running Bellman-Ford from an arbitrary vertex within each strongly connected component to detect negative cycles within that SCC.
Detection of negative weight cycles within strongly connected components by running Bellman-Ford to check for relaxing edges indefinitely.
Constructing a condensation graph where edges have weights -1 if source or target components contain negative cycles, 0 otherwise, to model reachability with negative cycles.
Computing all pairs shortest paths on the condensation graph, which is a DAG, with adjusted weights to propagate negative cycle information.
Creating the graph 𝐺* by removing from the original graph all strongly connected components containing negative cycles, to enable shortest path computation without negative cycles.

concepts.canonical_name: Computing APSP on G-star using Johnson's Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: Applying Johnson's algorithm to compute shortest paths on the modified graph 𝐺* which has no negative weight cycles after removal of SCCs with negative cycles.

concepts.canonical_name: Final Distance Calculation from SCC Condensation and Modified Graph
concepts.short_definition: Determining shortest path distances between vertices by combining APSP results from the condensation graph and the graph with negative cycle SCCs removed, using rules for infinite distances.

concepts.canonical_name: Negative Cycle Reachability and Shortest Paths
concepts.short_definition: Criterion that 𝛿(u,v) = -∞ if and only if there exists a negative cycle reachable from u to v in the graph, affecting shortest path calculations.
Relationships defining that 𝛿(u,v) = +∞ if and only if u cannot reach v in the graph, meaning no path exists between them.

concepts.canonical_name: DAG All Pairs Shortest Paths (DAG APSP) Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: Algorithm to compute shortest paths in directed acyclic graphs efficiently, used as a component in APSP.
The specific time complexities of Kosaraju, Bellman-Ford, DAG APSP, Johnson, and other operations in the APSP context.
An optimal solution to a problem contains optimal solutions to its sub-problems.
A problem where given a set of activities each with a start and finish time, the goal is to select the maximum number of non-overlapping activities.
A subset of activities with no overlapping intervals that has maximum cardinality.
A greedy algorithm that selects the activity with earliest finish time to construct an optimal maximum-size set of non-conflicting activities.
Finding a path in a Directed Acyclic Graph that maximizes the sum of weights of edges or number of vertices.

concepts.canonical_name: Construction of Activity DAG for Scheduling
concepts.short_definition: Construction of a Directed Acyclic Graph where vertices represent activities and edges represent precedence from one activity to another if one ends before the other starts.
A framework for designing greedy algorithms involving ordering input and iteratively making greedy choices.

concepts.canonical_name: Good vs. Bad Greedy Choices for Interval Hitting Problem
concepts.short_definition: Evaluations of various candidate greedy choices for the interval hitting problem, identifying which lead to optimal or suboptimal solutions.
For an activity scheduled to start at time t with duration ti and due time di, lateness is max(0, t + ti − di).
A measure of how late an activity finishes compared to its due time, defined for a schedule S as the maximum lateness over all activities.
Notation to represent an activity as a tuple of its duration and due time, used to characterize scheduling problems.

concepts.canonical_name: Optimal schedule with no idle time
concepts.short_definition: An optimal schedule can always be found with no idle time between activities by pushing activities leftwards to eliminate gaps, improving or preserving lateness.
If an optimal schedule schedules activity a first with duration t, then the schedule restricted to the remaining activities with adjusted due dates (At) is also optimal for that subproblem.
There is an optimal schedule where the activity with the earliest due date is scheduled first, supporting greedy algorithms for minimizing maximum lateness.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy Algorithm for Scheduling to Minimize Maximum Lateness
concepts.short_definition: A greedy algorithm that schedules activities ordered by their due dates to minimize the maximum lateness of any activity.

A proof technique showing that the Greedy algorithm produces an optimal solution by using induction and the Greedy Choice Property, reducing the problem to a smaller subproblem where the inductive hypothesis applies.

concepts.canonical_name: Inductive Hypothesis in Greedy Algorithm Proof
concepts.short_definition: The assumption used in the induction step that the Greedy algorithm is optimal for a smaller subproblem formed by removing the first task and adjusting due dates.
Scheduling problems can be decomposed into smaller subproblems recursively, which allows proofs of optimality by induction on these subproblems.
A method to encode data symbols into bits so that the original data can be perfectly reconstructed from the encoded data.
A finite set of symbols, each with a known frequency of occurrence, used as input to the compression process.
An encoding scheme where each symbol from an alphabet is represented by a fixed number of bits equal to the ceiling of log base 2 of the alphabet size.
An encoding scheme where symbols are encoded into bitstrings of different lengths, typically shorter bitstrings are assigned to more frequent symbols.
An encoding scheme where no symbol's codeword is a prefix of any other symbol's codeword, ensuring unambiguous decoding.
A method of lossless data compression that uses prefix-free codes to represent symbols based on their frequencies, aiming to minimize the average codeword length.
To decode a bitstring encoded by Huffman codes, parse the bits left to right by traversing the code's binary tree (left=0, right=1) until a leaf node is reached, then output the corresponding symbol.

concepts.canonical_name: Frequency of Symbols in Huffman Coding
concepts.short_definition: The relative occurrence rate (count or probability) of each symbol used to construct Huffman codes, which influences the codeword length.
The sum of frequencies of nodes in a prefix-free-code tree, used to quantify its efficiency.
A binary tree representing codes where no code is a prefix of another, used for efficient encoding.
A prefix-free-code tree that minimizes the cost function over given symbol frequencies.
A binary tree where every vertex has either zero or two children, no node has only one child.
In any optimal prefix-free code tree, if a symbol has lower frequency than another, its code length is at least as large.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy Choice Property in Huffman Coding
concepts.short_definition: The property that in an optimal Huffman tree, the two lowest frequency nodes are siblings, which justifies the greedy choice of joining two smallest frequency nodes.
The property that the problem of building a minimum-cost prefix tree can be solved optimally by combining solutions to subproblems.
A binary tree constructed using a greedy algorithm from symbol frequencies, used to generate prefix codes for Huffman encoding.
The time complexity of building the Huffman tree is O(n log n), where n is the number of symbols, due to repeated priority queue operations.
A problem where given a row of coins with positive values, the goal is to select coins such that no two adjacent coins are chosen, maximizing the sum of selected coins.

concepts.canonical_name: Recursive Solution to Coin Row Problem
concepts.short_definition: A recursive approach to solving the coin row problem by considering choices for the first coin and recursing on the remaining coins accordingly.

concepts.canonical_name: Exponential Time Complexity in Recursive Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: A time complexity where the runtime grows proportionally to an exponential function of the input size, e.g., T(n) = Ω(2^(n/2)).

concepts.canonical_name: Inefficiency of Python List Slicing in Recursive Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: Python list slicing takes linear time proportional to the slice length, which causes inefficiency in recursive algorithms that use slicing repeatedly.

concepts.canonical_name: Memoization to Avoid Exponential Running Time
concepts.short_definition: A technique to improve recursive algorithms by storing intermediate results to avoid redundant computations leading to exponential time.
A recursive function whose time complexity grows exponentially due to repeatedly recomputing overlapping subproblems.
An algorithmic technique that solves problems by combining solutions to subproblems and storing such solutions to avoid redundant computation.
A dynamic programming approach that uses recursion with memoization to store computed results and avoid recomputation of subproblems.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity Reduction from Exponential to Linear
concepts.short_definition: Conversion of recursive exponential time complexity algorithms into linear time algorithms using memoization to avoid repeated computations.
An array or structure that stores intermediate results of subproblems in Dynamic Programming to avoid redundant computations.
A Dynamic Programming approach where the solution to the problem is built from the smallest subproblems up to the original problem by filling a memo table iteratively without recursion.
The time complexity of a bottom-up dynamic programming solution is O(n) because each of the n entries in the memo table is computed once in O(1) time.
The process of recognizing a recursive problem, understanding the sequence of decisions, and structuring the problem as subproblems solvable with dynamic programming.
Rewriting the recursive call inputs from subarrays to their indices to simplify and quantify the number of subproblems.
In dynamic programming, the memo array can be filled iteratively from the back to the front when the subproblems depend on subsequent elements.
Expressing the solution to a problem in terms of recursive calls that cover all possible choices and combining results using maximization or minimization.

concepts.canonical_name: Index-based Input for DP Recursive Calls
concepts.short_definition: Changing recursive calls to use indices (e.g., of an array) rather than other inputs, facilitating memoization and iterative solutions.

concepts.canonical_name: Pure Dynamic Programming Algorithm Without Recursion
concepts.short_definition: Implementing a dynamic programming solution by iteratively filling a memoization table in the correct order rather than using recursive top-down calls.
For each bowling pin, the choices are dropping a single pin, dropping two consecutive pins (scoring their product), or skipping dropping (with unlimited throws).
The division of the original problem into smaller problems whose solutions are stored in the memoization table.
The functional dependency describing how each entry of the memo table is computed from other entries.
A directed acyclic graph illustrating dependencies between memo table entries used to determine the order of computation.
Entries in the memoization table that do not depend on other entries and serve as initialization points for DP algorithms.
The method to derive the solution to the original problem from entries in the memoization table.
The calculation of the computational complexity, often the product of number of memo entries times the work per entry.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Recurrence Relation for Coin Row Problem
concepts.short_definition: The recursive relation M(i) = max{M(i + 1), A[i] + M(i + 2)} that defines the maximum value sums by deciding whether to pick or skip the current coin.
Computing values of M(i) in decreasing order of i to ensure dependencies M(i') with i'>i are known.
Base case M(i) = 0 if i ≥ n indicating no coins left to pick.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Time Complexity for Coin Row Problem
concepts.short_definition: Computational complexity of O(n) for computing all M(i) values with each computed in O(1).
The method of finding an optimal solution (not just its value) in a dynamic programming problem by storing decisions or parent pointers during computation.
A table P where each entry P(i) indicates whether the optimal solution includes the decision of picking item i, built based on comparing values from the memoization table M.

concepts.canonical_name: Bold Edge Visualization in DP Graph
concepts.short_definition: A visualization technique where edges corresponding to the chosen decisions in dynamic programming are highlighted (bolded) to trace the optimal solution path.
Following highlighted edges in the dependency graph or decisions in table P to reconstruct the optimal solution from a dynamic programming computation.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Algorithm for Coin Row Problem
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that uses a memoization table to find the maximum value and an optimal set of coins without selecting adjacent coins.
A property stating that optimal solutions to smaller subproblems can be combined to form an optimal solution to a larger problem.

concepts.canonical_name: Cut-and-Paste Argument for Optimality in DP
concepts.short_definition: An argument that if there were a better solution to a subproblem, replacing part of the current solution improves overall optimality, used to justify correctness in DP.

concepts.canonical_name: Relationship Between Solutions Picking and Not Picking First Coin in Coin Row Problem
concepts.short_definition: A correspondence that optimal solutions that pick the first coin extend from subproblem [c2,...,cn-1] and those that do not pick first coin correspond to subproblem [c1,...,cn-1].
A specific problem presumably discussed in the lecture, for which the Optimal Substructure Property is to be argued.
Computing LCS by recursively checking character matches and deciding whether to include or exclude characters, leading to exponential runtime.

concepts.canonical_name: Memoization technique in Dynamic Programming for LCS
concepts.short_definition: Adding a memo to store results of subproblems LCS(A[i :], B[j :]) to avoid redundant computations and improve runtime from exponential to polynomial.
The technique of storing the results of expensive function calls and reusing them when the same inputs occur again.
Finding the longest subsequence common to two sequences that appears in the same relative order but not necessarily contiguously.
Defines the length of the longest common subsequence of suffixes of two strings recursively using subproblems.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Analysis of DP for LCS
concepts.short_definition: Analysis showing that the dynamic programming solution for LCS runs in O(|A||B|) time by processing each cell once.
A bottom-up dynamic programming method to compute the length of the longest common subsequence between two sequences by filling a memoization table M with optimal subproblem solutions.
Given two strings A and B, the SCS problem is to find the length of the shortest string that contains both A and B as subsequences.
The method of proving the correctness of a dynamic programming algorithm by using the Optimal Substructure Property and induction.
Given an array of integers, find the longest subsequence where the elements are strictly increasing.
A recursive method to find the LIS by deciding at each position whether to include the current element if it is larger than the previously chosen element, or exclude it otherwise.

concepts.canonical_name: State parameter in recursive LIS to remember last picked element
concepts.short_definition: To enforce the increasing constraint in recursion, the function keeps track of the last selected element to ensure the next chosen element is always larger.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Approach for Longest Increasing Subsequence
concepts.short_definition: A method to compute the length of the longest increasing subsequence using a DP table M(i,j) which tracks the longest increasing subsequence length of suffix starting at i with constraint on previous index j.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming State Definition for LIS
concepts.short_definition: The DP state M(i,j) defined as the length of the longest increasing subsequence starting at index i that includes only elements larger than A[j], with the convention A[-1] = -∞.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Complexity of Memoized DP Solution for LIS
concepts.short_definition: The time complexity of the memoized dynamic programming approach for LIS is O(n²), where n is the length of the input array.

concepts.canonical_name: State Transition Formula for DP Solution of LIS
concepts.short_definition: The recurrence relation for the DP state: M(i, j) = max(M(i + 1, i) + 1 if A[i] > A[j], M(i + 1, j)).

concepts.canonical_name: Ordering of DP Table Filling for LIS
concepts.short_definition: The DP table M is filled in reverse lexicographical order since entry M(i, j) depends on entries with larger i.

concepts.canonical_name: Initial Conditions for DP Table in LIS
concepts.short_definition: For all j, M(n, j) = 0, representing the base cases for the DP where the suffix is empty.

concepts.canonical_name: Use of Index Instead of Element in DP State
concepts.short_definition: Using the index of the last chosen element in the DP state instead of the element itself simplifies the DP solution and prevents issues with duplicated elements or characters.

concepts.canonical_name: Modification of DP Algorithm for Nondecreasing Subsequences and Non-integers
concepts.short_definition: An adapted DP solution that works for sequences of English characters and computes longest nondecreasing subsequences in O(n) time.
Definition of subproblems M(i) representing the length of the longest increasing subsequence starting at A[i].
The recursive formula M(i) = 1 + max {M(j) : j > i and A[j] > A[i]} for computing LIS subproblems.
Ordering of subproblems in increasing order of i to ensure correct dependency resolution in DP.
The output for the problem is the maximum value of M over all indices.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Complexity of Naive LIS DP
concepts.short_definition: The naive DP for LIS runs in O(n^2) time because M has n entries, each computed in O(n).

concepts.canonical_name: Optimized LIS DP Using Range Queries
concepts.short_definition: Optimizing the LIS DP by implementing M with a balanced binary search tree to achieve O(n log n) runtime.

concepts.canonical_name: Multiset Data Structure for Range Queries
concepts.short_definition: Using multisets or balanced search trees keyed by values A[i] to support range maximum queries for LIS DP.
The problem of finding the contiguous subarray within a one-dimensional array of numbers which has the largest sum.
The problem of finding the contiguous subarray within a one-dimensional array of numbers which has the largest product.
A variable used to represent partial solutions or states in dynamic programming algorithms to efficiently build up a solution.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity O(n) for Contiguous Subarray Problems
concepts.short_definition: Algorithms that solve the maximum sum or product contiguous subarray problems within linear time, i.e., O(n) time complexity.

concepts.canonical_name: Maintaining State for Maximum Product Subarray Problem
concepts.short_definition: Keeping track of additional information such as maximum and minimum products at each position to handle negative numbers in maximum product subarray algorithms.
A problem of finding the optimal product of a subarray, accounting for sign (positive, negative, or zero) and maximizing or minimizing product based on the prefix's sign.

concepts.canonical_name: Transition equation for f=0 in DP problem
concepts.short_definition: When f=0, the transition chooses whether to start the substring or not; T(i,0) = max{T(i+1,0), A[i]*T(i+1,sign(A[i])) }.
The DP table entries T(i, f) depend on entries with larger i and so are filled starting at the end of the array.

concepts.canonical_name: Initialization of DP table in subarray product problem
concepts.short_definition: The initialization for all sign states at the array end is T(n,f) = 1 for all f.

concepts.canonical_name: Overall time complexity of DP solution
concepts.short_definition: The DP solution for the subarray product problem has O(n) entries each computed in O(1) time, for a total O(n) time complexity.
A method of solving shortest path problems by using the optimal subproblem property, computing distances incrementally.

concepts.canonical_name: Single-Source Shortest Paths (SSSP) in General Graphs
concepts.short_definition: Finding shortest paths from one source vertex to every other vertex in a graph that may contain cycles and possibly negative edge weights but no negative cycles.

concepts.canonical_name: Handling Cycles in Shortest Path Computations
concepts.short_definition: Use of edge count limits in dynamic programming to avoid cycles when computing shortest paths in graphs with cycles.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Table for Shortest Paths with Edge Limit
concepts.short_definition: Definition of T(v, k) as the weight of shortest path from source s to vertex v using at most k edges, with base cases and recurrence relations.

concepts.canonical_name: Bellman-Ford Algorithm Similarity in DP Shortest Paths
concepts.short_definition: The DP algorithm processes all edges of the graph multiple times in rounds, relaxing edges similarly to Bellman-Ford algorithm rounds.

concepts.canonical_name: Negative Cycle Detection via DP Table Check
concepts.short_definition: If for some vertex u, T(u, |V|) < T(u, |V| - 1), then the graph contains a negative cycle reachable from the source.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of DP Shortest Path Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The dynamic programming algorithm for shortest paths using edge limits runs in O(|V| * |E|) time due to processing each edge for each edge-count limit k.
A dynamic programming algorithm that computes the shortest paths between all pairs of vertices with complexity O(|V|^3), more efficient than naive generalizations of Bellman-Ford for dense graphs.
A DP table entry that represents the minimal weight of a path from u to v through intermediate vertices from the set [k + 1] ∪ {u,v}.
The method of detecting negative cycles by checking if T(|V|, u, u) < 0 for some vertex u in Floyd–Warshall's DP table.
The recurrence defining T(k,u,v) as the minimum of using node k as an intermediate or not: T(k,u,v) = min(T(k−1,u,k)+T(k−1,k,v), T(k−1,u,v)).

concepts.canonical_name: Dependency Graph of a DP Table
concepts.short_definition: A directed graph representing dependencies among subproblems in a DP solution, where nodes are subproblems and edges indicate that one subproblem depends on another.

concepts.canonical_name: Transformation of Maximization Problems to Shortest Path Problems using Negative Weights
concepts.short_definition: A technique that converts maximization problems into shortest path problems by negating weights, enabling use of shortest path algorithms.
Modeling dynamic programming subproblems as nodes and dependencies as edges in a graph to apply graph algorithms like shortest path.
A maximization problem where a sandwich of length L needs to be optimally cut to maximize the total value of pieces based on a value function v(ℓ) for lengths ℓ.
An approach that attempts to take the most valuable sandwich piece per unit length at each step, which can fail for the Sandwich Cutting problem.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Recurrence for Sandwich Cutting
concepts.short_definition: The recurrence relation T(ℓ) = max over 1≤i≤ℓ of v[i] + T(ℓ−i) defines the optimal value achievable by cutting a sandwich of length ℓ.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Algorithm for Subset Sum
concepts.short_definition: A table T(ℓ, i) is constructed where T(ℓ, i) indicates if there exists a subset of elements from A indexed i to n that sums to ℓ, computed using a recurrence to decide the Subset Sum problem.

concepts.canonical_name: Running Time of the DP Algorithm for Subset Sum
concepts.short_definition: The Dynamic Programming algorithm for Subset Sum runs in O(Ln) time, where L is the target sum and n is the number of elements.
The running time of the Sandwich Cutting algorithm is O(L²), where L is the input integer.
The input size for Subset Sum is n + 1, consisting of one integer L and n integers in set A.

concepts.canonical_name: Reduction from Partition to Subset Sum
concepts.short_definition: The process of converting Partition problem instances to equivalent Subset Sum problem instances to use Subset Sum algorithms for Partition.
Determine if a set of n positive integers can be split into two subsets having equal sums.
A computational model where input integers fit in w-bit words; running times can depend on w.
An algorithm computing the greatest common divisor of two integers in pseudopolynomial time.
A variation of the Subset Sum problem where the set A can include negative numbers, removing the positivity restriction.

concepts.canonical_name: Reduction from Negative Subset Sum to Subset Sum
concepts.short_definition: A method to transform a Negative Subset Sum problem instance into an equivalent Subset Sum problem instance by adjusting elements and the target using an offset to handle negative numbers.
A subset of the set A whose elements sum exactly to the target value L.

concepts.canonical_name: Handling Non-Positive Elements in Subset Sum
concepts.short_definition: The technique of adding a large constant M to all elements in set A (and adjusting the target L) to make all elements positive, facilitating reduction from Negative Subset Sum to Subset Sum.
Study of when a problem lacks an efficient algorithm for its solution.
A search space whose size grows exponentially with the size of input, e.g., number of permutations of [n].
Reducing an optimization problem to a decision problem via techniques such as binary search.
The class of decision problems solvable by an algorithm in polynomial time, representing efficient computation.
The class of problems solvable in exponential time, specifically 2^(poly(n)) time algorithms.
The class of decision problems solvable using polynomial amount of memory (space).
The set of decision problems for which a solution can be verified in polynomial time given a certificate.
A proposed solution or witness to a decision problem instance whose length is polynomially bounded and can be checked by a verifier to confirm the solution.
An algorithm that accepts a problem instance and a certificate and runs in polynomial time to confirm whether the certificate proves a YES instance.

concepts.canonical_name: Relationship P is subset of NP
concepts.short_definition: Any problem solvable in polynomial time can be verified in polynomial time with a trivial certificate; thus, P is a subset of NP.
