In computational complexity theory, certain well-known complexity classes are contained one within another, e.g., P is contained in NP, which is contained in PSPACE, which is contained in EXPTIME.
For 3-colorability, a certificate is a coloring assignment to the graph's vertices; the verifier checks if adjacent vertices have different colors to confirm a valid coloring.

A decision problem where the input is a Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form with each clause containing exactly three literals, and the question is whether there exists an assignment of truth values making the formula true.
For 3SAT, the certificate is a candidate assignment to the Boolean variables; the verifier evaluates the formula under that assignment to verify if it evaluates to TRUE.

concepts.canonical_name: Reduction from partition problem to rectangle packing
concepts.short_definition: A polynomial-time reduction that transforms the partition problem into an instance of the rectangle packing problem to show NP-hardness.
The theory and study of what problems can be solved by algorithms (computers), including limits to computation.
Property of a computational model where a program either halts producing an output or runs forever without halting.
The fundamental impossibility of solving certain problems with any algorithm, no matter how much time is provided.
A finite or infinite sequence of bits (0s and 1s).
The application of a program P to input x, denoted P(x), yielding a computation or output.
The property that a program terminates (halts) on all inputs, necessary for computing a function.
A function f for which there exists a program P that computes f, halting on all inputs and returning correct output.
The argument using cardinality and pigeonhole principle to show that there exist functions that no program of a given length can compute.

concepts.canonical_name: Turing's Diagonalization Argument for the Halting Problem
concepts.short_definition: A proof by contradiction showing the halting problem is undecidable by constructing a program that contradicts the existence of a halting algorithm H.
A proof technique that shows the nonexistence of certain functions or algorithms by constructing a contradiction using diagonal and anti-diagonal elements, originally invented by Georg Cantor.
The concept that every interesting property of programs is not decidable by any algorithm, a result related to Rice's Theorem.
Given a program Q, determine if Q halts on all inputs (YES) or not (NO). This problem is undecidable.
A proof technique showing that if TOTALITY were decidable, then HALT would be decidable by constructing an algorithm using a hypothetical TOTALITY algorithm.
Given two programs P and Q, decide if they output YES on exactly the same inputs (YES) or not (NO). This problem is undecidable.
The EQUIV problem of deciding program equivalence is undecidable.
A proof that if EQUIV were decidable, then the HALT problem would be decidable by constructing an algorithm from a hypothetical EQUIV algorithm.
A property of certain problems that they cannot be decided algorithmically; no program can always correctly answer the question for all inputs.
The problem of deciding whether a multivariate polynomial equation with integer coefficients has an integer solution.
The Matiyasevich-Robinson-Davis-Putnam theorem which shows that Hilbert's Tenth Problem is undecidable; that is, no algorithm can decide whether a Diophantine equation has solutions in integers.
A measure of the length of the shortest program that outputs a given string, capturing the string's algorithmic complexity.
A self-referential paradox related to definitions like "the smallest positive integer not definable in under eleven words," pointing to limitations in formal systems and complexity notions.
Use of quantum entanglement by provers to enable a polynomial-time verifier to decide the HALT problem by interrogating two provers who cannot communicate.
Given a finite set of n×n integer matrices, deciding if the zero matrix can be expressed as a finite product of those matrices; this problem is Turing-Hard/undecidable.
Given two finitely generated groups defined by generators and relations, deciding if the groups are isomorphic; this problem is undecidable.

concepts.canonical_name: Conway's Game of Life Reachability Problem
concepts.short_definition: Given an initial configuration, deciding whether Conway’s Game of Life ever reaches a particular configuration; this problem is undecidable.
Property of problems expressive enough to encode general computation, thus including undecidable problems.
A problem that is both Turing-Hard and computable, meaning it can compute any computation and is also computable.
Games that are as computationally complex as Turing Machines, making questions like 'Can I win?' undecidable.
The study and implications of computability theory as it applies to the design and analysis of video games, demonstrating how some games can embody complex computational problems.

concepts.canonical_name: Ban of Certain Games on Apple’s App Store
concepts.short_definition: The restriction of games like Baba is You, Braid, and Magic: the Gathering Arena due to their computability or complexity properties that conflict with platform policies.
Use of the LATEX document preparation system to write and format homework solutions for clarity and conciseness.
The set of instructions regarding submission methods, deadlines, and formats for homework assignments.
Rules and ethical guidelines restricting how students may work together on assignments.
The process of determining the time complexity of an algorithm containing loops within loops, by multiplying the number of iterations of each loop.
A formal mathematical argument establishing tight upper and lower bounds for an algorithm's runtime.
The sequence of operations performed during the execution of an algorithm on a specific input.
Given an array of integers, output an index i such that the element at i is no smaller than any of its neighbors.
The concept of adding two functions with known asymptotic bounds and studying the asymptotic bound of their sum.
The concept of composing two functions with known asymptotic bounds and studying the asymptotic bound of their composition.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm design for finding smallest missing integer greater than or equal to S
concepts.short_definition: Designing an algorithm to find the smallest integer greater than or equal to a target integer S that is not present in a strictly increasing integer array A.
Writing code to implement a described algorithm to solve a particular problem.
A path through a weighted DAG whose total sum of edge weights is an even number.

concepts.canonical_name: Shortest Even Path Problem in DAG
concepts.short_definition: Finding the path from a source node to every other node that has the smallest sum of weights and an even total weight.
Techniques to improve the runtime efficiency of a dynamic programming algorithm, such as removing redundant computations or using prefix sums to achieve linear time complexity.

A combinatorial optimization problem where a sandwich is made from sections of bread filled with Firm, Medium, or Silken tofu pieces with specific length requirements and tastiness scores, aiming to maximize total tastiness without consecutive pieces of the same consistency, except the last piece can be shorter.
Computing the maximum sum of tastiness scores over all sections for a tofu sandwich arrangement respecting piece length and consistency constraints using DP.
A target problem (likely Shortest Path Subset Problem or similar) used as a reference for reductions in combinatorial optimization to show problem relationships.
The study of strategic decision making where players alternate moves with the goal of optimizing their own outcomes.
A strategy that maximizes a player's outcome assuming the opponent also plays optimally.
The shortest path between two nodes in a grid graph, moving only across shared edges and avoiding forbidden cells.
A dynamic programming approach to count the number of distinct paths satisfying constraints in a grid in O(n^2) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Optimal Shortest Path with Maximum Upgrades
concepts.short_definition: A shortest path in the grid that collects the maximum number of upgrades along any shortest path.
Movement allowed only between grid squares sharing edges, forbidden to enter grid squares containing viruses.
The design or proposal of a data organization method to store, manage, and facilitate access to data efficiently.
The official process for submitting solutions and code for automated checking in an algorithms course.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming for Shortest Even Path
concepts.short_definition: A recursive approach using subproblems E[u] and O[u] to compute shortest paths with even or odd total weight from a source node s to nodes u in the graph.

concepts.canonical_name: Prefix Sums for Efficient Range Sum Computation
concepts.short_definition: Precomputing prefix sums of ingredient tastiness arrays (F, M, S) to enable constant-time computation of sums over arbitrary intervals in the DP.

concepts.canonical_name: Sliding Window Sum Technique for DP Optimization
concepts.short_definition: Using auxiliary arrays to store the sums of sliding windows of size f, m, or s over ingredient tastiness arrays to achieve O(n) runtime for the DP.

concepts.canonical_name: Many-one Reduction from Sandwich DP Problem to Shortest Path Problem (SPSP)
concepts.short_definition: A polynomial-time reduction that maps an instance of the sandwich maximum tastiness problem to a shortest path problem graph, preserving correctness so that the shortest path distance corresponds to the maximum tastiness.
A metric where the "shortest" path is defined as the path maximizing the sum of edge weights.
A method to precompute sums of prefix segments of an array to enable efficient segment sum queries.
A method to construct a graph from problem states and transitions with weighted edges to enable shortest or longest path computations.
A game involving dividing a sandwich with sections of integer tastiness values between two players taking turns to eat or cut the sandwich, aiming to maximize their own total tastiness.

concepts.canonical_name: Maximizing Own Score Also Maximizes Score Difference
concepts.short_definition: In the Tasty Sandwich Division problem, a move that maximizes Ditto's total tastiness D also maximizes the difference D − P between Ditto's and Psyduck's totals.
Optimization problem where two players (Ditto and opponent) pick sections to maximize their tastiness difference, with total tastiness constant.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming for Optimal Play in Section Picking Game
concepts.short_definition: DP algorithm to compute the value of D−P assuming optimal play, using subproblems defined by remaining sections and player's turn.

concepts.canonical_name: Optimized O(n) Dynamic Programming Recurrence for Section Picking Game
concepts.short_definition: An improved DP recurrence f(i) = max{ti + f(i + 1), ti − f(i + 1)} using absolute value, reducing complexity to Θ(n).
A route from a start grid square to an exit grid square moving only through adjacent edges, minimizing the number of visited squares.
An algorithm design technique used to efficiently compute optimal paths and count number of paths in a grid by breaking down the problem into subproblems.
A method of identifying cells in an n by n grid by coordinates (i, j) with (1, 1) at the upper left and (n, n) at the bottom right.
A representation of grid cell values using a two-dimensional array L where L[i][j] denotes the contents of grid square (i, j).

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Subproblems for Path Optimization
concepts.short_definition: Formulating two types of subproblems: one to compute maximum upgrades from cell (i, j) to (n, n), and another to count the number of optimal paths achieving that maximum, both defined on paths of length (n - i) + (n - j) + 1.
The indices i and j used in subproblems and grid references range from 1 to n + 1 inclusive, extending beyond the grid size for boundary conditions.
The process of modeling positions containing viruses as blocked cells with no path originating from them, represented by setting their path value to negative infinity and path count to zero.
An indicator function m(i, j) that is 1 if a cell contains an upgrade, affecting the path score by being added to the maximum of future path scores.
The property that dependency relations among subproblems do not form cycles, ensuring a well-defined order of evaluation.

concepts.canonical_name: Base Case in Dynamic Programming for Grid Path Problems
concepts.short_definition: Initialization conditions for functions k and x on grid squares, specifying starting values and invalid indices.
The notation x(i, j) denotes the element at row i and column j of a matrix x.
Writing a Python function that realizes a given algorithm according to its specification or pseudocode.
Given a graph G=(V,E), decide if there exists a function ϕ: V→{r,g,b} such that adjacent vertices have different colors.
Given a collection S of subsets of universe U, output YES iff there exists a subset T ⊆ S that partitions U.
Proof that the Exact Boolean Cover problem is NP-complete, via reduction from 3COLOR.
Proof that the Vertex Cover problem is NP-complete.
Given a graph G=(V,E) and integer k, decide if there exists a subset S ⊆ V of size ≤ k that intersects every edge in E.
A language for which there exists a Turing machine that halts and accepts for strings in the language and halts and rejects for strings not in the language.
A language for which there exists a Turing machine that halts and accepts for strings in the language, but may not halt for strings not in the language.
Given a language L, its complement consists of all strings not in L.

A method in computational complexity theory used to construct problems or algorithms to prove separations between complexity classes, typically by defining functions or deciders that differ from all algorithms within a class on infinitely many inputs.
A Turing machine or algorithm that, for every input, halts and either accepts or rejects, thereby deciding membership in a language.
The assertion or proof that the class of recursive languages (R) is not equal to the class of languages decidable in polynomial time (P).
A bijection between sets where the function and its inverse are both computable functions.
A provided solution to problems intended for study or verification of problem-solving approaches.
Problems designed for student practice, not requiring coding in this context, meant to reinforce understanding and prepare for exams.
Topics and problem types that may appear on examinations and require understanding by students.
A polynomial-time transformation from the 3COLOR problem to the Vertex Cover problem, proving that Vertex Cover is NP-hard.
Running two algorithms simultaneously on the same input to combine their outputs for decision-making.
A computable function f such that every polynomial time algorithm halts within f(n) steps for cofinitely many inputs of length n.

concepts.canonical_name: Constructing a Language Outside Polynomial Time
concepts.short_definition: Defining a language via a diagonalization method so that it disagrees with every polynomial time algorithm on infinitely many inputs, thus is not in P but is in R.
The requirement to provide rigorous justification or proof for claims made in algorithm analysis, including runtime and correctness.
The practice of writing algorithm solutions in a clear and straightforward manner to facilitate grading and understanding.
The use of LATEX for preparing and submitting clear, professional algorithm solutions in PDF format.
Rules and procedures on how to submit algorithm problem set solutions, including use of Gradescope and ensuring pages are selected for feedback.
The policy governing collaboration and academic honesty for problem set submissions in the algorithms course.
The system at https://alg.mit.edu for automated checking of Python code related to algorithm problem sets.
The procedure of adjusting index values returned by recursive calls to reflect their position in the original array.
If f1 ∈O(f2) and g1 ∈O(g2), then f1 + g1 ∈O(f2 + g2).
A method to check if f(n) ∈ O(g(n)) by examining the limit of f(n)/g(n) as n→∞.

concepts.canonical_name: Asymptotic solution to recurrence with f(n) = Θ(n log n)
concepts.short_definition: The asymptotic solution to T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n log n) is T(n) ∈ Θ(n log^2 n).
Using induction on powers of two to prove asymptotic bounds on recursive functions.

concepts.canonical_name: Modified Binary Search for Missing Integer
concepts.short_definition: A variation of binary search designed to find the smallest integer greater than or equal to s that is missing from a strictly increasing integer array.

concepts.canonical_name: Reduction to Binary Search for Missing Integer
concepts.short_definition: A method to find the missing integer by reducing the problem to binary searches on transformed arrays involving the input array and offsets.
An array in which each element is strictly greater than the previous element.
A sequence of integers where each number in the sequence increments by exactly one from the previous number.

concepts.canonical_name: Divide and Conquer Algorithm for Missing Number
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that locates the missing element in an array of integers by recursively examining subarrays based on the presence or absence of consecutive sequences.
A method of proving an algorithm's correctness by showing base cases and inductive steps using strong induction, often by showing the algorithm works for input sizes and their halves.
The correctness of an algorithm that searches for an element in an array by recursively exploring either the left or right half depending on comparison, proved using strong induction.
A property of an array where each element is strictly greater than its predecessor, often used to prove sorting or search correctness.
A technique of defining auxiliary arrays like B derived from A to facilitate proof of search correctness by considering inequalities and bounds.
Analyzing the time complexity or runtime behavior of an algorithm, often involving recursive divide-and-conquer strategies reducing input size by roughly half each time.
Binary search operates in logarithmic time O(log n) by halving the search space each iteration.
A method of representing a natural number k using an array of length n, where each element corresponds to a digit in base n notation.
The operation that increases the stored number k by one in a base-n counter.
An operation that outputs the current stored number k and resets it to zero in a base-n counter.
The process of sorting elements based on integer keys, especially suited to non-comparison sorting algorithms when keys lie in a small range.
The process of re-sorting a dataset after a small change or update, which can sometimes be optimized beyond sorting the entire dataset from scratch.
Sorting strings where each string has the same fixed length, which can leverage algorithms like radix sort if the string length is small relative to log n.
Sorting data with physical constraints on movement, such as limited width for passing and restrictions on how items can be relocated, requiring specialized methods or algorithms.

concepts.canonical_name: Sorting by Rational Numbers with Close Values
concepts.short_definition: Sorting elements based on ratios (win rates), where small differences challenge precision and may affect the choice of sorting algorithm or comparison method.

concepts.canonical_name: OPPLARGER and OPPSMALLER Counts for Dual-Color Boxes Sorted by Width
concepts.short_definition: For two lists of boxes (red and white, each sorted by width), count for each box b the number of opposite color boxes with strictly larger length and width (OPPLARGER) and strictly smaller length and width (OPPSMALLER).
Algorithm that counts inversions in a sequence, useful for comparing orderings and counting relationships in O(n log n) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Divide and Conquer Algorithm for LARGER and SMALLER Counts Sorted by Length
concepts.short_definition: An O(n log n) divide and conquer algorithm to compute for each box b how many boxes have strictly larger length and width (LARGER(b)) and how many have strictly smaller length and width (SMALLER(b)), assuming boxes sorted by length.

concepts.canonical_name: Counting Triples of Boxes with Increasing Length and Width
concepts.short_definition: Design an O(n log n) algorithm to count triples (a,b,c) of boxes such that l(a)<l(b)<l(c) and w(a)<w(b)<w(c) without color or ordering assumptions.

concepts.canonical_name: Insert First Operation in Doubly Linked List
concepts.short_definition: An operation that inserts an item at the beginning (head) of the doubly linked list in worst-case Θ(1) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Delete First Operation in Doubly Linked List
concepts.short_definition: An operation that deletes the first item (head) of the doubly linked list in worst-case Θ(1) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Insert Last Operation in Doubly Linked List
concepts.short_definition: An operation that inserts an item at the end (tail) of the doubly linked list in worst-case Θ(1) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Delete Last Operation in Doubly Linked List
concepts.short_definition: An operation that deletes the last item (tail) of the doubly linked list in worst-case Θ(1) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Insert Mid Operation in Modified Doubly Linked List
concepts.short_definition: An operation that inserts an item at the middle index (⌊n/2⌋) of the doubly linked list, supporting worst-case Θ(1) time complexity in the modified data structure.

concepts.canonical_name: Delete Mid Operation in Modified Doubly Linked List
concepts.short_definition: An operation that deletes and returns the item at the middle index (⌊n/2⌋) of the doubly linked list, supporting worst-case Θ(1) time complexity in the modified data structure.
List operations that complete in worst-case Θ(1) time regardless of list size.
An asymptotic time complexity where a sorting algorithm runs in linear time proportional to the size of the input n.
A lower bound on the difference between distinct win rates computed as ratios of wins to battles for different Pokémons, specifically 1/(n−1)^2.

concepts.canonical_name: Integer Mapping of Win Rates via Scaling
concepts.short_definition: A process for mapping distinct fractional win rates wi/bi to distinct integers xi by scaling with (n−1)^2 and dividing by bi, enabling a radix sort for efficient sorting.
The principle that ordering of integer representations xi corresponds exactly to ordering of the original fractional win rates wi/bi, ensuring correctness of sorting method.

concepts.canonical_name: Partitioning a Set Based on Color in Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: A method where elements are categorized into groups based on color attributes, affecting subsequent computation such as zeroing specific counts based on color.
The process of setting a counter variable to zero to track the number of occurrences or processed items during execution.
Using a counter variable to keep track of how many white boxes have been processed in an algorithm or procedure.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm for counting boxes with larger or smaller dimensions
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that, given lists of boxes sorted by certain dimensions, counts how many boxes have strictly larger or smaller length and width than each box.

concepts.canonical_name: Proof of correctness for box dimension counting algorithm
concepts.short_definition: Logical reasoning that verifies the validity of the counting algorithm based on box size assumptions and processing order.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime analysis of box counting algorithm
concepts.short_definition: Analysis showing that the box counting algorithm runs in linear time Θ(n) due to constant-time operations and single pass through data.

concepts.canonical_name: Splitting a box into longer and shorter halves
concepts.short_definition: The process of dividing a box into two parts, one longer half and one shorter half, as a step in problem-solving or spatial reasoning.

concepts.canonical_name: Divide and Conquer Recursion on Longer Half
concepts.short_definition: A recursion strategy where at each step, the problem is split and recursion is applied on the longer half of the partitioned problem.
An operation or step in an algorithm that marks certain boxes by painting them red, often after processing or recursion steps.
An operation or step that involves setting boxes to a white color as part of a solution.
Understanding how for every bin b in a sorting or binning algorithm, the opposite bin (b.opp) contributes its larger and smaller elements to b's corresponding larger and smaller bins.

concepts.canonical_name: Merge step in Divide and Conquer
concepts.short_definition: The step of combining two sorted lists into one merged sorted list, preserving order and counts.
A method of partitioning a count or problem based on a chosen middle element to simplify analysis or computation.

concepts.canonical_name: Two-list approach for insert mid and delete mid
concepts.short_definition: Maintaining two doubly-linked lists such that the second has equal or one more element than the first, supporting insert mid and delete mid in Θ(1) by always operating on list2's front and rebalancing.
After each operation, restoring the size invariant by moving one element between list1 and list2 to keep list2 size equal or one more than list1.

concepts.canonical_name: Mid pointer approach for insert mid and delete mid
concepts.short_definition: Adding a mid pointer to a standard doubly-linked list pointing to the node at index ⌊n/2⌋ and updating it in Θ(1) time to support insert mid and delete mid.
Insert mid(x) implemented by splicing a new node before mid and adjusting mid pointer based on parity, in Θ(1) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Mid pointer update rules for standard operations
concepts.short_definition: Rules for updating mid pointer after insert first and delete first operations to maintain correctness, based on list size parity.

concepts.canonical_name: Middle Pointer Update in Doubly Linked List
concepts.short_definition: The logic for updating the middle pointer of a doubly linked list during insertions and deletions at the end, based on the parity of the list size.
Operations on a doubly linked list that take constant time, including pointer updates for middle element.

concepts.canonical_name: Parity-based Decision for Mid Pointer Adjustment
concepts.short_definition: Using the parity (odd or even) of the list size n to decide whether to move the middle pointer forward or backward during insert or delete operations.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm for Union of Intervals with Integer Starts
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that merges intervals whose start points are integers into a disjoint union in O(n) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm for Union of Intervals with Intervals Longer Than One Hour
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that merges intervals where each interval has length greater than one hour, running in O(n) time using solution from integer start case.
A pair of Grunts (x, y), with x < y, such that the sum of their Pokemon counts equals p.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm with O(n log n) Worst-Case Runtime
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm designed to find B (number of battle pairs) and the minimal x* battle pair with guaranteed worst-case runtime of O(n log n).
An algorithm designed to find B and (x* , y*) with expected runtime of O(n).

concepts.canonical_name: Reconstructing PreOrder Traversal from InOrder and PostOrder
concepts.short_definition: Algorithmic problem of determining the PreOrder traversal of a binary tree given its InOrder and PostOrder traversals, under the assumption of unique node values.

concepts.canonical_name: Hashing Optimization in Tree Traversal Reconstruction
concepts.short_definition: The technique of using hashing to accelerate the mapping from node values to indices during the reconstruction of PreOrder traversal from InOrder and PostOrder traversals, achieving expected O(n) time complexity.

A binary search tree implementation following the functional programming paradigm where the tree structure is immutable and never modified after creation, using class attributes for item, left subtree, and right subtree.
The set of items represented by a BST T is the union of its root item and the sets represented by its left and right subtrees.
A function that takes a BST and an integer key and returns True if the key is in the BST's set, and False otherwise.
A function that takes a BST and an integer key and outputs a new BST whose set is the union of the original set and the key, without modifying the original BST.

concepts.canonical_name: Functional Programming Paradigm in Data Structures
concepts.short_definition: An approach to programming where data structures are immutable and changes produce new versions rather than modifying existing ones.
The condition that all interval start times ai are integers, which allows for certain linear-time sorting algorithms to be applied.

concepts.canonical_name: Proof of Correctness for Interval Union Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The argument that after sorting and merging overlapping intervals in order, the resulting disjoint intervals correctly represent the union of the original intervals.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Analysis of Counting Sort Interval Union
concepts.short_definition: The justification that counting sort takes Θ(n) time under given conditions and merging intervals also completes in Θ(n), resulting in overall Θ(n) runtime.

concepts.canonical_name: Reduction of General Interval Union to Integer Start Times Case
concepts.short_definition: A method that reduces the problem of computing the union of intervals with arbitrary start times, under an additional assumption on minimum interval length, to the previously solved integer start times case.

concepts.canonical_name: Existence of an Integer Between Two Real Numbers
concepts.short_definition: For any two real numbers a and b where a < b, there exists at least one integer c such that a < c < b.
The method or process to calculate the set difference between two intervals, specifically in this case between intervals like [n - ci, n - ai].
The operation of replacing an interval [x, y] with [n - y, n - x], effectively reflecting the interval relative to n.
Vectors whose components are complex numbers, often denoted using i for the imaginary unit.
The process of calculating individual components (such as ci and bi) of a given vector using prior calculations or formulas.
A function that given finite sets of intervals with the same union returns a minimal set of intervals representing that union without overlap.
A self-inverting transformation of intervals defined as g(I) = {{n −x : x ∈ I} : I ∈ I} which commutes with the union function f.
A proof technique using cases on disjoint vs overlapping intervals to prove correctness of interval functions applying transformations.
Performing interval computations such as finding n − ci and unions via Θ(n) linear scans over n intervals.

concepts.canonical_name: Limitations of COUNTING-SORT for Interval Union
concepts.short_definition: Counting sort does not merge intervals aggressively enough leading to overlapping output intervals, hence inappropriate for interval union tasks where disjoint intervals are required.
A variable that accumulates a count or sum as a process progresses, often used to track progress or optimum values in iterative algorithms.
The current best or optimum value(s) maintained dynamically during the execution of an algorithm, updated as better solutions are found.
The technique of maintaining the original positions of elements in a sequence prior to sorting, typically by pairing each element with its original index.
A time complexity denoting that an algorithm's runtime grows proportionally to n log n, typical for efficient comparison sorts.
A procedure for identifying pairs of elements (x, y) satisfying certain conditions, such as x < y and a relation between values at these indices.
The procedure of initializing variables B, (x*, y*) and a sorted sequence {ci} according to specific algorithm steps.
Setting initial index variables i and j at the start (0) and end (n−1) positions of a data structure, typically an array or list, to enable bidirectional traversal.

concepts.canonical_name: Two-pointer technique for pairing elements in sorted list
concepts.short_definition: An algorithmic method using two indices moving through a sorted list from opposite ends to find pairs that satisfy a sum condition.
The process of initializing the current best solution (x∗, y∗) to start values before optimization begins, here set to (n, n).
Checking existence of a key in a dictionary or map data structure and retrieving its associated value.
The expected O(1) time complexity for insertion and find operations in a hash table for n insertions and find operations.
Analysis showing that creating the hash table and performing n find operations leads to an expected total runtime of Θ(n).
Using a hash-based data structure to map node values to indices in order traversal to enable O(1) lookups of root positions during reconstruction.

concepts.canonical_name: Expected O(n) runtime for tree traversal reconstruction using hashing
concepts.short_definition: The time complexity analysis showing that using a hashmap to lookup root indices during tree reconstruction results in expected linear time complexity.
A function that removes a key from an immutable BST producing a new BST that lacks the key without modifying the original.

concepts.canonical_name: Set of elements represented by BST
concepts.short_definition: The mathematical set of all keys stored in a BST, defined recursively as the union of root item and all elements in its left and right subtrees.

concepts.canonical_name: BST runtime analysis linear in tree height
concepts.short_definition: The property that operations like insert and delete take time proportional to the height of the BST, which is the longest path from root to a leaf.
Two fundamental rotation operations on binary trees: rotate-right pivots a node leftward, and rotate-left pivots a node rightward to restore balance.
The process of removing a node from a data structure by swapping or rearranging elements to maintain structure integrity.

concepts.canonical_name: Element Swapping in AVL Tree Restoration
concepts.short_definition: The process of swapping elements to restore AVL tree balance before performing rotations in rebalancing.

concepts.canonical_name: Set Data Structure with Composite Keys
concepts.short_definition: A set data structure where each element has two keys: one comparable and one hashable; elements identified uniquely by the ordered pair of these keys.

concepts.canonical_name: Find Operation in Sets with Composite Keys
concepts.short_definition: An operation to locate elements in a set using one or both keys from composite key sets, returning an element matching the key(s).

concepts.canonical_name: Delete Operation in Sets with Composite Keys
concepts.short_definition: An operation to remove elements from a set using one or both keys from composite key sets, where deleting by single key removes all elements matching that key.
A data structure designed to track athletes' long jump distances and determine prize winners according to a threshold and recency rule.
An operation recording an athlete's latest long jump distance in the data structure.
An operation that outputs the prize winner's name based on a minimum distance threshold and the most recent eligible jump.
The property that the data structure uses O(n) space, where n is the total number of athletes who have participated so far.

concepts.canonical_name: Data Structure for Dynamic Player Recruitment
concepts.short_definition: A data structure that supports insertion, deletion, and querying (finding the best player under certain cost constraints) efficiently in O(log n) time.
Operation to add a new player (element) into the data structure representing the recruitment options.
Operation to remove a player (element) from the data structure representing recruitment options.

concepts.canonical_name: Find Best Player with Cost Constraint
concepts.short_definition: Query operation to find the highest rated player whose cost does not exceed a given budget m.

concepts.canonical_name: Find Best Player with Cost Range Constraint
concepts.short_definition: Query operation to find the highest rated player whose cost is between m/2 and m inclusive.
Rotations are tree restructuring operations that maintain the binary search tree property while balancing the tree, including right and left rotations.
Swapping a node to be deleted with its successor (minimum in right subtree) until it becomes a leaf node during AVL tree deletion.
Swapping a node to be deleted with its predecessor (maximum in left subtree) until it becomes a leaf node during AVL tree deletion.

concepts.canonical_name: Nested Data Structures for Dual-Key Set
concepts.short_definition: A data structure design using two nested structures: an AVL tree keyed by one key, containing hash sets keyed by the other key, and a hash set keyed by the second key, containing AVL trees keyed by the first key, enabling efficient FIND and DELETE operations by either key.

concepts.canonical_name: Set Data Structure with Dual Keys
concepts.short_definition: A SET data structure storing elements identified uniquely by an ordered pair of keys (k1,k2), allowing FIND and DELETE operations using either key individually or both keys together.

concepts.canonical_name: Complexity Analysis of Dual-Key Set Operations
concepts.short_definition: The time complexity characterization of FIND, DELETE, and INSERT operations in a nested dual-key SET data structure, including worst-case, amortized, and expected time bounds.

concepts.canonical_name: Data Structure using Two AVL Trees for Long Jump
concepts.short_definition: A composite data structure that uses two AVL trees: one storing records of jumps in order of time with augmentations, and another mapping athlete names to nodes, to efficiently support JUMP and PRIZE operations.
The property that the augmented value MAX(T) of an AVL subtree T correctly stores the maximum distance among records in T's subtree, maintained via comparisons at each node.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithmic Time Complexity of AVL Tree Operations
concepts.short_definition: AVL tree insertions, deletions, and queries operate in O(log n) time.
A correctness argument for PRIZE, showing that recursive traversal correctly identifies the most recent eligible athlete or defaults to Srini if none qualify.
A recursive procedure to find the prize winner by comparing subtree augmentations with threshold t to decide traversal direction in DISTANCES AVL tree.

concepts.canonical_name: Range Query in Binary Search Tree
concepts.short_definition: A method to find records within a specified range in a binary search tree, using recursive traversal and subtree pruning.

concepts.canonical_name: Augmented Binary Search Tree for timestamped records
concepts.short_definition: A binary search tree structure augmented with metadata such as counters and timestamps to support efficient range queries and updates on records.
A technique to maintain efficient time and space bounds by occasionally rebuilding a data structure from scratch when certain counters exceed thresholds.

concepts.canonical_name: Augmentation of Binary Search Tree with Subtree Maximum Rating
concepts.short_definition: An augmentation of each subtree in a binary search tree storing the player with the maximum rating in that subtree, enabling efficient queries.
Given a budget m, find the highest rated player whose cost is at most m using the augmented AVL tree.
The concept that an empty tree is considered to have a rating of negative infinity and should output a special symbol ⊥ when queried.
A method of determining the next recursive step based on the root cost comparison to a threshold m; if the root cost is greater than m, recurse on the left subtree.

concepts.canonical_name: Recursive Algorithm for Best Rating Selection
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that, given a root cost at most m, recursively explores right branches and compares outcomes with the root player and left augmentation to find the best rating.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Analysis of Recursive Search Similar to AVL Find
concepts.short_definition: Analyzing the runtime complexity of the recursive best rating selection algorithm, showing it matches the runtime characteristics of an AVL tree find operation.
A tree data structure with no nodes, meaning it contains no players or elements.
The cost attribute associated with a player, used for filtering players whose cost is at most a given value m.
An output symbol representing 'no value' or 'no suitable player found', returned by the algorithm when no qualifying players exist.
A method where a function calls itself on subtrees to solve problems in binary trees.
The division of players in a tree based on whether their costs are less than or equal to a given threshold m, mapping them to the left subtree if their cost is at most m.
An augmentation in BST nodes storing the minimum cost among all elements in the subtree rooted at that node.

concepts.canonical_name: Recursive Find Best Operation in Augmented BST
concepts.short_definition: A recursive method to find the best element (e.g., minimal cost) in an augmented BST whose cost is at most m.
The concept of outputting a special symbol (⊥) when a certain condition (root augmentation larger than m) in an algorithm is met, indicating a failure or invalid state.
A method of solving a problem by recursively processing the right subcomponent or right side of a data structure or problem instance, conditional on a constraint on augmentation.
The cost value associated with the root node of a decision tree, representing the evaluation metric or resource consumption at the root.

concepts.canonical_name: Root Player Selection in Decision Trees
concepts.short_definition: The procedure of selecting the root player when the root node of the decision tree has a cost at most a given threshold m.
The runtime complexity of searching (finding) an element in an AVL tree, which is logarithmic in the number of nodes due to AVL balance properties.
A method of proving correctness by considering all possible cases separately and showing correctness in each case.
A root augmentation refers to an augmenting path starting from the root in a matching problem, used to improve the matching by increasing its cardinality or weight.
A cost threshold m above which players' costs are considered too high, used to determine when no acceptable augmentation exists and the algorithm should terminate with failure (return ⊥).

concepts.canonical_name: Failure Return Condition in Matching Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: The condition under which the matching algorithm returns failure (⊥) indicating no improvement is possible, specifically when all players have costs exceeding a threshold m.
The notion that if the right augmentation of a tree is at most m, then there exists a player in the right subtree with cost at most m.
In a binary tree, players (nodes) in the right subtree with augmentation at most m have cost less than or equal to any player in the left subtree or at the root, making them better in comparison.
The principle that the best player in the right subtree, under the given augmentation conditions, is also the best player in the entire tree.

concepts.canonical_name: Comparison of Subtree Player Costs in a Binary Tree
concepts.short_definition: The idea that if the right subtree's augmentation cost exceeds a threshold m, and the root's cost is at most m, then players in the right subtree are too expensive, and players in the left subtree are worse than the root, making the root the best player whose cost is at most m.

concepts.canonical_name: Augmented Binary Search Tree for Range Queries
concepts.short_definition: A data structure that maintains, for each subtree, augmentations such as best player, minimum key, and maximum key to enable efficient logarithmic time queries on ranges of costs.

concepts.canonical_name: Maintaining O(log n) Time Complexity for Insert, Delete, and Find Best
concepts.short_definition: Ensuring that insert, delete, and find best operations all run in logarithmic time despite the augmentations and additional constraints.
The condition involving the minimum key in a tree being greater than a specific value m.
The condition involving the maximum key in a tree being less than a specific fraction of a value m/2.
The concept of intervals on the real number line, specifically intervals defined by division of a parameter m, such as [m/2, m], and understanding their properties and meaning in algorithms.
A process or method to enhance a data structure or algorithm by modifying or updating it to improve performance or correctness.
A principle where if the root node's cost exceeds a threshold m, the search algorithm recurses on the left subtree to find acceptable solutions.
The correctness argument that a recursive algorithm produces the correct output based on mutually exclusive steps and case analysis.
The analysis of the runtime complexity of a recursive algorithm using mutually exclusive steps and recursion tree properties obtaining O(log n) runtime.
Dividing a problem into cases based on the eligibility or cost range of nodes and analyzing each separately in a recursive algorithm.

concepts.canonical_name: Mirror Recursive Functions: find_best_atmost and find_best_atleast
concepts.short_definition: Two symmetric recursive functions used to find the highest rated player whose cost is at most or at least a given value m, respectively.
The process of solving a problem by calling the same function or procedure with smaller inputs repeatedly.
A recursive method to find the best (highest rated) player within a given cost range [m/2, m] in an AVL tree of players, leveraging subtree cost bounds and ratings.

concepts.canonical_name: Augmentation of AVL tree nodes with min_cost
concepts.short_definition: Storing the minimum cost among all players in the subtree rooted at a node, to enable pruning and fast decision making in queries.

concepts.canonical_name: Augmentation of AVL tree nodes with max_cost
concepts.short_definition: Storing the maximum cost among all players in the subtree rooted at a node, to enable pruning and fast decision making in queries.
The function runs in O(log n) time because it either descends the AVL tree to a leaf or performs O(log n) operations at a step, totaling O(log n) complexity.
Each player is represented as a pair (cost, rating) where cost is a numerical value and rating is a score used to find best players.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph with locked doors and keys
concepts.short_definition: A graph model where locations are nodes and doors as edges, each door has a lock type; keys to these locks are found at certain locations.
Finding a minimum-door-passing path in a graph where node traversal depends on having keys that open locked edges.
Using BFS extended with state to track keys collected and reachable nodes to find constrained shortest paths in graphs.
Using a limited number of lock picks to bypass locked doors without keys in pathfinding to minimize door passages.
A rule stating that certain classes must be completed before others can be taken.
An ordering or grouping of classes respecting all prerequisite constraints to produce a schedule.

concepts.canonical_name: Minimizing Semester Count in Course Scheduling
concepts.short_definition: The problem of arranging courses to complete a target course in the fewest semesters possible.
A constraint limiting course schedules to taking only one class per semester.
Course scheduling without limits on the number of classes per semester; allows taking multiple classes in the same semester.
A directed graph where every vertex has an edge to itself (a self-loop).
A function f on vertices of a graph such that for every vertex v, f(v) is an out-neighbor of v in the graph.
The iterative application of a movement function f, where f^{0}(v)=v and f^{i+1}(v)=f(f^{i}(v)).

concepts.canonical_name: Hide and Seek Game on Directed Graphs
concepts.short_definition: A game where two players start at vertices of a directed graph and move according to respective movement functions, with one having a head start. One player tries to evade, the other tries to capture by occupying the same vertex at the same time.

concepts.canonical_name: Naïve Evade Strategy in Hide and Seek
concepts.short_definition: A strategy where the evader goes to the vertex farthest reachable from the seeker and stays there to maximize evasion time.

concepts.canonical_name: Linear Time Algorithm to Maximize Evasion Time
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm running in time linear in the size of the graph that computes a movement function for the evader to maximize the time before capture, regardless of the seeker's strategy.

concepts.canonical_name: Linear Time Algorithm to Minimize Capture Time
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm running in linear time that, given the evader's movement function, finds the seeker's movement function minimizing the time to capture or determines capture is impossible.
Use of division with remainder to reduce runtime complexity, hinted as a better approach than naive iteration to achieve linear time complexity in the algorithm.
Representing a function f: V → V as a list where f(i) encodes the image of vertex i under f.

concepts.canonical_name: State space graph with key and pizza possession states
concepts.short_definition: A graph construction representing each location combined with boolean states indicating possession of keys and pizza, used to encode all possible states of Liza's exploration of the labyrinth.

concepts.canonical_name: Breadth-First Search (BFS) in augmented state graph
concepts.short_definition: Using BFS to find shortest path in the constructed state space graph that represents Liza's traversal with keys and pizzas, minimizing the number of doors crossed.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph duplication for representing multiple key possession states
concepts.short_definition: The technique of duplicating nodes in a graph to represent multiple possible states of key possessions, resulting in a larger state-space graph encoding all possible states.

concepts.canonical_name: Linear time algorithm for shortest path in state-augmented graph
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that constructs the augmented graph with key and pizza possession states and uses BFS to find the shortest path, achieving O(|L| + |D|) time complexity.

concepts.canonical_name: State Space Representation with Lock Picks
concepts.short_definition: A method to model Liza's movement through locations including the number of lock picks remaining as part of the state for traversal algorithms.

concepts.canonical_name: Path Finding with Lock Picks and Keys
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm to find a path from start back to start that collects at least one pizza and minimizes the number of door passes, using keys and lock picks to pass doors.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Complexity in Graph Search Algorithms with State Expansion
concepts.short_definition: The analysis and understanding that expanding the vertex set by a factor of O(k) increases the runtime by a factor of O(k).
Constructing a directed graph where vertices represent classes and edges represent prerequisite relationships.
Using DFS on the graph to determine a topological order of classes by finish times, identifying valid course orders respecting prerequisites.
A topological ordering of a prerequisite graph corresponds to a valid linear schedule of courses respecting prerequisites.

concepts.canonical_name: Linear Time Algorithm for Prerequisite Scheduling with One Class per Semester
concepts.short_definition: Algorithm to produce a schedule with one class per semester in linear time minimizing semesters needed by performing DFS topological sorting on the reverse prerequisite graph.
Justification that DFS finishing times produce a valid topological order scheduling prerequisites before dependent classes and detect cycles indicating no valid schedule.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm Runtime Analysis for DFS-based Scheduling
concepts.short_definition: The time complexity of constructing the graph and performing DFS is linear in the number of classes and prerequisite edges.
The process of defining and creating a graph data structure G according to problem specifications or prior instructions.
A function defined on a subset of a set, possibly not defined for all inputs from the domain.

concepts.canonical_name: Function from a Set to the Natural Numbers
concepts.short_definition: A function that assigns each element of a set V a natural number in N.
An ordering of classes such that for every directed edge from class v to class u, v comes before u in the order.
Computing the value f(v) for each class v by setting f(v) to be 1 plus the maximum f(u) among all out-neighbors u of v or 0 if there are no out-neighbors.
For a vertex v in a directed graph, its out-neighbors are the vertices u where there is a directed edge from v to u.
An algorithm that assigns courses to semesters ensuring all prerequisites are taken before the dependent course.
An invariant that the scheduling function f assigns to each course the earliest semester in which it can be taken, respecting prerequisites.
A prerequisite relation where a course u must be completed in an earlier semester than course v if u is a prerequisite of v.

concepts.canonical_name: Strategy for Evading Capture in Directed Graph
concepts.short_definition: A strategy implemented via movement functions to maximize the time before one player (Hoothoot) is caught by another (Skitty) on a graph.
A specific example graph and initial positions where the naive strategy of going to the farthest reachable vertex and waiting fails to maximize evasion time.
The process of adding a constant k to all shortest path distances from a source node except the distance from the source to itself (δS(vS)).

concepts.canonical_name: Maximizing δS(x) under finite δH(x) constraint
concepts.short_definition: The problem of finding the value x such that the variation in entropy δS(x) is maximized while ensuring the variation in energy δH(x) remains finite.

concepts.canonical_name: Time to Reach a Vertex in a Graph
concepts.short_definition: A metric indicating the time it takes for a player or entity to reach a particular vertex in a graph during a game or process.
A mathematical operation involving division resulting in a quotient and remainder, useful in modular arithmetic and algorithm design.

concepts.canonical_name: Iterative Computation of Locations in a Graph
concepts.short_definition: Computing the positions or states of an entity (here, Hoothoot) over time by iteratively applying a function or relation and recording the sequence, typically until a repetition or cycle is detected.
Identifying the first repeated vertex or state in an iterative sequence to detect cycles, indicating repeating behavior or states.
Use of the remainder operation to adjust indices cyclically within algorithmic computations.

concepts.canonical_name: Computation of Sequential Locations in a Graph
concepts.short_definition: The process of determining the positions of an entity (Hoothoot) over a series of time steps up to a specified time index k' plus the size of vertex set |V|, typically in a graph or network context.
A condition to determine when to stop an iterative training process based on the change in the training score and a threshold.
A method for dividing two numbers step-by-step, especially useful for polynomials or multi-digit integers, typically operating in linear time relative to input size.
A simple search method that checks each element sequentially to find a target or to compare elements.

concepts.canonical_name: Function Repeat Detection in a Sequence
concepts.short_definition: Detecting the first repeated position and length of cycle of a function iterated from a start point.
A function from vertices to vertices that maps Skitty's optimal move at each vertex to catch Hoothoot assuming Skitty starts at vertex 0.

concepts.canonical_name: Modulo Operation to Reduce Time Parameter
concepts.short_definition: Using modulo arithmetic on the head start time k to handle repeated cycles in Hoothoot's movement function.
The requirement to explain and prove the time efficiency of an algorithm, including worst-case or expected runtimes.
The requirement to prove the correctness of an algorithm or data structure solution to a problem for full credit.
The practice of providing clear and concise algorithmic or data structure descriptions, avoiding convoluted and obtuse explanations to ensure clarity and better grading outcomes.
A theoretical lower bound on the runtime of algorithms based on comparisons between elements, often used to prove that certain tasks cannot be done faster than a specific time complexity.
An algorithm whose running time matches the lower bound for a problem's time complexity up to constant factors, representing the most efficient known solution in terms of growth rate.
The process of coding an algorithm in a programming language to produce executable software matching the algorithmic design.
An s-t path such that the traveler is never within distance k of any mine located at certain intersections.
The problem of finding the shortest path between two intersections that remains at least distance k away from all mines.
The distance range within which the proximity fuse of a mine is triggered or dangerous.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm for shortest k-safe path given fuse range
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that finds a shortest s-t path that is k-safe when the range k of proximity fuses is known.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm for maximum k for shortest k-safe path
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that finds a shortest k-safe path where k is as large as possible such that such a path exists.
An algorithm to find shortest paths from a source vertex s to a target vertex t in a weighted graph using a heuristic function h.
A function h : V → [0, ∞) estimating the shortest distance from any vertex v to the target t, used to guide the A* search.
A graph G′ with weight function w′(u, v) = w(u, v) + h(v) − h(u), used in A* to adjust edge weights according to heuristic h.
A heuristic h satisfying the triangle inequality: for every edge (u,v), h(u) ≤ h(v) + w(u, v).
A heuristic h such that for every vertex v, h(v) ≤ δ(v, t), i.e., h never overestimates the true shortest distance to the target t.
The operation of building a min-heap from an array of elements takes O(n) time.
Removing the root element from a heap and re-heapifying takes O(log n) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Sorting Lower Bound for k Elements
concepts.short_definition: To sort k elements requires at least Ω(k log k) time in the comparison model.

concepts.canonical_name: Asymptotically Optimal Algorithm for Magikarp Jump Contest
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that outputs the selection order of top-jumping Magikarps in O(n + k log n) time by building a min-heap and popping top elements k times.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Pruning Based on Distance Threshold
concepts.short_definition: Removing vertices from the graph that are within distance less than k of any mine in order to find k-safe paths.

concepts.canonical_name: Distance Computation from Set of Nodes
concepts.short_definition: Calculating the shortest distance from every node to the nearest node in a given set M in a weighted graph.
A graph where edges have weights and no direction, represented as G=(V,E) where V is a set of vertices and E is a set of edges, each with a weight.
An edge connecting two vertices in a weighted graph, characterized by an unordered pair of vertices {u,v} and a numerical weight representing length or cost.
The operation of removing vertices from a graph based on a condition related to distances (e.g., deleting any vertex v where the distance δ(u, v) is less than a threshold k).

concepts.canonical_name: Distance from Closest Mine in Graph
concepts.short_definition: For each vertex, the minimum distance to the nearest mine vertex in the graph.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm Complexity O(n log n + m)
concepts.short_definition: An algorithmic runtime complexity often associated with graph algorithms using priority queues and adjacency lists, where n is the number of vertices and m is the number of edges.
The probability of observed data under a Gaussian process model given hyperparameters, used for model selection.
The process of tuning Gaussian process kernel parameters by maximizing the marginal likelihood to improve model fit.

concepts.canonical_name: Predictive Distribution in Gaussian Process Regression
concepts.short_definition: The distribution predicted by a Gaussian process for new inputs, characterized by a mean and covariance based on training data and kernel parameters.
A statistical method for estimating model parameters by maximizing the likelihood function based on observed data.
The set of parameters defining the kernel function in a Gaussian process, controlling aspects like smoothness and lengthscale.
Choosing Gaussian process model hyperparameters by maximizing marginal likelihood to best explain observed data.
The set of inputs over which a function is defined, especially in context of optimization and regression.
Formulation of regression as a problem of finding function parameters that minimize a loss function over a data set.
A distance metric where the length of a path is defined by the maximum minimum edge weight along the path, affecting how shortest paths are computed.

concepts.canonical_name: Shortest Path Distance δ′(s, v) under the Max-Min Metric
concepts.short_definition: The shortest path distance from source vertex s to vertex v computed using the max-min metric.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Vertex Deletion Based on Distance Comparison
concepts.short_definition: The operation of deleting vertices in a graph where the updated shortest distance from a source vertex s to vertex v is less than that to vertex t, i.e. δ′(s, v) < δ′(s, t).
The process of adjusting data point weights to reflect original or desired distributions during model training or evaluation.
A metric used in graph algorithms where path costs are combined using minimum and addition operations, useful in shortest path problems.
The complexity measure related to the number of nodes and edges in a graph, often denoted as n and m respectively.
The cost c(u, v) associated with traveling along a directed edge from city u to city v, which can be positive or negative.

concepts.canonical_name: Pokémon Center as Starting and Ending Node
concepts.short_definition: Designated special nodes in the graph where Purrloin must start each day and can end journeys; specifically Nimbasa City Pokémon Center is the start point.
The constraint that Purrloin cannot lose more than k coins in a single day of travel.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm for Finding Reachable Cities with Cost Constraints
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm with O(n^2 log n) time complexity to find all cities that can be explored by Purrloin under the given cost and daily constraints, ending at the starting Pokémon Center.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm to Find Cheapest Path in Directed Weighted Graph
concepts.short_definition: An O(n^3) algorithm to find the minimum cost path from the Nimbasa City Pokémon Center to Nuvema Town and back, considering edge costs which can be positive or negative.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm Improvement to O(n^2 log n) Time for Cheapest Path
concepts.short_definition: A modification of the previous method to find the cheapest round trip path in improved O(n^2 log n) time complexity.
A graph where all edge weights are zero or positive.
A graph where no cycle has a sum of edge weights less than zero, ensuring shortest paths are well-defined.
The path having the maximum total length from a given start node to each reachable node in a directed graph, possibly infinite if cycles exist.

concepts.canonical_name: Infinite Longest Path Due to Cycles
concepts.short_definition: If a strongly connected component of size greater than 1 is reachable from start node and leads to a target node, the longest path length is infinite.
Algorithmic technique to compute longest paths in a Directed Acyclic Graph by negating weights and performing shortest path relaxations.

concepts.canonical_name: Negative and Positive Weight Negation Trick
concepts.short_definition: A technique that negates edge weights to transform longest path problems into shortest path problems on DAGs.
A shortest path problem in a graph where costs on edges can be negative but the total cost is constrained by a threshold k per day.

concepts.canonical_name: O(n² log n) Algorithm for Graph Exploration
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm with O(n² log n) time complexity designed to find all cities reachable under given constraints of cost and day limitations.
A constraint on traveling routes requiring that the net loss (cost) over any daily cycle must not exceed a given value k.
The set of nodes in a graph, denoted as V, representing entities such as cities in a network.
Constructing a graph by forming edges between vertex pairs only if a certain condition on a distance or weight function is satisfied.
A subset of a graph's vertices and edges that forms a graph itself, maintaining the direction of edges.
Building a new graph G' whose vertices correspond to Pokémon Centers (subset S), and edges represent allowed paths Purrloin can take, useful for planning daily travels.
Purrloin can visit a city v if the sum of the minimum distance from S to v and from v to S is at most k.
A function used to reweight graph edges to allow non-negative weights enabling Dijkstra's algorithm to be used for shortest paths computation.

concepts.canonical_name: Step 4 Optimization in Graph Path Problem
concepts.short_definition: Selecting the optimal pair of vertices u, v in a graph for which a route constraint is satisfied, minimizing a function over combined distance weights.

concepts.canonical_name: Shortest paths in weighted directed graph
concepts.short_definition: The problem of finding minimum-weight paths from each vertex to every other vertex in a directed graph with weighted edges.
The specific due dates by which homework or assignments must be submitted.
The process of submitting code to an automated system for verification and testing against predefined tests.
Providing brief and clear descriptions in solutions to avoid low marks due to convoluted or obtuse explanations.
A scheduling problem where one must select a subset of intervals so that no two overlap and the number of selected intervals is maximized or some coverage condition is met.
Finding a minimum size subset of intervals that cover a specified union of intervals or time period.
An O(n log n) greedy algorithm that selects intervals in a way that ensures minimum coverage size by prioritizing intervals with earliest finishing times or left boundaries.
The problem of scheduling tasks each with a profit and a deadline such that the chosen schedule maximizes total profit without missing deadlines.
The principle that an optimal schedule for tasks that take unit time each and have integral deadlines can be assumed to schedule tasks at integral time slots.

concepts.canonical_name: Maximum Profit Inclusion in Optimal Schedule
concepts.short_definition: The principle that any optimal schedule for this problem includes the task with maximum profit (here HP restoration).
A representation of a positive rational number as a sum of distinct unit fractions, i.e., fractions with numerator 1 and distinct positive integer denominators.
An algorithm that decomposes a fraction x/y into a sum of distinct unit fractions using a greedy approach, typically by subtracting the largest possible unit fraction at each step.

concepts.canonical_name: Computational Complexity of Egyptian Fraction Decomposition
concepts.short_definition: The study of time complexity for algorithms decomposing fractions into Egyptian fractions. In particular, no algorithm can do this in polynomial time with respect to the numerator x for certain cases.
Finding a minimum size set of intervals from a set to cover all given time intervals.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy Choice Property for Interval Cover
concepts.short_definition: In a set of intervals that cover a timeline, among intervals that start earliest, there exists one with the latest end time that can be chosen to preserve minimal coverage.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy Algorithm for Minimum Interval Cover
concepts.short_definition: An O(n log n) greedy algorithm that sorts intervals by start time and repeatedly selects intervals following the greedy choice property to cover all intervals with minimal selection.
A greedy strategy that selects intervals starting with those having the earliest start time to form a solution set.
The operation of finding all elements that are common to two sets.
A property where one interval fully includes another interval within its bounds.
A list of intervals ordered by a specific key, often by start or end times, facilitating efficient interval scheduling algorithms.
The starting point or time value of an interval.
The ending point or time value of an interval.
A set of intervals in which no intervals overlap, i.e., any two intervals have non-overlapping time ranges.
A method in clustering where if one cluster's element set is entirely contained within another's, the smaller cluster is discarded to simplify the clustering results.
A subset of intervals that covers a given set while having the smallest possible number of intervals.
Adjusting intervals by shortening their start or end points during iterations to avoid overlapping coverage while maintaining correctness.
There exists an optimal schedule where leftover containers are eaten at integral time units, starting from time 0, such that all are consumed before their expiration times.

concepts.canonical_name: Inclusion of maximum HP leftover in an optimal schedule
concepts.short_definition: Any optimal schedule for eating leftover containers must include the container with the maximum health point (HP) restoration value.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy algorithm for scheduling leftovers to maximize HP restoration
concepts.short_definition: A greedy O(n log n) algorithm that sorts leftovers by expiration time, uses a max-heap prioritized by HP, and schedules leftovers in decreasing order of expiration time to maximize total HP restored.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy choice property for leftover scheduling problem
concepts.short_definition: The choice to schedule the leftover with the highest expiration time and highest HP value last is optimal; exchanging selected leftovers preserves or improves schedule optimality.

concepts.canonical_name: Priority Queue Operations in Leftover Scheduling
concepts.short_definition: Using priority queues to insert and extract the leftover items based on their HP values during scheduling, with complexity O(log n) per operation.

concepts.canonical_name: AVL Tree for Expiration Time Management
concepts.short_definition: Using an AVL tree data structure constructed from expiration times to efficiently assign scheduling times to leftovers in the algorithm.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Complexity of Leftover Scheduling Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The total time complexity of the leftover scheduling algorithm is Θ(n log n), accounting for sorting and priority queue operations.
A scheduling technique where a leftover item with maximum health points (HP) can replace a previously scheduled leftover to maintain or improve overall health points and optimal schedule.
A schedule arrangement that maximizes the overall health points (HP) or objective function, ensuring no better schedule exists.
The process of scheduling leftovers represented as pairs (height h, time t) with the highest HP value in a valid order to optimize overall HP.

concepts.canonical_name: Scheduling algorithm for leftovers using AVL data structure
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that schedules leftovers by placing the leftover with maximum HP at the largest available time less than or equal to its timestamp, removing that time from an AVL data structure, repeating until no leftovers remain.
Proof of correctness of an algorithm using induction on the size of the input, assuming correctness for inputs of size k and proving for k+1.
An algorithm that schedules leftovers by adjusting expiration times and deciding optimal eating times based on expiration constraints.
Adjusting the expiration time of a leftover item to the minimum of its floor expiration time and 1 in order to decide scheduling.
When there is a single leftover item, the optimal scheduling might be not scheduling if expiration time is less than 1 or scheduling at time 0 if expiration is after 1.
The assumption that the algorithm works optimally for a smaller problem size, used to extend the proof to a larger problem size.
The nth harmonic number Hn is the sum of reciprocals of the first n positive integers.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Algorithm for Merging Strings
concepts.short_definition: A dynamic programming algorithm to determine if two strings A and B can be merged (interleaved) to form a third string C, assuming |C| = |A| + |B|, in O(|A||B|) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Restriction on Consecutive Characters from One String in Merging
concepts.short_definition: A DP algorithm to check if strings A and B can be merged to form C, with the additional restriction that no more than 3 consecutive characters from A are used in sequence during merging, still in O(|A||B|) time.
The maximum possible total mana expended to open chests under the worst sequence of safe and mimic chests, given a limit on how many mimics can be opened.
Partitioning a sequence of positive integers into four subsequences to maximize the minimum sum among these subsequences.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm for Maximum Quality Quarter Partition
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm to find the maximum possible minimum sum among four subsequences partitioned from a sequence, with a runtime of O(m^3 n).
Using dynamic programming techniques to solve sequence partitioning problems efficiently.
The problem of checking if a string C can be formed by merging two strings A and B in order, preserving the relative order of characters in A and B.

concepts.canonical_name: Subproblem Definition in Dynamic Programming for String Merging
concepts.short_definition: Defines a subproblem T(i, j) as a boolean indicating whether one can merge suffixes A[i:] and B[j:] into suffix C[i + j:].
The concept of advancing either pointer i or pointer j when matching the next letter from strings A and B, respectively, in a recursive or dynamic programming solution.

concepts.canonical_name: Boolean Recurrence Relation for String Interleaving
concepts.short_definition: A logical OR recurrence relation T(i, j) that represents whether a substring combination matches, defined in terms of matching current characters and recursive checks after incrementing i or j.

concepts.canonical_name: Handling Index Out of Range in Recursive Conditions
concepts.short_definition: When an index in conditional statements goes out of range, these cases are assumed to be FALSE in the logical definition to prevent invalid accesses.

A base case in a recursive definition is a condition or scenario where the recursive process terminates, often specified as a condition on variables such as T(n,m) = TRUE to establish a stopping point.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Algorithm for String Interleaving
concepts.short_definition: A dynamic programming approach to determine if one string can be formed by interleaving two other strings under given constraints.

concepts.canonical_name: Restriction on Consecutive Characters from a String in Interleaving
concepts.short_definition: A constraint that limits the number of consecutive characters taken from one string (A) to at most 3 when interleaving with another string (B) to form a new string (C).

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of DP Table for Interleaving Strings
concepts.short_definition: The size and computation time of the DP table is O(nm) where n and m are the lengths of the two strings being interleaved.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Subproblems in Sequence Merging
concepts.short_definition: A subproblem formulation defining T(i, j, k) as TRUE iff one can merge suffixes of sequences A and B starting at indices i and j respectively into a merged sequence C so that the last k entries come from A, used to solve sequence merging problems.
The process of guessing which pointer to advance in a multi-pointer dynamic programming solution, ensuring constraints are satisfied and handling edge cases appropriately.
Ordering elements based on the sum of their grid coordinates (i+j) to create a topological order.
The size of the dynamic programming table T for problems involving parameters n and m is 4(n + 1)(m + 1), which belongs to O(nm) complexity class.

concepts.canonical_name: Constant Time Computation per Table Entry
concepts.short_definition: Each entry in the dynamic programming table T can be computed in constant time, leading to overall time complexity proportional to the table size.
The method of guessing which pointer (index) to advance in sequences A and B to match a combined sequence C, considering up to three-step advances and handling edge cases.

concepts.canonical_name: Recursive Transition Function in Sequence Matching T(i, j)
concepts.short_definition: A function defining transitions between states in terms of advancing pointers i and j in sequences A and B to match sequence C under specified conditions.

concepts.canonical_name: Boolean Base Case in Recursive Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: A base case in a recursive algorithm indicating the truth value for specific input parameters in the context of T(n, m).

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Dynamic Programming Table Computation
concepts.short_definition: The computational complexity of filling a dynamic programming table with dimensions related to input sizes n and m, resulting in O(nm) time if each entry is computed in constant time.

concepts.canonical_name: Worst-case Mana Cost DP for Frieren's Chest Problem
concepts.short_definition: A dynamic programming algorithm to compute the worst-case total mana cost for determining the boundary s of safe chests, given the mana costs m_i and a tolerance k of opening mimics, running in O(n^3 k) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Subproblem Definition for Frieren's Mant Cost DP
