concepts.short_definition: Definition of subproblems M(a,b,c) representing worst-case mana cost on subarray m[a:b] with up to c mimics allowed, used for DP formulation.

concepts.canonical_name: Recursive Formula for Worst-case Mana Cost DP
concepts.short_definition: The DP recurrence: M(a,b,c) = min over a≤q<b of (m_q + max(M(a,q,c−1), M(q+1,b,c)))

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity Analysis of O(n^3 k) DP
concepts.short_definition: Analysis showing the DP runs in time O(n^3 k) because of Θ(n^2 k) subproblems each taking O(n) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Improved DP Algorithm with O(n^2 k log n) Time
concepts.short_definition: A modification of the DP that leverages monotonicity properties and binary search to reduce runtime to O(n^2 k log n).
Observation that M is decreasing in a and increasing in b, allowing binary search over q to find an optimal split.

concepts.canonical_name: Binary Search Usage in DP Optimization
concepts.short_definition: Use of binary search to find q* where difference M(q+1,b,c)-M(a,q,c−1) changes sign, used to split minimization in the improved DP.

concepts.canonical_name: Range Query Data Structures in DP Optimization
concepts.short_definition: Use of AVL BST data structures storing M redundantly to answer prefix and suffix minimum range queries in O(log n) as part of the improved DP.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming State Definition for Partition
concepts.short_definition: A DP state defined as x(k, s1, s2, s3) indicating whether it is possible to partition the suffix A[k:] into four subsets with sums s1, s2, s3, and the remainder to the fourth subset.

concepts.canonical_name: Recurrence Relation for Quarter Partition DP
concepts.short_definition: The recursive formula for deciding x(k, s1, s2, s3) by placing the k-th element in one of the four subsets.

concepts.canonical_name: Pseudopolynomial Time Complexity of Quarter Partition
concepts.short_definition: The dynamic programming algorithm runs in O(m^3 n) pseudopolynomial time where m is sum of sequence elements and n is the number of elements.

concepts.canonical_name: State Space Reduction in Quarter Partition DP
concepts.short_definition: By starting from the base case and using reversed dependency graph, only O(4^n) true subproblems need to be considered, bounding worst-case runtime to O(4^n).

concepts.canonical_name: Alternative DP Formulation Using Sets of Tuples
concepts.short_definition: An alternative DP where x(k) is the set of all tuples (s1, s2, s3) possible by partitioning the suffix A[k:] and the transition adds element ak to each subset generating up to four new tuples per tuple in x(k+1).
Function m(s1, s2, s3) = min(s1, s2, s3, m - s1 - s2 - s3) representing the quality metric to maximize.
The property that a sequence x(k) satisfies certain given conditions or facts.

concepts.canonical_name: Number of Distinct Tuples in a Triple-indexed Set
concepts.short_definition: The maximum number of distinct tuples (s1, s2, s3) where each si ranges from 0 to m is (m+1)^3.
A method solving the partition problem into four subsets by defining subproblems recursively and storing intermediate results to compute maximum minimum subset sums efficiently.
A characterization of Big-Omega using limits: g(n) = Ω(f(n)) if lim n→∞ g(n)/f(n) > 0.
The characterization of functions by their dominant growth term ignoring constants, including constant, logarithmic, linear, quadratic, polynomial, and exponential growth types.
Comparing the growth of polynomial functions asymptotically, e.g., na vs. nb.
Showing that logarithms with different constant bases are asymptotically equivalent, i.e., loga n = Θ(logb n) for constants a,b >1.
An approximation expressing n! as Θ(sqrt(n) * (n/e)^n).

concepts.canonical_name: Asymptotic Bound Comparisons involving Logs and Powers
concepts.short_definition: Understanding relationships like n^a = O(n^a (log n)^b) and the absence of tight bounds in certain cases.

concepts.canonical_name: Relationship Between Logarithmic and Polynomial Growth
concepts.short_definition: Showing that (log n)^a = O(n^b) for positive constants a,b.

concepts.canonical_name: Asymptotic Growth of n log n
concepts.short_definition: Classifying n log n within the hierarchy of asymptotic complexities, including proving n log n = Ω(n^a) and n log n = O(2^n) for constants a.
Comparing growth rates of factorial functions and their logarithms, e.g., (6n)! vs n! and log((6n)!) vs log(n!).
A technique to solve recurrence relations by guessing the solution and proving it via substitution.
A formula that provides a general solution to a large class of recurrence relations.

concepts.canonical_name: Recurrence Relation of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)
concepts.short_definition: A type of recurrence relation where a problem of size n is solved by recursively solving a subproblem of size n/b a times and doing additional work f(n).
The three cases of the Master Theorem that determine the asymptotic solution based on the relation between f(n) and n^(log_b a).

concepts.canonical_name: Simplified Master Theorem for Polynomial f(n)
concepts.short_definition: A simplified form of the Master Theorem for recurrences where f(n) = Θ(n^c), determining asymptotic behavior by comparing c to log_b a.

concepts.canonical_name: Asymptotic Growth Functions in Recurrence Analysis
concepts.short_definition: Functions f(n) used to represent additional work in recurrence relations analyzed asymptotically to determine dominating work at tree levels.
A tight bound on the growth rate of a function using Big Theta (Θ) notation, describing the function's limiting behavior as input size grows.
The recurrence relation that characterizes the running time of the binary search algorithm.
A notation to describe the asymptotic growth rates of polynomial functions, e.g., using Big Omega (Ω) to express lower bounds.
Mathematical rules for manipulating logarithms, including that log(ab) = log(a) + log(b) and log(a^b) = b log(a).
The product of all positive integers up to n, denoted n!, with rapid growth rate used in combinatorics and analysis.

concepts.canonical_name: Asymptotic Complexity Class n log n
concepts.short_definition: A complexity class representing growth rates on the order of n log n, commonly appearing in algorithm analysis.

concepts.canonical_name: Asymptotic Growth of Functions involving powers and logarithms
concepts.short_definition: Understanding and comparing growth rates of functions involving powers of n and logarithmic factors.

concepts.canonical_name: Asymptotic Growth Comparison of Logarithmic and Polynomial Functions
concepts.short_definition: The concept that logarithmic functions raised to a positive constant power grow slower than any polynomial function, formally (log n)^a = O(n^b) for positive constants a and b.

concepts.canonical_name: Limit Behavior of Functions as n Approaches Infinity
concepts.short_definition: The concept of evaluating functions or their ratios by taking limits as the input n approaches infinity to understand relative growth rates.
A calculus technique used to evaluate limits of indeterminate forms by differentiating numerator and denominator.
A notation to describe an upper bound of a function's growth rate asymptotically.
The characteristic growth of functions involving log n, especially in combination with polynomial terms such as nlog n.
A growth rate where functions increase proportionally to some constant base raised to the power of the input size, e.g., 2^n.

concepts.canonical_name: Relationship Between Polynomial and Exponential Functions
concepts.short_definition: The concept that exponential functions grow faster asymptotically than polynomial or polylogarithmic functions, e.g., nlog n = O(2^n).
In the Master Theorem, when f(n) = O(n^{log_b a - ε}) for some ε > 0, then T(n) = Θ(n^{log_b a}), and work done at leaves dominates.
In the Master Theorem, when f(n) = Θ(n^{log_b a} log^k n) for some k ≥ 0, then T(n) = Θ(n^{log_b a} log^{k+1} n), and work balanced across the tree.
In the Master Theorem, when f(n) = Ω(n^{log_b a + ε}) and af(n/b) ≤ cf(n) for some constants c < 1, ε > 0, then T(n) = Θ(f(n)), work done at root dominates.
A recurrence relation expressing T(n) as 2 times T(n-1) plus a constant.
The asymptotic complexity result of the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n −1) + Θ(1) is T(n) = O(2^n).

concepts.canonical_name: Binary Tree Height Interpretation of Recurrence
concepts.short_definition: Interpretation of the recurrence as modeling work done on a binary tree of height n, with Θ(1) work per node.
The sum of the geometric series Σ from i=0 to n of 2^i equals 2 * 2^n - 1, which relates to the total work done.
A divide-and-conquer recurrence relation where the problem of size n is divided into 2 subproblems of size n/2 plus a linear amount of additional work.

concepts.canonical_name: Solution to Recurrence T(n) = Θ(n log n)
concepts.short_definition: The asymptotic time complexity result for the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n), which resolves to Theta of n log n.
A recurrence relation describing the running time which divides a problem into two subproblems of half size plus constant additional work.
A method for solving recurrences that generalizes the Master Theorem.
A specific recurrence relation expressing T(n) in terms of T(n/2) plus a linear term Θ(n).
The asymptotic tight bound representing linear time complexity.

concepts.canonical_name: Recursion Tree Height Logarithmic in n
concepts.short_definition: The height of the recursion tree is proportional to log base 2 of n.

concepts.canonical_name: Recurrence Relation T(n) = T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + n
concepts.short_definition: A recursive function defined by T(n) in terms of smaller inputs n/5 and 7n/10 plus n.
Asymptotic tight bound indicating function grows linearly in n.
The method to determine the big-Theta time complexity of recursive definitions such as T(n) = T(n-1) + Theta(n) by summation of work at each recursive call height.
The formula and concept that the sum of the first n natural numbers is n(n+1)/2, which is Theta(n^2).
A divide-and-conquer algorithm for multiplying large numbers more efficiently than the standard grade school method, using a recurrence T(n) = 3T(n/2) + Cn.

concepts.canonical_name: Induction Proof for Karatsuba's Algorithm Correctness
concepts.short_definition: A proof by mathematical induction on n that Karatsuba’s algorithm correctly computes the product of two n-digit integers.
The handling of the recursion base case in Karatsuba's multiplication algorithm, typically by stopping recursion and performing standard multiplication on sufficiently small inputs.
The part of Karatsuba's algorithm where the problem is divided into smaller subproblems and combined using the Karatsuba method.
A generalization of Karatsuba's multiplication algorithm with a parameter k, achieving faster asymptotic runtimes by splitting the problem into more parts.
The recurrence relation T(n) = (2k−1)T(n/k) + O(n) describing the runtime of Toom-Cook multiplication parameterized by k.
A basic, elementary method for addition typically taught to young children, involving simple digit-wise addition and carry handling.

concepts.canonical_name: Recurrence Relation Analysis Using Recurrence Trees
concepts.short_definition: Analyzing recurrences by representing them with recurrence trees, calculating contributions at each level and total cost across levels.

concepts.canonical_name: Recurrence for T(n) ≤ T(n/2) + O(n) and Solution T(n) = O(n)
concepts.short_definition: Specific recurrence where each call splits the problem into one subproblem of half size plus linear work, solved by total linear time.

concepts.canonical_name: Recurrence for Naive Divide-and-Conquer Multiplication T(n) ≤ 4T(n/2) + O(n)
concepts.short_definition: Recurrence describing the naive divide-and-conquer multiplication algorithm runtime, relating to four subproblems of half size plus linear work.

concepts.canonical_name: Divide and Conquer Recurrence Tree Analysis
concepts.short_definition: Analyzing recursive algorithms using the recurrence tree method, considering levels, subproblem sizes, and number of nodes at each level.
A series of the form a + ar + ar^2 + ... whose sum can be expressed in closed form when |r|<1.
The number of levels in a recursive call tree, often related to the logarithm of the problem size for divide-and-conquer algorithms.
A method using mathematical induction to prove that a guess solution to a recurrence relation, such as T(n) = O(n log n), is correct.
The number of recursive calls or subproblems generated at each level of the recursion tree, affecting the total number of nodes at each level.

concepts.canonical_name: Cost per Node at Recursion Tree Level
concepts.short_definition: The amount of work done at each node of a recursion tree at level i, often expressed in terms of the input size related to that level.
The sum of the costs of all nodes at all levels of the recursion tree, used to find the total complexity of the recursive algorithm.
The sum of series involving powers of two, for example sum of 2^i for i up to log n.

concepts.canonical_name: Total Cost Calculation in Algorithm Analysis
concepts.short_definition: The method of calculating the total cost by summing the costs over rows or iterations, especially in recursive or iterative algorithms.
Properties and manipulations of logarithms involving powers, such as converting expressions like a^{log_b c} into equivalent forms.
The step in an inductive proof showing that if the property holds for smaller inputs, it holds for n.
In Karatsuba's algorithm, recursive calls are made on inputs that are roughly half the size (n/2) plus one digit due to carries from addition, especially when n is odd.
The time complexity of Toom-Cook multiplication shown to be O(n^{log_k(2k-1)}) for parameter k.

concepts.canonical_name: Big-O Notation Dependency on Parameter k
concepts.short_definition: In Toom-Cook multiplication, the hidden constant in the big-O notation depends on the parameter k, affecting the practical runtime despite the asymptotic expression.

concepts.canonical_name: Limitations of Toom-Cook Multiplication with Large k
concepts.short_definition: Although large k can produce near linear runtime, setting k = n is not feasible due to dependencies of constants on k and practical constraints.

concepts.canonical_name: Approximation to Linear Time by Toom-Cook Multiplication
concepts.short_definition: By choosing sufficiently large k, Toom-Cook multiplication can approximate a runtime of O(n^{1+ϵ}) for any ϵ > 0, approaching but not reaching linear time.
An algorithm that iteratively checks whether any two students have the same birthday and returns a pair if found, otherwise None.

concepts.canonical_name: Birthday algorithm worst-case runtime lower bound
concepts.short_definition: Theoretical minimum time complexity for the worst-case execution of the birthday algorithm.
An array originally sorted in ascending order but rotated by an unknown number of positions k, causing indices to shift by k modulo n.

concepts.canonical_name: Binary search in rotated sorted arrays
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that performs binary search on arrays that are sorted and then rotated, to efficiently find elements or the rotation parameter k in O(log n) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime complexity O(log n) for integer square root
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that computes the integer square root of a positive integer n with logarithmic time complexity.

concepts.canonical_name: Finding the root of a monotone function in O(log |α|) time
concepts.short_definition: Algorithm to find the unique root α of a monotone integer function that returns {-1, 0, 1}, with runtime logarithmic in |α|.
A problem or algorithmic challenge to identify an element in a data structure that is not smaller than its neighbors.

concepts.canonical_name: Brute Force Algorithm for Finding Shared Birthdays
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that selects one student, compares their birthday to every other student's to find if any share the same birthday and year, and continues recursively removing checked students until a match is found or none exists.
A proof technique that establishes the truth of a statement for all natural numbers by proving a base case and an inductive step.
The correctness of the birthday algorithm proven by induction, demonstrating it correctly identifies whether any two students share the same birthday.
An algorithm to determine if any two students in a set have the same birthday by comparing birthdays and using recursion to check subsets.

concepts.canonical_name: Worst-case Runtime Complexity of Birthday Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: An upper bound on the runtime of the birthday_match algorithm in the worst-case scenario, expressed as a function of input size n.

concepts.canonical_name: Arithmetic Series Summation in Runtime Analysis
concepts.short_definition: The use of the arithmetic series formula to sum the total work across recursive calls, leading to runtime estimates such as n(n+1)/2.
A guaranteed minimal runtime that an algorithm takes in the worst-case inputs, shown by constructing an input that forces the algorithm to take at least that much time.
The number of positions by which a sorted array has been rotated; equivalent to the index of the minimum element in the rotated array.
An O(log n) recursive algorithm to find the rotation index k in a rotated sorted array by locating the minimum element via binary search comparing middle, start, and end elements.

concepts.canonical_name: Correctness Proof of Rotation Index Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: An inductive proof validating that the recursive algorithm correctly returns the index of the minimum element (rotation index) in a rotated sorted array.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Complexity of Rotation Index Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The time complexity of the rotation index finding algorithm is O(log n), achieved by recursively reducing the input size by half each time.
An O(log n) algorithm that checks which half of the rotated sorted array is properly sorted to apply binary search optimally to find if a number x exists in the array.
A recurrence relation describing the time complexity of a divide and conquer algorithm where the input size is halved each recursive step and constant work is done per step.
The approach of finding an element in a partially sorted array by exploiting sorted subarrays separated by a breakpoint k.
The process of determining the time complexity of an algorithm based on its operations and input size.

concepts.canonical_name: Binary Search for Integer Square Root
concepts.short_definition: Algorithm to find the floor of the square root of a positive integer n using a binary search approach between 1 and n.
An invariant stating that the floor of the square root of n is always contained in the current interval [a, b].
The technique of proving correctness of the loop invariant by induction on the number of iterations of the loop.
A value α for which the function f(α) = 0.
An algorithm that starts from a point and exponentially increases the search interval size to find a range containing the target, then applies binary search within that range.
A data structure where elements are stored in nodes linked via pointers, implementing the Sequence interface.
A resizable array data structure supporting Sequence interface operations, with efficient amortized operations.
A technique or algorithm to find if a linked list contains a cycle and determine properties like cycle length, often with constraints such as linear time and constant space.
An approach to use a data structure only through its defined interface without accessing its internal representation.

A method to implement the Queue interface using two Stacks, one storing the front half in reverse order and the other the back half, with enqueue and dequeue operations implemented via these stacks including a flip operation to reverse elements from one stack to another when needed.

The operation that moves all elements from the back stack B to the front stack F by popping all elements from B and pushing them onto F, reversing their order for proper queue sequencing; only performed when F is empty.

concepts.canonical_name: Amortized Analysis of Two-Stack Queue Operations
concepts.short_definition: The runtime analysis showing that enqueue, dequeue, and peek operations on two-stack queue implementation run in amortized O(1) time by charging the cost of the flip operation across multiple enqueue operations.
A technique using two indices/pointers to represent subranges within a single array to efficiently manage operations at both ends.
A method to resize a dynamic array to have free space on both ends by allocating twice the size to ensure amortized O(1) inserts at both ends.

concepts.canonical_name: Two Dynamic Arrays (Front and Back) Method
concepts.short_definition: An alternative implementation using two dynamic arrays, representing front and back portions, to support efficient insertions and deletions at both ends of a sequence.

concepts.canonical_name: Indexing Method in Two-Array Dynamic Sequence
concepts.short_definition: Indexing into a two-array sequence by reversing indices in the front array and offsetting in the back array.
Analyzing how costly splitting the arrays into halves can be amortized over many constant-time operations, ensuring overall amortized O(1) deletes.

concepts.canonical_name: Concatenation of Reversed Front and Back Arrays
concepts.short_definition: Returning the full sequence as a list by reversing the front array and concatenating with the back array.

concepts.canonical_name: Cycle length determination in linked list
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm to find the number of nodes in the cycle of a linked list by counting nodes between repeated visits to a node in the cycle once detected.

concepts.canonical_name: Constant space complexity in cycle detection
concepts.short_definition: The property of performing cycle detection and length determination using only a fixed number of pointer variables, without using extra data structures proportional to the list size.

concepts.canonical_name: Queue interface with O(1) amortized time operations
concepts.short_definition: An abstract data type supporting enqueue and dequeue operations each taking O(1) amortized time.

concepts.canonical_name: Stack interface implemented with single queue and constant extra space
concepts.short_definition: Using one QUEUE as a black box and constant extra space to implement the STACK interface, i.e. LIFO behavior.

concepts.canonical_name: Cycle queue method for stack push operation
concepts.short_definition: Simulate stack push by enqueueing the new element, then rotating the queue by dequeuing and enqueuing all the other elements once to keep the LIFO order.

concepts.canonical_name: Stack pop and peek operations with single queue
concepts.short_definition: Stack pop and peek can be implemented to run in constant time by matching stack pop order with queue dequeue order using the described implementation.
Algorithms that build up a solution by processing inputs one at a time incrementally, such as insertion sort and selection sort.

concepts.canonical_name: Set Interface Implementation Using Sorted Array
concepts.short_definition: Implementing the Set ADT using a sorted array, with operations such as insert, delete, and search, each having specific runtimes.

concepts.canonical_name: Set Interface Implementation Using Sorted Doubly Linked List
concepts.short_definition: Implementing the Set ADT using a sorted doubly linked list, with operations such as insert, delete, and search, and analyzing their runtimes.
Algorithm to determine the minimum number of platforms required at a train station given sorted arrival and departure times of trains.

concepts.canonical_name: Brute Force Algorithm for Inversion Counting
concepts.short_definition: The naive algorithm that counts inversions by checking every pair of elements and has a quadratic runtime.

concepts.canonical_name: Efficient Inversion Counting Algorithm Using Divide and Conquer
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that counts inversions more efficiently than brute force by using divide and conquer techniques such as a modified merge sort.

concepts.canonical_name: Sorted Array Implementation of Set Interface
concepts.short_definition: Using a sorted array to implement set operations such as build, find min/max, iteration, search, insertion, and deletion.
The computational time complexity for operations such as building, searching, iterating, inserting, and deleting elements in an array.
A doubly linked list in which elements are kept in sorted order, allowing ordered traversal with head and tail pointers.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Find Minimum and Maximum in Sorted Doubly Linked List
concepts.short_definition: The runtime to find the minimum or maximum elements is O(1) using head and tail pointers respectively in a sorted doubly linked list.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Iteration in Sorted Doubly Linked List
concepts.short_definition: The runtime to iterate over all elements in order is O(n), by scanning through the list.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Find, Find Next, and Find Previous in Sorted Doubly Linked List
concepts.short_definition: Finding an element or the next or previous element requires scanning through the list, taking O(n) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Insert and Delete in Sorted Doubly Linked List
concepts.short_definition: Insert and delete operations require scanning through the list to find the right spot and take O(n) time.
The smallest number of train platforms required at a station so that all arriving trains can be accommodated without waiting, given arrival and departure times.
Tracking the number of trains currently in the station by incrementing on train arrivals and decrementing on departures to deduce the maximum concurrency.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of O(n) for Merging
concepts.short_definition: The analysis showing that merging two sorted lists of size n takes linear time O(n) with constant time per merge step.

concepts.canonical_name: Divide and Conquer Approach to Inversion Counting
concepts.short_definition: An algorithmic technique to count how many pairs a[i], a[j] of an array are out of order (inversions) using recursive division and merging of subarrays.
A measure of how unsorted an array is determined by counting pairs of elements that are out of order relative to their indices.

concepts.canonical_name: Brute Force Algorithm for Counting Inversions
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm using a nested loop to count pairs of elements where a preceding element is greater than a following one by exhaustive search.
Inversions where both indices come from the same half of the array in a divide-and-conquer approach.
Count the number of inversions across the two halves of the array during the merge step by comparing elements of each sorted subarray.

concepts.canonical_name: Recurrence Relation of the Inversion Counting Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The time complexity of the divide and conquer inversion counting algorithm satisfies T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), same as merge sort, yielding O(n log n) runtime.
The process of inserting an element into an ordered array at the correct position to maintain order, possibly replacing existing elements with the same key.
The process of deleting an element with a specific key from an ordered array, using binary search to locate it.

concepts.canonical_name: Find Next Element by Key in Ordered Array
concepts.short_definition: Finding the smallest element whose key is greater than a given key in a sorted array, using binary search.

concepts.canonical_name: Find Previous Element by Key in Ordered Array
concepts.short_definition: Finding the largest element whose key is less than a given key in a sorted array, using binary search.

concepts.canonical_name: Naive Quadratic Time Algorithm for Duplicates
concepts.short_definition: A simple algorithm to solve the duplicates problem in worst-case time O(n^2) by comparing each element to every other element.
An algorithm that solves the duplicates problem in worst-case O(n log n) time by sorting the array and checking for adjacent equal elements.

concepts.canonical_name: Hashing-based Expected Linear Time Duplicate Detection
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm using hash functions and hash tables to solve the duplicates problem in expected O(n) time by detecting collisions during insertions.

concepts.canonical_name: Constant Time Duplicate Detection for Limited Range (k < n)
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm solving the duplicates problem in worst-case O(1) time when the maximum integer k is less than the number of array elements n, exploiting the limited domain to guarantee detection.

concepts.canonical_name: Linear Time Duplicate Detection for Limited Range (n ≤ k)
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm solving the duplicates problem in worst-case O(k) time when the number of elements n is less than or equal to the maximum integer k, by counting or direct access methods.
An algorithm to sort a set of n strings each having k English characters in linear time with respect to n and k.

concepts.canonical_name: Linear Time Integer Sorting Algorithm with Range Constraints
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that sorts n integers in a given range [−n^{49}, ..., n^{50}] using a linear time algorithm that exploits range-bound properties.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm for Counting Similar Pairs of Strings Differing by One Character in Linear Time
concepts.short_definition: A linear time algorithm that counts the number of pairs of 8-character strings differing by exactly one character, assuming no two strings are identical.
A hash function h mapping a tuple of t integers to an integer in {0,...,m-1} for prime m, computed in O(t) time, satisfying the Simple Uniform Hashing Assumption.
A hash computation method for tuples that computes sequentially h1 = h(a1), h2 = h(h1, a2), ..., ht = h(h_{t-1}, a_t) to enable efficient hashing of large sequences.

concepts.canonical_name: Data Structure for Probabilistic Membership Testing with False Positives
concepts.short_definition: A data structure built in O(tn) that uses O(n) space to check if a tuple is in a list of bad tuples with at most 1% false positive probability and no false negatives, and O(t) lookup time.
A theoretical lower bound on the number of comparisons needed to find a particular element or property in a set under the comparison model.
Data structures using an array indexed by keys to represent sets directly, enabling constant time membership queries and updates for keys in a bounded universe.
A collision resolution technique in hashing where each hash table slot holds a linked list of all keys that hash to that slot.

concepts.canonical_name: Brute Force Algorithm for Duplicate Detection
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that checks all pairs of elements in an array to find duplicates, running in O(n^2) time by comparing each pair directly.
After sorting an array, scanning through adjacent pairs to check if any two consecutive elements are equal to find duplicates.
The ratio of the number of stored keys n to the number of hash table buckets m, denoted by α = n/m, influencing chain lengths and performance.

concepts.canonical_name: Expected Chain Length in Chaining Hash Table
concepts.short_definition: The expected length of the linked list or chain at any hash bucket, which is approximately the load factor α = n/m.
An algorithm to find duplicates in a list by inserting each element into a hash table and checking for existing entries in expected O(n) time.
A sorting algorithm that runs in linear time under certain input assumptions, often using direct access arrays.
The minimum number of comparisons required to sort n distinct elements using any comparison-based sorting algorithm.
Two kerberos strings are similar if they differ by exactly one character.
An algorithm to count the number of pairs of kerberos strings that differ by exactly one character, designed to run in linear time.
Sorting a list of fixed-length strings by iteratively sorting on each character position, often used for efficient linear-time sorting under constant-length assumptions.

concepts.canonical_name: Counting Similar Pairs Using Radix Sort
concepts.short_definition: A method to count pairs of strings differing by exactly one character by iteratively sorting the strings ignoring each character position, then counting consecutive equal strings to identify similar pairs efficiently.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Radix Sort with Fixed-Length Keys
concepts.short_definition: The total time complexity of performing Radix sort multiple times on a list of n strings with constant length is O(n), given each iteration runs in O(n) and the number of iterations is constant.
Using a hash function to process tuples of integers into a hash value within a modular range, computed in time proportional to the tuple length, under the Simple Uniform Hashing Assumption.
The computational complexity of a preprocessing algorithm expressed as O(tn), where t and n represent algorithmic parameters.
The amount of memory space utilized by a preprocessing algorithm, expressed as O(n), where n represents the size of the data structure.
The probability that a lookup operation erroneously indicates presence of a tuple that is not actually stored, bounded here by 1%.
Using hashed fingerprints of tuples instead of storing the full tuples can reduce memory usage from Ω(tn) to O(n) at the cost of a small false positive rate.

concepts.canonical_name: BST Operations: Find, Insert, Delete, Successor
concepts.short_definition: Core operations on a binary search tree including searching for a key (find), adding a key (insert), removing a key (delete), and finding the successor of a node.
Techniques to order element insertions into a BST to maximize or minimize the BST's height.

concepts.canonical_name: In-order Traversal Sort Property of BST
concepts.short_definition: The property that performing an in-order traversal of a BST yields the elements in sorted order.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm to Construct Balanced BST from Array
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm to construct a BST with height O(log n) from n elements in O(n log n) time, assuming n is one less than a power of two.

concepts.canonical_name: BST Successor Relationship When Node Has No Right Child
concepts.short_definition: For nodes x and y in a BST, if y is the successor of x and x has no right child, then y is an ancestor of x and x is in the left subtree of y.
An argument that an iterative procedure to traverse a tree in a traversal order runs in O(n) time where n is the number of nodes.
The method of traversing a tree data structure by iteratively yielding nodes using a subtree-first approach and successor linkage.
A data structure representing a node in a binary tree, containing an item and links to left child, right child, and parent nodes.
The process of traversing all nodes in a subtree rooted at a given binary node in order, yielding each node.
The node with the smallest key (or leftmost node) in the subtree rooted at a given binary node.
The node that follows a given node in an in-order traversal of the binary tree, or None if the given node is the last.
The node that precedes a given node in an in-order traversal of the binary tree, or None if the given node is the first.
Inserting node B into the subtree before node A according to in-order traversal order, maintaining binary tree structure.

concepts.canonical_name: Subtree Deletion in Binary Search Tree
concepts.short_definition: A method for deleting a node in a binary search tree by swapping it with its predecessor or successor and recursively deleting the swapped node if it has children, or simply removing it if it is a leaf.
Procedure to find a key in a binary search tree by comparing it with the current node and traversing left or right accordingly.

concepts.canonical_name: BST Delete Operation with Two Children
concepts.short_definition: Deletion in a BST when the node has two children involves swapping with the minimum node in the right subtree, then deleting the swapped node which becomes a leaf.

concepts.canonical_name: BST Delete Operation with One Child
concepts.short_definition: Deletion in a BST when the node has one child involves swapping with the max node in the left subtree, then deleting the swapped node.
The process of finding the next higher value node (successor) in a BST, which involves moving up to the parent and grandparent nodes when the node has no children.

concepts.canonical_name: Insertion order and tree height relationship in BST
concepts.short_definition: The order in which nodes are inserted into a BST affects the height of the resulting tree; inserting in ascending order creates a skewed tree with maximal height, whereas balanced insertion order minimizes height.
The sequence in which nodes are inserted into a binary tree, affecting its structure and height.

concepts.canonical_name: In-order Traversal of a BST Yields a Sorted Array
concepts.short_definition: The result that performing an in-order traversal on a Binary Search Tree produces the node values in sorted order.
The height of a balanced binary search tree built with n = 2^k - 1 nodes is k - 1, which is O(log n).

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity Recurrence Relation for Balanced BST Construction
concepts.short_definition: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1) solves to T(n) = O(n), describing the tree-building runtime.

concepts.canonical_name: Overall Time Complexity of Constructing Balanced BST from Unsorted Array
concepts.short_definition: The overall time to construct the balanced BST is O(n log n) due to sorting and linear-time tree construction.
The node that comes immediately after a given node x in the in-order traversal of a BST.

concepts.canonical_name: Least Common Ancestor in Binary Search Tree
concepts.short_definition: The lowest node in a BST that has two given nodes as descendants (where each node can be a descendant of itself).
A node y is an ancestor of node x if y lies on the path from the root of the BST to x.

concepts.canonical_name: Left Subtree in Binary Search Tree
concepts.short_definition: The subtree rooted at the left child of a node y, containing nodes with values less than y.
The proof that an iterative tree traversal procedure runs in O(n) time by analyzing edge and node visit counts.
A method that returns the next node in the in-order traversal sequence of a binary tree from a given node.
The concept that in a tree traversal each edge is traversed at most twice, once downwards and once upwards.

concepts.canonical_name: Node Visit Count in Tree Traversal
concepts.short_definition: Every node in a tree is traversed at most three times during the traversal: once from the parent and once from each child.
A simple implementation of a binary tree node with item, left, right, and parent pointers plus traversal helper methods.
A node in a binary search tree with pointers to left and right children and its parent, supporting subtree navigation and modification.
A recursive method to find a node with a given key in the subtree rooted at a given node, operating in O(h) time where h is the height of the tree.
A method to find the node with the smallest key greater than a given key within the subtree rooted at a node, operating in O(h) time.
A method to insert a new node into the BST subtree rooted at a node preserving BST properties and operating in O(h) time.
Inserts a node B into the BST so that B comes after node A in in-order traversal, preserving tree structure, operating in O(h) time.
A set data structure implemented with a binary search tree to support insertion, deletion, find, and iteration operations efficiently.

concepts.canonical_name: BST minimum and maximum find operations
concepts.short_definition: Methods to find the minimum and maximum key items in the BST, using subtree_first and subtree_last respectively.
A method to find an item by key in the set implemented by BST, returning the item if found or None otherwise.
Methods to find the next larger or previous smaller item relative to a key in the set BST implementation.
Inserts an item into the BST set, creating a new node and inserting it at the appropriate position, updating size and root accordingly.
Deletes an item by key from the BST set, finding the corresponding node then deleting it properly, updating size and root as needed.
The height of a variant of AVL trees where skew is allowed up to 2, still bounded in O(log n).

concepts.canonical_name: Iterator NEXT Operation on AVL Tree
concepts.short_definition: The operation that returns the next node in the traversal of an AVL tree, which can be amortized constant time or improved to worst-case constant time.
An operation time guarantee that the operation completes in constant time in all cases.

concepts.canonical_name: Unordered SET data structure with multiple keys
concepts.short_definition: A data structure supporting efficient INSERT, FIND, and DELETE operations using two unique keys: one comparable key and one hashable key.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime analysis of data structure operations
concepts.short_definition: Understanding the time complexity (worst-case, amortized, or expected) for operations like INSERT, FIND, and DELETE in a data structure supporting multiple keys.

concepts.canonical_name: Recurrence Relation for number of nodes in an AVL-2 Tree
concepts.short_definition: The recursive formula nh = nh−1 + nh−3 + 1 describing the minimum number of nodes at height h for AVL-2 Trees.

concepts.canonical_name: Big O notation for Height Bound
concepts.short_definition: The asymptotic upper bound of the tree height, here shown as O(log n) for AVL and AVL-2 trees.

concepts.canonical_name: Cross-Linking AVL Tree with Doubly-Linked List
concepts.short_definition: A technique to augment AVL tree nodes with pointers to predecessor and successor to allow NEXT operation in iteration to run in worst-case constant time.

concepts.canonical_name: AVL Tree Node Augmentation with Successor Pointer Only
concepts.short_definition: A variation of the AVL tree augmentation using only a successor pointer, updating successor pointers during insertion or deletion using FINDPREV in O(log n) time.

concepts.canonical_name: AVL Tree Insertion and Deletion Impact on Linked List
concepts.short_definition: Insertion involves adding a leaf node whose parent is either predecessor or successor; deletion removes the node from both tree and linked list, maintaining data structure consistency.

concepts.canonical_name: Cross-Linked Data Structure for Dual-Key Access
concepts.short_definition: A combined data structure linking an AVL tree keyed by k1 and a hash table keyed by k2 to allow efficient INSERT, FIND, and DELETE operations by either key.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Complexity of Hash Table Operations
concepts.short_definition: Using hashing with chaining, FIND on the hash table runs in expected O(1) time assuming uniform hashing distribution.

concepts.canonical_name: Amortized and Expected Runtime for Insert and Delete in Cross-Linked Data Structure
concepts.short_definition: INSERT and DELETE operations require updates to both AVL tree and hash table, resulting in amortized and expected O(log n) runtime.
The method of inserting a node into a binary search tree while maintaining its order property.

concepts.canonical_name: Finding Minimum in Binary Search Tree
concepts.short_definition: The method to find the minimum value stored in a binary search tree, typically by traversing to the leftmost node.

concepts.canonical_name: Finding Next Node in Binary Search Tree
concepts.short_definition: Method to find the node with the smallest key greater than a given key in the binary search tree.

concepts.canonical_name: Finding Previous Node in Binary Search Tree
concepts.short_definition: Method to find the node with the largest key smaller than a given key in the binary search tree.

concepts.canonical_name: Binary Search Tree Iteration in Order
concepts.short_definition: An iterator method yielding the items of the binary search tree in sorted order.

concepts.canonical_name: Building a Binary Search Tree from a Collection
concepts.short_definition: Method to construct a binary search tree by inserting elements from a given collection sequentially.
A branch of statistics dealing with the properties of order in a set of elements, such as finding medians or other quantiles within data structures, often used in algorithms.
An operation on a set of integers returning the minimum positive difference between any two elements of the set.
Constraints that prevent certain queries from being maintained as augmentations within a data structure, such as inability to update or maintain them efficiently.
An augmentation using an ordered triple capturing minimum differences to allow constant time computation of a complex query like CLOSEST().

concepts.canonical_name: Dual Representation of Key and Augmentation in BST
concepts.short_definition: A concept where key and augmentation roles in a binary search tree can be swapped to represent data differently, maintaining correctness and efficiency.
An augmentation storing the median key of a BST subtree at each node, used for order-statistics queries.
An augmentation that maintains the k largest values in the subtree of a binary search tree node.

concepts.canonical_name: Counting Odd Values Augmentation in BST
concepts.short_definition: An augmentation that counts the number of odd integers within the subtree of a BST node.

concepts.canonical_name: Left Subtree Height Augmentation in BST
concepts.short_definition: An augmentation that stores the height of the left subtree under a BST node.
A data structure maintaining a sequence of n bits supporting efficient updates and queries.
An operation flip(i) that flips the bit at index i in a bit sequence.
An operation ones_upto(i) that returns the count of bits set to one in the prefix up to index i.
An augmentation storing a triple of minimum, closest difference, and maximum values in a subtree to allow computing CLOSEST in constant time.
Using the augmentation triple, CLOSEST() can be returned in constant time at any node by combination of subtree data and root data.

concepts.canonical_name: Interval Tree Augmented by Minimum Left Endpoint
concepts.short_definition: An interval tree keyed by the right endpoint b of intervals [a,b], augmented at each node with the minimum left endpoint a in its subtree to support efficient interval intersection queries.

concepts.canonical_name: Interval-Search in Interval Tree keyed by b
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm to find an interval intersecting a given interval [a,b] in an interval tree keyed by b, by recursively searching based on minimum a augmentation and interval intersection conditions.

concepts.canonical_name: Correctness Proof of Interval Tree keyed by b
concepts.short_definition: An inductive proof showing that the interval-search algorithm correctly returns an intersecting interval if one exists, based on subtree minimum a augmentation and interval ordering keyed by right endpoints b.
An augmentation at node v equal to the median of the keys in the subtree rooted at v.

concepts.canonical_name: Three Biggest Values in Subtree Augmentation
concepts.short_definition: An augmentation at node v that stores the three biggest values in the subtree rooted at v.
The process of computing an augmentation at node v efficiently from the augmentations of its children nodes.
Some augmentations cannot be computed efficiently from just the augmentations of the children nodes and the value at v, due to identical child augmentations leading to different correct results at v.

concepts.canonical_name: Ones Upto Operation on a Bit Sequence
concepts.short_definition: An operation that returns the number of bits set to one up to a specified index in a sequence of bits.

concepts.canonical_name: Binary Tree with Augmented Nodes for Bit Sequences
concepts.short_definition: A binary tree data structure where each node stores a bit and an augmentation of the number of ones in its subtree, enabling efficient prefix queries and updates.
An augmentation that stores the number of 1 bits in the subtree rooted at each node, computed from children in O(1) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Get Node at Index in Binary Tree Sequence
concepts.short_definition: A method to find the node at the ith index in the sequence represented by an augmented binary tree, used to access or update bits.

concepts.canonical_name: Flip Operation Implementation Using Augmented Binary Tree
concepts.short_definition: Flipping a bit at index i involves finding the ith node, toggling its bit, then updating subtree ones in the node and its ancestors in O(log n) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Ones Upto Operation Implementation Using Augmented Binary Tree
concepts.short_definition: Calculating the number of ones up to index i by traversing the binary tree, adding counts of left subtree ones and node bits when moving to the right child, in O(log n) time.
A recursive function that returns the number of 1 bits in the prefix up to index i using subtree sizes and subtree ones in the binary tree.

concepts.canonical_name: Sequence AVL Tree with Size Augmentation
concepts.short_definition: An AVL tree variant that maintains subtree sizes for efficient operations on sequences, supporting node access by index and size updates.

concepts.canonical_name: Subtree Node Access by Index in AVL Sequence Tree
concepts.short_definition: A method to locate the node at a given index i in an AVL-based sequence tree by traversing subtree sizes recursively in O(log n) time.
A binary search tree data structure implementing set operations such as insert, delete, find, find_min, find_max, find_next, and find_prev.
A method to locate a node in a subtree whose key matches a specified value, or the closest ancestor or node as per the find variant.
A method to find the largest node in a subtree with key strictly less than a given key.

concepts.canonical_name: Delete Operation in Binary Search Tree
concepts.short_definition: The method to remove a node with a specified key from the binary search tree, updating root and size accordingly.
Methods to store graphs in data structures, commonly including adjacency lists and adjacency matrices.
A data structure that supports push and pop operations, where elements are added and removed from the top (LIFO).

concepts.canonical_name: Path with Minimal Number of Red Edges in a Colored Graph
concepts.short_definition: The problem of finding a path from source to target in an unweighted graph where edges have colors, minimizing the count of red edges on the path.
A computational problem that involves graphs, such as pathfinding or connectivity inquiries.
The matrix obtained by swapping the rows and columns of the original matrix; the entry at (i,j) becomes the entry at (j,i).

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Graph Reversal Using Adjacency List
concepts.short_definition: The runtime to reverse a directed graph represented as an adjacency list is O(|V| + |E|).

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Graph Reversal Using Adjacency Matrix
concepts.short_definition: The runtime to reverse a directed graph represented as an adjacency matrix is O(|V|^2) due to transposing the matrix.

concepts.canonical_name: Depth-First Search (DFS) Implementation Using a Stack
concepts.short_definition: A method to perform DFS traversal by using a stack data structure to manage vertices, utilizing push and pop operations to explore graph vertices.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Path Reconstruction Using Parent Pointers
concepts.short_definition: Technique to reconstruct a path in a graph by following parent pointers from the destination to the source.
A property of a directed graph indicating whether there is a path from some vertices to others, including the concepts of strong connectivity.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Acyclicity and Isomorphism to Condensation Graph
concepts.short_definition: The property that the condensation graph GC is isomorphic to the original graph G if and only if G is acyclic.

concepts.canonical_name: Cycle Detection Using Single Full DFS
concepts.short_definition: A technique to detect cycles in a directed graph by performing only one full depth-first search traversal.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm for Minimal Forced Opening of Lock Boxes
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm designed to determine the smallest set of boxes that must be forcibly opened to access all boxes given keys inside boxes and possibly multiple copies of keys, including forced opening with a rusty crowbar.
A property of a graph where there exists a path between every pair of vertices, indicating the graph is connected.
A designated node representing a connected component of a graph, used to represent that component in condensed structures.
An algorithm that constructs the condensation graph of G by identifying connected components, choosing leaders, and creating edges between leaders for edges between components in G.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Condensation Graph Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The complexity of the algorithm to build the condensation graph is O(|V| + |E|), where V is the set of vertices and E is the set of edges in the original graph.
The problem of determining whether a directed graph contains a cycle, i.e., a path starting and ending at the same vertex.
A bijection between the vertex sets of two graphs that preserves the edge relation, making the graphs structurally identical.

A problem involving n lock boxes and m keys where each box has a distinct lock and keys are stored inside boxes, requiring finding the smallest set of boxes to force open to access all keys and thus open all boxes.

concepts.canonical_name: Directed Graph Construction for Key-Box Problem
concepts.short_definition: Modeling the lock boxes and keys as a directed graph where nodes represent boxes and an edge u->v means box u contains the key to box v.

concepts.canonical_name: Source Strongly Connected Components in Condensation Graph
concepts.short_definition: Strongly connected components that have no incoming edges in the condensation graph, indicating they must be forced open to access all boxes.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm to Find Minimum Boxes to Force Open
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm which computes the number of source strongly connected components in the condensation graph to determine the minimal set of boxes to open forcibly, performed in O(n + m) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Representation of Islands and Routes
concepts.short_definition: Modeling the Orange Islands and traversable routes as an undirected graph G=(V, E) where vertices represent islands and edges represent routes.
Each route {u, v} between islands has an associated positive integer cost cu,v in Power Points required to traverse it.
The problem of deciding whether a Pokémon can reach a specific island from Shamouti Island given a fixed maximum budget of Power Points (PP) to spend navigating routes.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm Design with Time Complexity O(k|E|) for Reachability
concepts.short_definition: Designing an algorithm that determines reachability within a Power Point budget k with time complexity proportional to k multiplied by number of edges |E|.

concepts.canonical_name: Flying and Swimming Mode with Rest Constraint
concepts.short_definition: A traversal model where a Pokémon can either swim across routes spending cu,v PP or fly spending 1 PP, but must rest after flying before flying again, requiring swimming before flying next time.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm Design for Reachability with Flying and Rest Constraint in O(k|E|) Time
concepts.short_definition: Algorithm to decide whether a Pokémon can reach a destination under alternating flying and swimming with resting constraint, within k PP, running in time O(k|E|).

concepts.canonical_name: Co-traveling Pokémon Reachability with Different Movement Costs and Resting Constraints
concepts.short_definition: The problem where two Pokémon travel together with distinct movement modes and costs, flying requires resting, and determining reachability within a budget with combined constraints.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm Design for Co-traveling Pokémon Reachability in O(k^2|E|) Time
concepts.short_definition: Algorithm to decide whether two Pokémon traveling with given rules can reach destination in time O(k^2|E|) where k is the max PP budget.
Assigning positive integer costs to edges representing the Power Point cost to navigate routes between islands in the graph.
A technique that transforms a graph by subdividing edges into chains of edges to encode costs or capacities, effectively increasing the number of vertices and edges.
An algorithm running time proportional to the product of k and the number of edges |E|, indicating a scalable approach where k is a parameter and |E| is the edge count.

concepts.canonical_name: Swim and Fly Route Costs Model
concepts.short_definition: A model where swimming across a route has cost cu,v PP and flying costs 1 PP; flying cannot be repeated consecutively without swimming in between.
An algorithm that decides whether a location is reachable under cost and flying restrictions using the state-expanded graph and BFS.

concepts.canonical_name: State Space Graph Construction for PP Tracking
concepts.short_definition: A graph construction approach where vertices represent triples encoding the island, and the remaining PP of Squirtle and Fletchling, used to model travel capabilities and restrictions.

concepts.canonical_name: Travel Cost Rules for Squirtle and Fletchling
concepts.short_definition: The rules defining how Squirtle can swim spending cu,v PP, and Fletchling can fly spending 5 PP with rest requirements, impacting state transitions in the graph.
An algorithm running in time proportional to k squared times the number of edges to decide if Squirtle and Fletchling can reach Trovita Island under the travel and PP constraints.
The transitions in the constructed graph changing positions and PP values according to movement rules, including flying and swimming and the resting constraint for Fletchling.
An algorithm to convert an arbitrary array into a heap in linear time by iteratively applying heapification from the bottom nodes up to the root.

concepts.canonical_name: Finding Minimum Element in Max Heap
concepts.short_definition: The process or method to locate the smallest element within a max heap, which is not stored at a specific node but must be found by inspecting relevant nodes.
The process and complexity of converting a max heap to a min heap or vice versa.
A data structure supporting efficient insertions, deletions, and maintenance of the k highest-scoring players without necessarily maintaining their internal ranking.
Sorting an array in which each element is at most k positions away from its sorted position.
An array where the position of each element differs from its position in the sorted array by at most k.

concepts.canonical_name: Insertion Sort Time Complexity on k-proximate array
concepts.short_definition: Insertion sort runs in O(nk) time when sorting a k-proximate array without changes.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm to sort k-proximate array in O(n log k) time
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm that sorts a k-proximate array in O(n log k) time, more efficient than general sorting for small k.

concepts.canonical_name: Leaf Nodes in a Binary Heap
concepts.short_definition: The nodes in the bottom level of a binary heap that have no children, typically about n/2 for a heap of n elements.

concepts.canonical_name: Search Time Complexity in a Max Heap for Minimum Element
concepts.short_definition: The time complexity required to find the minimum element in a max heap is Omega(n), since all leaf nodes must be examined.
Returning the highest-scoring set of k players in O(1) time by returning a pointer to an existing array rather than constructing the array anew.
Constructing a min-heap of size k from the first k players in O(k) time.
Constructing a max-heap of size n-k from the array of players with scores lower than the top k.
Maintaining pointers between elements in three heaps, to reflect movements and enable efficient updates.
Removing the highest-scoring player and their score from the data structure in O(log n) time.
The process of building a heap from n elements can be done in O(n log k) time, which is more efficient than inserting elements one by one.
A min-heap can be compactly maintained as an array which allows access to the highest-ranking elements in O(1) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Insertion into Combined Heaps Hk and Hn-k
concepts.short_definition: Insertion procedure for a new player involves comparing scores with the min-heap root, selectively popping and inserting players between heaps Hk and Hn-k, maintaining heap pointers, all in O(log n) time.
Deletion of a player from Hk involves popping from Hn, deleting from Hk, popping max from Hn-k, and reinserting to maintain size, all achievable in O(log n) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Use of AVL Trees for Top-k Notation
concepts.short_definition: An AVL tree can be used instead of a min-heap to store the top k players if a compact array corresponding to players can be maintained and returned in O(1) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Min-Heap Sorting Algorithm for k-proximate array
concepts.short_definition: A sorting algorithm that uses a min-heap of size k+1 to sort a k-proximate array in O(n log k) time by repeatedly inserting and deleting the minimum.
The operation of removing elements from data structures such as lists or trees, with computational cost analysis.
Analyzing the time complexity and efficiency of Dijkstra's algorithm with respect to graph size and data structures used.
Selected nodes within a graph considered for specific shortest path computations, such as starting nodes for distance calculations.

concepts.canonical_name: Algorithm for Closest Special Node Distance
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm to find the minimum distance from each node in a graph to its closest special node efficiently, in O(|E| + |V| log |V|) time.

concepts.canonical_name: Shortest Path with Constraints on Surveillance Cameras
concepts.short_definition: Finding shortest paths in a graph where the path should not include edges with surveillance cameras more than once.
Finding a path between two points that minimizes the probability of an adverse event, here the probability of destroying the bike along trails with independent destruction probabilities.
The probability p(e) associated with each trail e that the bike will be destroyed if Ash cycles along that trail, assuming independence across trails.
Events whose probabilities multiply because the occurrence of one event does not affect the probability of others.
The assumption that arithmetic operations such as addition, multiplication, and comparison take constant time.
The set of vertices for which the shortest path from the source has been determined and finalized during Dijkstra's algorithm execution.

concepts.canonical_name: Distance Label Updates in Dijkstra's Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The process where the tentative shortest distance d[v] for vertices v is updated one or more times during the algorithm, before finalizing the shortest path.
For each node v in a graph, the shortest distance from the nearest special node among s1, s2, ..., sk.
Adding an extra node s* connected to all special nodes with zero-weight edges to simplify shortest path calculations from any special node.
Starting Dijkstra's algorithm with zero distance estimates for all special nodes and infinity for others to find closest special node distances.
The runtime of the described algorithm combining a supernode and Dijkstra's algorithm, dependent on number of edges and vertices.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Construction for Camera Visibility Constraint
concepts.short_definition: Constructing a layered graph where vertices represent intersections annotated with the number of cameras seen so far, and edges represent possible moves respecting the camera visibility constraint.

concepts.canonical_name: Shortest Path with at most One Camera Constraint
concepts.short_definition: Finding the shortest path from start to target that is observed by at most one surveillance camera road, either none or exactly one.

concepts.canonical_name: Path Reconstruction from Shortest Path Computation
concepts.short_definition: Recovering the sequence of vertices/edges in the shortest path by backtracking from recorded optimal edges during shortest path computations.

concepts.canonical_name: Safest path problem with probabilistic edge failure
concepts.short_definition: Finding a path in a graph that minimizes the probability of an undesired event occurring on any edge along the path, assuming independent edge probabilities.
Transforming edge probabilities p(e) of failure into weights w(e) = 1 - p(e) representing success probabilities to facilitate algorithmic pathfinding.

concepts.canonical_name: Dijkstra's algorithm with custom semiring operations
concepts.short_definition: Applying Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm using a customized algebraic structure with (0,1) as identity elements, max and multiplication operators replacing the usual min and addition to find the path maximizing product of weights.

concepts.canonical_name: Fibonacci Heap optimization for Dijkstra's algorithm
concepts.short_definition: Using Fibonacci Heaps to implement the priority queue in Dijkstra's algorithm to achieve O(m + n log n) time complexity.

concepts.canonical_name: Weighted Edges in Single-Source Shortest Path (SSSP) Problems
concepts.short_definition: The challenge introduced by edges that have weights, including negative weights, in shortest path problems from a single source vertex.
The process of updating the shortest known distance to vertices by checking if a new path improves the previous distance estimate.
A conceptual graph used for analysis with layers corresponding to edges used in the path to enforce the counting of edges in shortest path computations.

concepts.canonical_name: Shortest Path with Maximum Total Fun Optimization
concepts.short_definition: Finding a path or meeting point in a weighted graph where the weights represent fun values (which can be negative), to maximize the sum of fun for all participants traveling along paths.

concepts.canonical_name: Graph Representation of Currency Exchange Arbitrage
concepts.short_definition: Using graph models with weighted edges corresponding to exchange rates to analyze arbitrage opportunities and detect profitable loops.
A situation where a cyclic path in a weighted graph yields a net gain in value, signaling profitable cycles in currency or item exchanges.
A situation where starting with some amount of a commodity, through a sequence of exchanges, one ends up with more of the same commodity than initially started with.
A deal represented as a tuple (A, x, B, y), indicating the exchange of x units of commodity A for y units of commodity B, with x and y positive integers.
An algorithm that, given an array of commodity exchange deals, finds a sequence of trades that results in more of a commodity than the initial amount, or determines that no such opportunity exists.

concepts.canonical_name: Single-Source Shortest Path Problem with Negative Weights
concepts.short_definition: The problem of finding shortest paths from a single source vertex to all other vertices in a graph that may have edges with negative weights.
Weighting edges in the directed graph by the negative of the road's fun level to transform the problem of maximizing fun into a shortest path problem minimizing total edge weights.
Representing commodities as vertices and exchange deals as directed edges with weights modeled from exchange ratios, to analyze trade opportunities.
A method to detect cycles in a graph whose edge weights sum to a negative value, indicating a gain or arbitrage possibility in commodity exchange models.
Transforming multiplicative trade ratios into additive weights via logarithms for use in shortest path algorithms detecting arbitrage.
Introducing an auxiliary vertex connected to all other vertices with zero-weight edges to enable Bellman-Ford to detect negative cycles in disconnected graphs.

concepts.canonical_name: Modified Bellman-Ford for Maximum Product Path
concepts.short_definition: A variation of Bellman-Ford that updates distances multiplicatively to detect cycles with product of edges greater than 1, indicating arbitrage.

concepts.canonical_name: Time Complexity of Bellman-Ford on Commodity Exchange Graph
concepts.short_definition: Analysis showing that the runtime is O(n^2) where n is the number of deals, due to at most O(n) vertices and edges.
A variant of Bellman-Ford that uses edge weights defined as ratios and maximizes the product of weights along paths using a supersource with edges of weight 1 to all vertices.
A method to assign new weights to edges by adding potentials to vertices, to remove negative weights while preserving shortest paths.

concepts.canonical_name: Effect of Uniform Increment on Edge Weights in Shortest Paths
concepts.short_definition: Adding a constant value to all edge weights does not necessarily preserve shortest paths in a weighted graph.
A constraint that the path cannot travel more than m miles between vertices that have Pokémon Centers.

concepts.canonical_name: Useful Nodes in Directed Weighted Graphs
concepts.short_definition: Vertices that lie on at least one minimum-weight path between two distinct vertices s and t in a directed weighted graph with no negative cycles.
An O(|V|^3)-time algorithm to determine which vertices in a directed weighted graph are useful by checking membership in shortest paths between all node pairs.

concepts.canonical_name: Shortest Path Problem with Distance Constraint
concepts.short_definition: Finding a shortest path between two nodes s and t in a weighted undirected graph such that no segment between consecutive Pok�emon Centers exceeds a distance m.

concepts.canonical_name: Construction of Auxiliary Graph for Distance-Constrained Path
concepts.short_definition: A method to form a new graph G' whose vertices are Pok�emon Centers, connecting pairs with edges weighted by shortest paths not exceeding distance m, to enforce the travel distance constraint.

concepts.canonical_name: Reconstruction of Shortest Path from Parent Pointers
concepts.short_definition: Using stored parent pointers from shortest path computations to reconstruct the actual shortest path route between two nodes.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Analysis of Johnson's and Dijkstra's Algorithms
concepts.short_definition: Determining the computational complexity of the overall algorithm, including Johnson's APSP and Dijkstra's SSSP on the auxiliary graph and path reconstruction.

concepts.canonical_name: Limitations of Supernode Approach for Distance-Constrained Paths
concepts.short_definition: The inadequacy of adding a supernode connected to all Pok�emon Centers to solve the distance constraint problem because it ignores individual inter-center distances.
For vertices s, t, and v, the minimum length of a path from s to t that goes through v equals the sum of shortest distances from s to v and from v to t, i.e. δ(s, v) + δ(v, t).

concepts.canonical_name: Interval Covering Problem with Unit Intervals
concepts.short_definition: Given a set of points on the real line, the problem of finding the minimum number of unit-length intervals needed to cover all the points.

concepts.canonical_name: Process Scheduling to Minimize Average Finishing Time
concepts.short_definition: The problem of finding an order of scheduling processes to minimize the average completion time, where each process takes a given amount of time to complete sequentially.
An optimization problem where you can take fractional amounts of items with given weights and values to maximize total value without exceeding a weight limit.
A problem where given an amount V and unlimited coins of given denominations, the goal is to find the minimum number of coins needed to make change for V.
The process of ordering input followed by iterating through to apply the greedy choice in a greedy algorithm.
A closed real interval of the form [a, a+1] covering points on the real line of length exactly one.
An interval of length one on the real line, typically used in problems involving interval coverage and point sets.
The principle that the product of two negative numbers is a positive number.
The process and method to solve the exercise numbered 3.7 in the given course context.

concepts.canonical_name: Proof of Optimality of Greedy Algorithm for Fractional Knapsack
concepts.short_definition: A proof that selecting metals in decreasing order of value/weight ratio and taking as much as possible from each leads to an optimal solution in the fractional knapsack problem.
A method for making change by repeatedly choosing the largest possible coin denomination until the total value is reached.

concepts.canonical_name: Optimal Substructure in Coin Change Problem
concepts.short_definition: A property indicating that an optimal solution to the coin change problem can be constructed from optimal solutions of subproblems.

concepts.canonical_name: Limitations of Greedy Algorithm in Coin Change
concepts.short_definition: Cases where the greedy algorithm does not yield the optimal solution for coin change problems, such as with coin denominations 1, 10, and 25.
The specific set of coin denominations {1, 5, 10, 25} used in the United States, for which the greedy algorithm for making change is optimal.

concepts.canonical_name: Largest Possible Denomination in a Value Set
concepts.short_definition: The concept that the largest denomination coin or bill present in a value set V must satisfy certain inequalities depending on the total value range.
The idea that multiple smaller denomination coins can be replaced by a higher denomination coin if it does not exceed the total value, used to optimize or simplify coin sets.

concepts.canonical_name: Representation of integer values using currency denominations
concepts.short_definition: A method for expressing values as sums of different currency notes, emphasizing substitutions based on largest denominations.

concepts.canonical_name: Substitution of smaller denominations with larger denominations in currency sums
concepts.short_definition: Replacing multiple smaller currency denominations with an equivalent single larger denomination to simplify representation.
A sequence where the differences between successive numbers strictly alternate between positive and negative.
The problem of finding the longest subsequence of a given sequence that forms a wiggle sequence.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy Algorithm for Longest Wiggle Subsequence
concepts.short_definition: A greedy algorithm approach to compute the longest wiggle subsequence by selecting elements that maintain wiggle property in an optimal way.

concepts.canonical_name: Optimal Wiggle Subsequence Includes First Element
concepts.short_definition: In the longest wiggle subsequence problem, there is always an optimal solution that includes the first element A[0].
If a sequence A starts by increasing, every optimal wiggle subsequence that includes A[0] also starts by increasing.

concepts.canonical_name: Guest Invitation Problem with Known Pairs Constraint
concepts.short_definition: Computing the largest set of guests to invite such that each guest knows at least five other guests, given a list of pairs of people who know each other.

concepts.canonical_name: O(n^2)-Time Algorithm for Guest Invitation Problem
concepts.short_definition: An algorithm with O(n^2) time complexity that computes the largest possible number of guests to invite given the friendship pairs and the constraint on knowing at least five other guests.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Analysis of Greedy Algorithm in Guest Invitation Problem
concepts.short_definition: The greedy algorithm runs in O(n^2) time by initializing adjacency lists in O(n^2) and iteratively performing removal and updates in O(n) time for up to n guests.

concepts.canonical_name: Correctness Proof of Greedy Algorithm via Induction
concepts.short_definition: A proof that the greedy algorithm for the guest invitation problem produces an optimal solution by induction on the number of guests.
An element in the sequence which is either a local maximum (greater than neighbors) or local minimum (less than neighbors), including the last element as a local extremum.

concepts.canonical_name: Greedy Choice Property for Wiggle Subsequence
concepts.short_definition: The property that the greedy choice of local extremum leads to an optimal longest wiggle subsequence.

concepts.canonical_name: Runtime Analysis of Greedy Wiggle Subsequence Algorithm
concepts.short_definition: The greedy algorithm runs in linear time by sequentially scanning for local extrema and building the subsequence.
A wiggle subsequence which includes A[0] and starts by moving in the same direction as the first element in the sequence.
A recursive method that explores all possible outcomes without pruning, leading to an exponential time complexity.
Transforming a recursive solution into an iterative one to solve the same problem without recursion.
A problem involving a player and dealer drawing cards from an ordered deck to maximize number of rounds won under certain rules.

concepts.canonical_name: Dynamic Programming Algorithm for Maximum Non-Crossing Matching on a Circular Wafer
concepts.short_definition: An O(n^3)-time dynamic programming algorithm to match computing units to power sources placed evenly along the perimeter of a circular wafer, maximizing the number of powered computing units connected by non-crossing wires, with the constraint that wires may not connect adjacent ports.
A simplified blackjack game where a player and dealer draw cards from a known ordered deck, and the player may draw an additional card to try to beat the dealer's sum without exceeding 21.

concepts.canonical_name: Recursive Dynamic Programming Approach for Simplified Blackjack
concepts.short_definition: An O(n) time algorithm solving the maximal rounds the player can win using recursive decomposition, testing whether the player draws an additional card or not, including memoization to avoid recomputation.

concepts.canonical_name: Recurrence Relation for Simplified Blackjack DP
concepts.short_definition: The recurrence x(i) = max{w(ci + ci+1, ci+2 + ci+3) + x(i+4), w(ci + ci+1, ci+2 + ci+3 + ci+4) + x(i+5)} where w(d,p) = 1 if player wins the round (d < p ≤ 21) else 0, describes player choice to draw an extra card or not and future wins.

concepts.canonical_name: Recursive Solution for Maximum Rounds Won in BlackJack
